abstract: A technique for segmenting sounds using processing based on mam(cid:173) malian early auditory processing is presented. The technique is based on features in sound which neuron spike recording suggests are detected in the cochlear nucleus. The sound signal is band(cid:173) passed and each signal processed to enhance onsets and offsets. The onset and offset signals are compressed, then clustered both in time and across frequency channels using a network of integrate(cid:173) and-fire neurons. Onsets and offsets are signalled by spikes, and the timing of these spikes used to segment the sound.

paragraphs: This paper presents a way to divide sound into segments using the timing of sound beginnings and endings. Its design is inspired by early mammalian auditory processing, particularly features that recordings of neuronal spikes suggest are detected in the cochlear nucleus. The focus is on turning acoustic changes into useful temporal boundaries.

The incoming sound is first separated into frequency bands. Processing within each band emphasizes onsets and offsets, and the resulting signals are compressed. A network of integrate-and-fire neurons then groups these events across time and across frequency channels, bringing together information that was initially represented in separate bands.

Spikes signal the detected onsets and offsets, and their timing determines the sound segmentation. The contribution is a processing chain that links frequency-specific changes to a common representation in event times. Grouping across channels matters because the segmentation decision can draw on related changes throughout the frequency representation, while the spiking network supplies the timing information used to mark boundaries.
summary.tldr: An auditory-inspired spiking network segments sound by grouping onset and offset events across time and frequency.

title: Onset-based Sound Segmentation

abstract: In cellular telephone systems, an important problem is to dynamically allocate the communication resource (channels) so as to maximize service in a stochastic caller environment. This problem is naturally formulated as a dynamic programming problem and we use a reinforcement learning (RL) method to find dynamic channel allocation policies that are better than previous heuristic solutions. The policies obtained perform well for a broad variety of call traffic patterns. We present results on a large cellular system with approximately 4949 states.
originalAbstract: In cellular telephone systems, an important problem is to dynamically allocate the communication resource (channels) so as to maximize service in a stochastic caller environment. This problem is naturally formulated as a dynamic programming problem and we use a reinforcement learning (RL) method to find dynamic channel allocation policies that are better than previous heuristic solutions. The policies obtained perform well for a broad variety of call traffic patterns. We present results on a large cellular system with approximately 4949 states.

paragraphs: Cellular telephone systems must allocate communication channels while call demand changes unpredictably. The paper treats this as a sequential decision problem: channel-allocation choices are made in a stochastic caller environment, with the objective of maximizing service. This framing connects resource allocation to dynamic programming.

The authors use reinforcement learning to find dynamic allocation policies. A policy specifies how the system should assign its communication resources as conditions change. Learning such a policy provides a way to address the dynamic programming problem and derive allocation behavior suited to the evolving traffic environment.

The resulting policies outperform previous heuristic solutions and perform well across a broad variety of call-traffic patterns. The abstract also reports results on a large cellular system. These findings matter in two related ways: learned policies improve the stated service-allocation task, and their usefulness extends across several demand patterns. The contribution demonstrates reinforcement learning as a practical approach to managing shared communication resources under uncertain demand.
summary.tldr: Reinforcement learning produces cellular channel-allocation policies that outperform prior heuristics across varied call-traffic patterns.

title: Reinforcement Learning for Dynamic Channel Allocation in Cellular Telephone Systems

abstract: This paper shows how the prices of option contracts traded in finan(cid:173) cial markets can be tracked sequentially by means of the Extended Kalman Filter algorithm. I consider call and put option pairs with identical strike price and time of maturity as a two output nonlin(cid:173) ear system. The Black-Scholes approach popular in Finance liter(cid:173) ature and the Radial Basis Functions neural network are used in modelling the nonlinear system generating these observations. I show how both these systems may be identified recursively using the EKF algorithm. I present results of simulations on some FTSE 100 Index options data and discuss the implications of viewing the pricing problem in this sequential manner.

The Black-Scholes approach popular in Finance liter(cid:173) ature and the Radial Basis Functions neural network are used in modelling the nonlinear system generating these observations. paragraphs: The paper treats option pricing as a sequential tracking problem. It pairs a call option and a put option with the same strike price and maturity, representing their prices as two outputs of one nonlinear system. This formulation places the related observations within a common model that can be updated as data arrive.

Two alternatives describe the nonlinear system: the Black-Scholes approach and a radial basis function neural network. The author shows how an Extended Kalman Filter can identify either system recursively. The shared estimation procedure allows both a financial model and a neural representation to participate in the same sequential treatment of observed option prices.

The paper presents simulation results using FTSE 100 Index options data and discusses the implications of this perspective. Its contribution is the recursive formulation and its application to both modeling approaches. Viewing prices sequentially makes updating the estimated system part of the pricing task, with the call-put pairing defining the two-output observations that the filter follows over time.
summary.tldr: An Extended Kalman Filter recursively tracks paired call and put prices using either Black-Scholes or a radial basis function network.

title: Sequential Tracking in Pricing Financial Options using Model Based and Neural Network Approaches

abstract: The problem of reinforcement learning in a non-Markov environment is explored using a dynamic Bayesian network, where conditional indepen(cid:173) dence assumptions between random variables are compactly represented by network parameters. The parameters are learned on-line, and approx(cid:173) imations are used to perform inference and to compute the optimal value function. The relative effects of inference and value function approxi(cid:173) mations on the quality of the final policy are investigated, by learning to solve a moderately difficult driving task. The two value function approx(cid:173) imations, linear and quadratic, were found to perform similarly, but the quadratic model was more sensitive to initialization. Both performed be(cid:173) low the level of human performance on the task. The dynamic Bayesian network performed comparably to a model using a localist hidden state representation, while requiring exponentially fewer parameters.

paragraphs: This paper studies reinforcement learning when the current observation does not provide a complete Markov description of the environment. It uses a dynamic Bayesian network to represent conditional independence among variables compactly. The network's parameters are learned online, so the representation is updated as experience arrives.

The method uses approximations both for inference and for computing the optimal value function. These serve different roles: inference concerns the environment's hidden state, while the value function concerns the desirability of future behavior. The authors investigate how approximations in each part affect the final policy using a moderately difficult driving task.

Linear and quadratic value-function approximations perform similarly on that task, although the quadratic version is more sensitive to initialization. Both remain below human performance. The dynamic Bayesian network achieves performance comparable to a model with a localist hidden-state representation while requiring exponentially fewer parameters. The result supports the compactness of the factored representation without claiming that it solves the task at a human level.
summary.tldr: A learned dynamic Bayesian network matches a localist model on a driving task with exponentially fewer parameters, while remaining below human performance.

title: Learning Factored Representations for Partially Observable Markov Decision Processes

abstract: Function approximation is essential to reinforcement learning, but the standard approach of approximating a value function and deter(cid:173) mining a policy from it has so far proven theoretically intractable. In this paper we explore an alternative approach in which the policy is explicitly represented by its own function approximator, indepen(cid:173) dent of the value function, and is updated according to the gradient of expected reward with respect to the policy parameters. Williams's REINFORCE method and actor-critic methods are examples of this approach. Our main new result is to show that the gradient can be written in a form suitable for estimation from experience aided by an approximate action-value or advantage function. Using this result, we prove for the first time that a version of policy iteration with arbitrary differentiable function approximation is convergent to a locally optimal policy. Large applications of reinforcement learning (RL) require the use of generalizing func(cid:173) tion approximators such neural networks, decision-trees, or instance-based methods. The dominant approach for the last decade has been the value-function approach, in which all function approximation effort goes into estimating a value function, with the action-selection policy represented implicitly as the "greedy" policy with respect to the estimated values (e.g., as the policy that selects in each state the action with highest estimated value). The value-function approach has worked well in many appli(cid:173) cations, but has several limitations. First, it is oriented toward finding deterministic policies, whereas the optimal policy is often stochastic, selecting different actions with specific probabilities (e.g., see Singh, Jaakkola, and Jordan, 1994). Second, an arbi(cid:173) trarily small change in the estimated value of an action can cause it to be, or not be, selected. Such discontinuous changes have been identified as a key obstacle to estab(cid:173) lishing convergence assurances for algorithms following the value-function approach (Bertsekas and Tsitsiklis, 1996). For example, Q-Iearning, Sarsa, and dynamic pro(cid:173) gramming methods have all been shown unable to converge to any policy for simple MDPs and simple function approximators (Gordon, 1995, 1996; Baird, 1995; Tsit(cid:173) siklis and van Roy, 1996; Bertsekas and Tsitsiklis, 1996). This can occur even if the best approximation is found at each step before changing the policy, and whether the notion of "best" is in the mean-squared-error sense or the slightly different senses of residual-gradient, temporal-difference, and dynamic-programming methods. In this paper we explore an alternative approach to function approximation in RL.

paragraphs: This paper studies reinforcement learning with a policy represented by its own function approximator, separately from the value function. The policy parameters are updated in the direction that increases expected reward. This provides a direct way to improve action selection while allowing the policy to choose actions probabilistically.

The motivation includes a difficulty with deriving actions greedily from approximate values: a tiny value change can abruptly switch the selected action. Such discontinuities obstruct convergence analysis. The paper's main result expresses the policy gradient in a form that can be estimated from experience with help from an approximate action-value or advantage function.

Using that result, the authors prove convergence to a locally optimal policy for a version of policy iteration with arbitrary differentiable function approximation. The scope matters: the guarantee concerns the analyzed version of the algorithm and local optimality. The contribution gives direct policy optimization a theoretical foundation while retaining a useful role for approximate value estimates in guiding policy updates.
summary.tldr: An experience-estimable policy-gradient formula supports a convergence proof to a locally optimal policy for a version of approximate policy iteration.

title: Policy Gradient Methods for Reinforcement Learning with Function Approximation

abstract: We combine the replica approach from statistical physics with a varia- tional approach to analyze learning curves analytically. We apply the method to Gaussian process regression. As a main result we derive ap- proximative relations between empirical error measures, the generaliza- tion error and the posterior variance.
originalAbstract: We combine the replica approach from statistical physics with a varia- tional approach to analyze learning curves analytically. We apply the method to Gaussian process regression. As a main result we derive ap- proximative relations between empirical error measures, the generaliza- tion error and the posterior variance.

paragraphs: This paper develops an analytical approach to learning curves, which describe how learning performance changes with the amount of training data. The authors combine the replica approach from statistical physics with a variational approach. Their aim is to obtain mathematical relationships that help explain learning behavior.

They apply the combined method to Gaussian process regression. The analysis connects three quantities: error measures calculated from observed data, generalization error on new data, and posterior variance, which describes uncertainty within the fitted probabilistic model. These quantities address related but distinct questions about how well a model fits, predicts, and represents uncertainty.

The main result is a set of approximate relationships among those quantities. This matters because it provides an analytical connection between measurements available from data and properties of predictive performance. The approximation qualification is central: the paper reports approximate relations, not exact identities equating empirical error, generalization error, and posterior variance. Its stated application is Gaussian process regression, where those connections form the substance of the learning-curve analysis.
summary.tldr: A combined replica and variational analysis derives approximate links between empirical error, generalization error, and posterior variance in Gaussian process regression.

title: A Variational Approach to Learning Curves

abstract: The Minimax Probability Machine Classiﬁcation (MPMC) framework [Lanckriet et al., 2002] builds classiﬁers by minimizing the maximum probability of misclassiﬁcation, and gives direct estimates of the proba- bilistic accuracy bound Ω. The only assumptions that MPMC makes is that good estimates of means and covariance matrices of the classes exist. However, as with Support Vector Machines, MPMC is computationally expensive and requires extensive cross validation experiments to choose kernels and kernel parameters that give good performance. In this paper we address the computational cost of MPMC by proposing an algorithm that constructs nonlinear sparse MPMC (SMPMC) models by incremen- tally adding basis functions (i.e. kernels) one at a time – greedily select- ing the next one that maximizes the accuracy bound Ω. SMPMC auto- matically chooses both kernel parameters and feature weights without us- ing computationally expensive cross validation. Therefore the SMPMC algorithm simultaneously addresses the problem of kernel selection and feature selection (i.e. feature weighting), based solely on maximizing the accuracy bound Ω. Experimental results indicate that we can obtain reli- able bounds Ω, as well as test set accuracies that are comparable to state of the art classiﬁcation algorithms.

paragraphs: Minimax Probability Machine Classification builds classifiers by minimizing the worst-case probability of error and supplies a probabilistic accuracy bound. Its stated assumption is that good estimates of class means and covariance matrices are available. The paper addresses the computational expense of this framework, including costly cross-validation for choosing kernels and their parameters.

The proposed sparse method builds a nonlinear model incrementally, adding one kernel basis function at a time. Each step greedily chooses the addition that maximizes the accuracy bound. The same criterion guides kernel parameters and feature weights, bringing kernel selection and feature weighting into the model-building procedure without expensive cross-validation.

Experiments indicate that the method obtains reliable accuracy bounds and test accuracy comparable to state-of-the-art classifiers. The contribution is therefore both computational and organizational: a single bound guides several choices that otherwise require separate searches. The reported empirical comparability concerns the resulting classifiers, while the reliability of the framework remains tied to its assumption about estimating class statistics.
summary.tldr: A greedy sparse minimax classifier selects kernels and feature weights by maximizing an accuracy bound, avoiding expensive cross-validation.

title: Sparse Greedy Minimax Probability Machine Classification

abstract: In this paper, we provide a general theorem that establishes a correspon- dence between surrogate loss functions in classiﬁcation and the family of f-divergences. Moreover, we provide constructive procedures for determining the f-divergence induced by a given surrogate loss, and conversely for ﬁnding all surrogate loss functions that realize a given f-divergence. Next we introduce the notion of universal equivalence among loss functions and corresponding f-divergences, and provide nec- essary and sufﬁcient conditions for universal equivalence to hold. These ideas have applications to classiﬁcation problems that also involve a com- ponent of experiment design; in particular, we leverage our results to prove consistency of a procedure for learning a classiﬁer under decen- tralization requirements.

Moreover, we provide constructive procedures for determining the f-divergence induced by a given surrogate loss, and conversely for ﬁnding all surrogate loss functions that realize a given f-divergence. Next we introduce the notion of universal equivalence among loss functions and corresponding f-divergences, and provide nec- essary and sufﬁcient conditions for universal equivalence to hold. These ideas have applications to classiﬁcation problems that also involve a com- ponent of experiment design; in particular, we leverage our results to prove consistency of a procedure for learning a classiﬁer under decen- tralization requirements.

paragraphs: This paper connects two ways of describing classification problems: surrogate losses, which define penalties used in learning, and f-divergences, which measure differences between probability distributions. A general theorem establishes a correspondence between these objects. The result offers a shared mathematical language for studying choices that otherwise appear to belong to different parts of a learning problem.

The correspondence is constructive. The authors give procedures for finding the divergence associated with a surrogate loss and for finding all surrogate losses that realize a specified divergence. They also define universal equivalence among losses and their corresponding divergences, then establish conditions that are both necessary and sufficient for that equivalence.

These ideas apply when classification also requires decisions about experimental design. The authors use the theory to prove consistency for a classifier-learning procedure subject to decentralization requirements. The contribution therefore extends beyond translating between mathematical objects: the correspondence and equivalence results support a learning guarantee in a setting with constraints on how classification is organized.
summary.tldr: The paper connects surrogate classification losses with f-divergences and uses that theory to prove consistency under decentralization requirements.

title: Divergences, surrogate loss functions and experimental design

abstract: Active learning refers to algorithmic frameworks aimed at selecting training data points in order to reduce the number of required training data points and/or im- prove the generalization performance of a learning method. In this paper, we present an asymptotic analysis of active learning for generalized linear models. Our analysis holds under the common practical situation of model misspeciﬁca- tion, and is based on realistic assumptions regarding the nature of the sampling distributions, which are usually neither independent nor identical. We derive un- biased estimators of generalization performance, as well as estimators of expected reduction in generalization error after adding a new training data point, that allow us to optimize its sampling distribution through a convex optimization problem. Our analysis naturally leads to an algorithm for sequential active learning which is applicable for all tasks supported by generalized linear models (e.g., binary clas- siﬁcation, multi-class classiﬁcation, regression) and can be applied in non-linear settings through the use of Mercer kernels.

paragraphs: Active learning chooses which training examples to acquire, with the aim of using fewer examples or improving generalization. This paper analyzes that choice for generalized linear models when the model is misspecified. Its analysis also accommodates sampling distributions that are generally neither independent nor identical, a relevant feature of sequentially selected training data.

The authors derive unbiased estimators of generalization performance and estimators of the expected error reduction from adding another training point. These quantities connect the choice of new data to its anticipated effect on prediction. They then formulate optimization of the sampling distribution as a convex problem, giving a concrete procedure for directing data acquisition.

The analysis is asymptotic and leads naturally to a sequential active learning algorithm. Its stated scope includes the tasks supported by generalized linear models, such as binary classification, multiclass classification, and regression. Mercer kernels extend its applicability to nonlinear settings. The contribution is thus a principled selection framework that explicitly accounts for model misspecification and the sampling structure created by active learning.
summary.tldr: An asymptotic analysis yields sequential active learning for misspecified generalized linear models by optimizing the expected benefit of new training data.

title: Active learning for misspecified generalized linear models

abstract: Data sets that characterize human activity over time through collections of timestamped events or counts are of increasing interest in application areas as humancomputer interaction, video surveillance, and Web data analysis. We propose a non-parametric Bayesian framework for modeling collections of such data. In particular, we use a Dirichlet process framework for learning a set of intensity functions corresponding to different categories, which form a basis set for representing individual time-periods (e.g., several days) depending on which categories the time-periods are assigned to. This allows the model to learn in a data-driven fashion what "factors" are generating the observations on a particular day, including (for example) weekday versus weekend effects or day-specific effects corresponding to unique (single-day) occurrences of unusual behavior, sharing information where appropriate to obtain improved estimates of the behavior associated with each category. Applications to realworld data sets of count data involving both vehicles and people are used to illustrate the technique.

paragraphs: Timestamped events and counts describe how activity changes over time, but different days can follow different patterns. This paper develops a nonparametric Bayesian framework for learning collections of such patterns. It represents activity through intensity functions that describe how frequently events occur across a time period.

A Dirichlet process framework learns categories and their associated intensity functions. These functions form a basis for representing individual periods according to their category assignments. The model can therefore discover recurring differences, such as weekday versus weekend behavior, as well as unusual effects associated with a single day.

An important part of the formulation is sharing information when periods belong to relevant categories. Shared evidence can improve estimates of category-specific behavior while the representation still accommodates distinctive occurrences. The authors illustrate the technique with real count datasets involving vehicles and people. The contribution is a data-driven way to organize temporal activity into reusable patterns and period-specific effects, rather than requiring those patterns to be fully specified beforehand.
summary.tldr: A Dirichlet process model learns recurring and day-specific activity profiles while sharing information across related time periods.

title: Learning Time-Intensity Profiles of Human Activity using Non-Parametric Bayesian Models

abstract: Efficient coding models predict that the optimal code for natural images is a population of oriented Gabor receptive fields. These results match response properties of neurons in primary visual cortex, but not those in the retina. Does the retina use an optimal code, and if so, what is it optimized for? Previous theories of retinal coding have assumed that the goal is to encode the maximal amount of information about the sensory signal. However, the image sampled by retinal photoreceptors is degraded both by the optics of the eye and by the photoreceptor noise. Therefore, de-blurring and de-noising of the retinal signal should be important aspects of retinal coding. Furthermore, the ideal retinal code should be robust to neural noise and make optimal use of all available neurons. Here we present a theoretical framework to derive codes that simultaneously satisfy all of these desiderata. When optimized for natural images, the model yields filters that show strong similarities to retinal ganglion cell (RGC) receptive fields. Importantly, the characteristics of receptive fields vary with retinal eccentricities where the optical blur and the number of RGCs are significantly different. The proposed model provides a unified account of retinal coding, and more generally, it may be viewed as an extension of the Wiener filter with an arbitrary number of noisy units.

paragraphs: Efficient coding theories can produce receptive fields resembling those in primary visual cortex, yet fail to explain retinal responses. This paper asks whether the retina is optimizing a different combination of objectives. The signal reaching it has already been blurred by the eye's optics and corrupted by photoreceptor noise, so preserving information alone does not capture every relevant demand.

The authors develop a theoretical framework that combines removal of blur and noise with robustness to neural noise and effective use of the available neurons. These requirements concern the population as a whole: the code must distribute useful visual information across a limited collection of noisy units while accounting for degradation at the input.

When optimized for natural images, the model produces filters strongly resembling retinal ganglion cell receptive fields. Their characteristics also vary with retinal eccentricity, where optical blur and ganglion cell numbers differ. The model therefore offers a unified account connecting retinal coding to these conditions. More generally, the authors interpret it as extending Wiener filtering to an arbitrary number of noisy units.
summary.tldr: A theory balancing image restoration, neural noise, and neuron availability produces filters resembling retinal receptive fields.

title: A Theory of Retinal Population Coding

abstract: Hierarchical probabilistic modeling of discrete data has emerged as a powerful tool for text analysis. Posterior inference in such models is intractable, and practitioners rely on approximate posterior inference methods such as variational inference or Gibbs sampling. There has been much research in designing better approximations, but there is yet little theoretical understanding of which of the available techniques are appropriate, and in which data analysis settings. In this paper we provide the beginnings of such understanding. We analyze the improvement that the recently proposed collapsed variational inference (CVB) provides over mean field variational inference (VB) in latent Dirichlet allocation. We prove that the difference in the tightness of the bound on the likelihood of a document decreases as $O(k-1) + \log m /m$, where $k$ is the number of topics in the model and $m$ is the number of words in a document. As a consequence, the advantage of CVB over VB is lost for long documents but increases with the number of topics. We demonstrate empirically that the theory holds, using simulated text data and two text corpora. We provide practical guidelines for choosing an approximation.

We analyze the improvement that the recently proposed collapsed variational inference (CVB) provides over mean field variational inference (VB) in latent Dirichlet allocation. We prove that the difference in the tightness of the bound on the likelihood of a document decreases as $O(k-1) + \log m /m$, where $k$ is the number of topics in the model and $m$ is the number of words in a document. As a consequence, the advantage of CVB over VB is lost for long documents but increases with the number of topics. We demonstrate empirically that the theory holds, using simulated text data and two text corpora. We provide practical guidelines for choosing an approximation.

paragraphs: Latent Dirichlet allocation requires approximate posterior inference because exact inference is intractable. Although many approximation methods exist, the paper addresses the limited theoretical understanding of when one is preferable to another. It focuses on the improvement offered by collapsed variational inference over mean-field variational inference.

The authors analyze how tightly the two methods bound a document’s likelihood. Their comparison depends on the number of topics and the number of words in the document. The stated consequence is that the collapsed method’s advantage disappears for long documents but increases with the number of topics, relating the approximation choice to identifiable properties of the modeling setting.

Experiments with simulated text and two text corpora support the theoretical analysis. The paper uses these findings to provide practical guidance for choosing an approximation. Its significance is a conditional account of relative performance: the comparison is grounded in likelihood-bound tightness and varies with document length and topic count, giving practitioners a more specific basis for selecting an inference method.
summary.tldr: Likelihood-bound analysis shows that collapsed variational inference’s advantage over mean-field inference in LDA diminishes for long documents and grows with topic count.

title: Relative Performance Guarantees for Approximate Inference in Latent Dirichlet Allocation

abstract: Motivated from real world problems, like object categorization, we study a particular mixed-norm regularization for Multiple Kernel Learning (MKL). It is assumed that the given set of kernels are grouped into distinct components where each component is crucial for the learning task at hand. The formulation hence employs $l_\infty$ regularization for promoting combinations at the component level and $l_1$ regularization for promoting sparsity among kernels in each component. While previous attempts have formulated this as a non-convex problem, the formulation given here is an instance of non-smooth convex optimization problem which admits an efficient Mirror-Descent (MD) based procedure. The MD procedure optimizes over product of simplexes, which is not a well-studied case in literature. Results on real-world datasets show that the new MKL formulation is well-suited for object categorization tasks and that the MD based algorithm outperforms state-of-the-art MKL solvers like \texttt{simpleMKL} in terms of computational effort.

The authors encode these preferences through a mixed-norm regularizer motivated by applications such as object categorization.

The formulation uses an infinity-norm regularizer to encourage combinations at the component level and an L1 regularizer to encourage sparsity inside each component. Although previous attempts produced nonconvex problems, this formulation is convex, though nonsmooth. The authors develop an efficient mirror-descent procedure that optimizes over a product of simplexes, matching the grouped structure of the kernel choices.

Experiments on real datasets indicate that the formulation is well suited to object categorization. The mirror-descent algorithm also requires less computational effort than state-of-the-art kernel-learning solvers such as simpleMKL in the reported comparisons. The contribution combines a task-specific structural assumption with a convex formulation and an optimization method designed for its constraints.
summary.tldr: A convex mixed-norm formulation combines essential kernel groups while selecting within groups, with an efficient mirror-descent solver.

title: On the Algorithmics and Applications of a Mixed-norm based Kernel Learning Formulation

abstract: In this paper we propose an approximated learning framework for large scale graphical models and derive message passing algorithms for learning their parameters efficiently. We first relate CRFs and structured SVMs and show that in the CRF's primal a variant of the log-partition function, known as soft-max, smoothly approximates the hinge loss function of structured SVMs. We then propose an intuitive approximation for structured prediction problems using Fenchel duality based on a local entropy approximation that computes the exact gradients of the approximated problem and is guaranteed to converge. Unlike existing approaches, this allow us to learn graphical models with cycles and very large number of parameters efficiently. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in an image denoising task. This task was previously solved by sharing parameters across cliques. In contrast, our algorithm is able to efficiently learn large number of parameters resulting in orders of magnitude better prediction.

paragraphs: Structured prediction models represent relationships among several output variables, making parameter learning demanding when graphical models contain cycles and many parameters. This paper develops an approximate learning framework and message-passing algorithms intended to make such large models practical. Its starting point connects conditional random fields with structured support vector machines.

The authors show that a soft-max form associated with the conditional random field objective smoothly approximates the structured SVM hinge loss. They then use Fenchel duality and a local entropy approximation to construct their learning procedure. The algorithm computes exact gradients for the approximate objective and has a convergence guarantee; those properties concern the approximated problem.

An image-denoising experiment demonstrates the approach. Earlier treatment of this task shared parameters across groups of interacting variables, whereas the proposed algorithm efficiently learns many parameters. The authors report prediction improvements of orders of magnitude in that experiment. The result illustrates the practical value of a tractable approximation that supports a much more extensively parameterized graphical model.
summary.tldr: A convergent message-passing framework learns large graphical models by optimizing a structured-prediction approximation with exact gradients.

title: A Primal-Dual Message-Passing Algorithm for Approximated Large Scale Structured Prediction

abstract: Domain adaptation algorithms seek to generalize a model trained in a source domain to a new target domain. In many practical cases, the source and target distributions can differ substantially, and in some cases crucial target features may not have support in the source domain. In this paper we introduce an algorithm that bridges the gap between source and target domains by slowly adding both the target features and instances in which the current algorithm is the most confident. Our algorithm is a variant of co-training, and we name it CODA (Co-training for domain adaptation). Unlike the original co-training work, we do not assume a particular feature split. Instead, for each iteration of co-training, we add target features and formulate a single optimization problem which simultaneously learns a target predictor, a split of the feature space into views, and a shared subset of source and target features to include in the predictor. CODA significantly out-performs the state-of-the-art on the 12-domain benchmark data set of Blitzer et al.. Indeed, over a wide range (65 of 84 comparisons) of target supervision, ranging from no labeled target data to a relatively large number of target labels, CODA achieves the best performance.

paragraphs: A model trained in one domain may struggle in another because the data distributions differ. Some features that matter in the target domain may even be absent from the source domain. This paper introduces CODA, a co-training approach that gradually incorporates target information to bridge that gap.

CODA progressively adds target features and target instances about which the current algorithm is most confident. It does not require a predetermined division of features into separate views. Instead, each iteration solves one optimization problem that jointly learns the target predictor, the division into views, and a shared subset of source and target features for the predictor.

On a benchmark containing twelve domains, CODA significantly outperforms the state of the art reported in the abstract. It achieves the best performance in 65 of 84 comparisons spanning no labeled target examples through relatively substantial target supervision. The findings support learning the feature views and the predictor together while gradually expanding the target information used. The results cover varied supervision levels without claiming that CODA wins every comparison.
summary.tldr: CODA gradually incorporates confident target information while jointly learning feature views and a predictor, improving domain adaptation across varied supervision levels.

title: Co-Training for Domain Adaptation

abstract: We describe a simple algorithm that runs in time poly(n,1/gamma,1/eps) and learns an unknown n-dimensional gamma-margin halfspace to accuracy 1-eps in the presence of malicious noise, when the noise rate is allowed to be as high as Theta(eps gamma sqrt(log(1/gamma))). Previous efficient algorithms could only learn to accuracy eps in the presence of malicious noise of rate at most Theta(eps gamma). Our algorithm does not work by optimizing a convex loss function. We show that no algorithm for learning gamma-margin halfspaces that minimizes a convex proxy for misclassification error can tolerate malicious noise at a rate greater than Theta(eps gamma); this may partially explain why previous algorithms could not achieve the higher noise tolerance of our new algorithm.

Previous efficient algorithms could only learn to accuracy eps in the presence of malicious noise of rate at most Theta(eps gamma). Our algorithm does not work by optimizing a convex loss function. We show that no algorithm for learning gamma-margin halfspaces that minimizes a convex proxy for misclassification error can tolerate malicious noise at a rate greater than Theta(eps gamma); this may partially explain why previous algorithms could not achieve the higher noise tolerance of our new algorithm.

paragraphs: The paper studies learning a linear decision boundary with margin gamma when some training data are maliciously corrupted. It presents an algorithm that achieves accuracy 1 minus epsilon in time polynomial in the dimension, inverse margin, and inverse target error. The central improvement is how much malicious noise the algorithm can tolerate.

The tolerated noise rate scales as epsilon times gamma times sqrt(log(1/gamma)). Earlier efficient algorithms reached a rate scaling as epsilon times gamma. The new result therefore adds a square-root logarithmic factor to the tolerated corruption level while retaining polynomial running time. The guarantee concerns the margin-based learning setting described in the paper.

The algorithm achieves this without minimizing a convex loss function. The authors also prove that methods minimizing a convex proxy for misclassification error cannot tolerate malicious noise beyond the order of epsilon times gamma in this setting. This links the improved guarantee to a change in learning strategy and offers a partial explanation for the lower noise tolerance of earlier methods.
summary.tldr: A polynomial-time halfspace learner tolerates more malicious noise than convex-proxy minimization can handle in the stated margin setting.

title: Learning large-margin halfspaces with more malicious noise

abstract: We consider the problem of identifying patterns in a data set that exhibit anomalous behavior, often referred to as anomaly detection. In most anomaly detection algorithms, the dissimilarity between data samples is calculated by a single criterion, such as Euclidean distance. However, in many cases there may not exist a single dissimilarity measure that captures all possible anomalous patterns. In such a case, multiple criteria can be defined, and one can test for anomalies by scalarizing the multiple criteria by taking some linear combination of them. If the importance of the different criteria are not known in advance, the algorithm may need to be executed multiple times with different choices of weights in the linear combination. In this paper, we introduce a novel non-parametric multi-criteria anomaly detection method using Pareto depth analysis (PDA). PDA uses the concept of Pareto optimality to detect anomalies under multiple criteria without having to run an algorithm multiple times with different choices of weights. The proposed PDA approach scales linearly in the number of criteria and is provably better than linear combinations of the criteria.

paragraphs: Anomaly detection often measures how unusual a sample is using one notion of dissimilarity, such as Euclidean distance. Some datasets contain unusual patterns that no single measure captures adequately. Combining several criteria with a weighted sum offers one approach, but unknown criterion importance can force repeated runs with different weight choices.

The paper introduces Pareto depth analysis, a nonparametric method for detecting anomalies across multiple criteria. It uses Pareto optimality to retain the comparison across criteria without repeatedly choosing weighted combinations. This changes how conflicting dissimilarity signals are handled: the method works with their joint ordering instead of requiring one fixed scalar summary.

The authors report that the approach scales linearly with the number of criteria and establish a provable advantage over linear combinations of those criteria. These contributions address both the cost of adding criteria and the drawbacks of exploring weight settings. The method is especially motivated by settings where several dissimilarity measures are meaningful but their relative importance is not known beforehand.
summary.tldr: Pareto depth analysis detects anomalies using multiple criteria without repeated weight selection and has a proved advantage over linear combinations.

title: Multi-criteria Anomaly Detection using Pareto Depth Analysis

abstract: A model connecting visual tracking and saliency has recently been proposed. This model is based on the saliency hypothesis for tracking which postulates that tracking is achieved by the top-down tuning, based on target features, of discriminant center-surround saliency mechanisms over time. In this work, we identify three main predictions that must hold if the hypothesis were true: 1) tracking reliability should be larger for salient than for non-salient targets, 2) tracking reliability should have a dependence on the defining variables of saliency, namely feature contrast and distractor heterogeneity, and must replicate the dependence of saliency on these variables, and 3) saliency and tracking can be implemented with common low level neural mechanisms. We confirm that the first two predictions hold by reporting results from a set of human behavior studies on the connection between saliency and tracking. We also show that the third prediction holds by constructing a common neurophysiologically plausible architecture that can computationally solve both saliency and tracking. This architecture is fully compliant with the standard physiological models of V1 and MT, and with what is known about attentional control in area LIP, while explaining the results of the human behavior experiments.

paragraphs: The paper tests a proposed connection between visual saliency and tracking. The hypothesis is that tracking works by tuning center-surround saliency mechanisms over time according to the target's features. Under this account, mechanisms that distinguish a visually prominent item from its surroundings also contribute to following that item.

The authors identify three predictions. Salient targets should be tracked more reliably; tracking should respond to feature contrast and distractor heterogeneity in the same way as saliency; and both tasks should be implementable using shared low-level neural mechanisms. Human behavioral studies confirm the first two predictions, connecting tracking performance to the variables that define saliency.

For the third prediction, the authors construct a shared, neurophysiologically plausible computational architecture that solves both tasks and explains the behavioral results. It is consistent with standard models of V1 and MT and known attentional control in LIP. The combined evidence supports the saliency hypothesis through behavioral correspondences and a plausible common implementation, without making that architecture a direct identification of the brain's actual circuitry.
summary.tldr: Behavioral studies and a shared neural architecture support the hypothesis that target-tuned saliency mechanisms contribute to visual tracking.

title: On the connections between saliency and tracking

abstract: In this paper, we take a statistical decision-theoretic viewpoint on social choice, putting a focus on the decision to be made on behalf of a system of agents. In our framework, we are given a statistical ranking model, a decision space, and a loss function defined on (parameter, decision) pairs, and formulate social choice mechanisms as decision rules that minimize expected loss. This suggests a general framework for the design and analysis of new social choice mechanisms. We compare Bayesian estimators, which minimize Bayesian expected loss, for the Mallows model and the Condorcet model respectively, and the Kemeny rule. We consider various normative properties, in addition to computational complexity and asymptotic behavior. In particular, we show that the Bayesian estimator for the Condorcet model satisfies some desired properties such as anonymity, neutrality, and monotonicity, can be computed in polynomial time, and is asymptotically different from the other two rules when the data are generated from the Condorcet model for some ground truth parameter.

paragraphs: Social choice concerns decisions made on behalf of multiple agents. This paper frames that task as statistical decision-making: specify a model of rankings, a set of possible decisions, and a loss describing how costly each decision would be for a given underlying parameter. A social choice mechanism then becomes a rule for minimizing expected loss.

This perspective makes the intended decision and its consequences explicit in the design of a voting or ranking rule. The authors compare Bayesian estimators for the Mallows and Condorcet ranking models with the Kemeny rule. They examine normative properties alongside computational complexity and behavior as the amount of data grows.

The Bayesian estimator for the Condorcet model satisfies anonymity, neutrality, and monotonicity, and can be computed in polynomial time. For some ground-truth parameters, when observations come from the Condorcet model, its asymptotic behavior differs from both alternatives. Thus, even with abundant data, the choice of statistical decision rule can matter. The framework provides a way to analyze that choice through explicit modeling assumptions and losses.
summary.tldr: The paper designs and compares social choice rules as statistical decisions that minimize expected loss.

title: A Statistical Decision-Theoretic Framework for Social Choice

abstract: This paper investigates stochastic and adversarial combinatorial multi-armed bandit problems. In the stochastic setting under semi-bandit feedback, we derive a problem-specific regret lower bound, and discuss its scaling with the dimension of the decision space. We propose ESCB, an algorithm that efficiently exploits the structure of the problem and provide a finite-time analysis of its regret. ESCB has better performance guarantees than existing algorithms, and significantly outperforms these algorithms in practice. In the adversarial setting under bandit feedback, we propose CombEXP, an algorithm with the same regret scaling as state-of-the-art algorithms, but with lower computational complexity for some combinatorial problems.

In the stochastic setting under semi-bandit feedback, we derive a problem-specific regret lower bound, and discuss its scaling with the dimension of the decision space. We propose ESCB, an algorithm that efficiently exploits the structure of the problem and provide a finite-time analysis of its regret. ESCB has better performance guarantees than existing algorithms, and significantly outperforms these algorithms in practice. paragraphs: Combinatorial bandit problems involve repeatedly choosing structured actions while learning from limited feedback. This paper studies two versions with different assumptions about rewards and observations. In the stochastic version, semi-bandit feedback reveals information about the selected components. In the adversarial version, bandit feedback supplies information about the chosen action as a whole.

For the stochastic setting, the authors derive a problem-specific lower bound on regret, the performance lost while learning. They examine how this unavoidable cost scales with the dimension of the decision space. They also introduce ESCB, which exploits the problem's structure, and analyze its regret over a finite time horizon. Its guarantees improve on existing algorithms, and the reported practical results show substantial improvements.

For the adversarial setting, the paper introduces CombEXP. Its regret scales like that of leading existing methods, while its computational complexity is lower for some combinatorial problems. These are distinct contributions: ESCB improves performance guarantees in the stochastic setting, whereas CombEXP offers a qualified computational improvement while preserving the established regret scaling.
summary.tldr: ESCB improves stochastic combinatorial bandit guarantees, while CombEXP preserves adversarial regret scaling with lower computational cost for some problems.

title: Combinatorial Bandits Revisited

abstract: Humans demonstrate remarkable abilities to predict physical events in dynamic scenes, and to infer the physical properties of objects from static images. We propose a generative model for solving these problems of physical scene understanding from real-world videos and images. At the core of our generative model is a 3D physics engine, operating on an object-based representation of physical properties, including mass, position, 3D shape, and friction. We can infer these latent properties using relatively brief runs of MCMC, which drive simulations in the physics engine to fit key features of visual observations. We further explore directly mapping visual inputs to physical properties, inverting a part of the generative process using deep learning. We name our model Galileo, and evaluate it on a video dataset with simple yet physically rich scenarios. Results show that Galileo is able to infer the physical properties of objects and predict the outcome of a variety of physical events, with an accuracy comparable to human subjects. Our study points towards an account of human vision with generative physical knowledge at its core, and various recognition models as helpers leading to efficient inference.

paragraphs: Galileo studies how visual observations can reveal physical properties and support predictions about future events. Its generative model places a three-dimensional physics engine at the center of scene understanding. Objects are represented through properties including mass, position, shape, and friction, which determine the simulations the engine produces.

The model infers hidden properties through relatively brief MCMC runs that drive simulations to fit important features of observed images and videos. The authors also explore a deep-learning route that maps visual inputs directly to physical properties. This reverses part of the generative process and provides another mechanism for inference.

Evaluation uses videos of simple scenes with rich physical behavior. Galileo infers object properties and predicts several kinds of physical events with accuracy comparable to human participants in those evaluations. The study supports a proposed account of vision in which generative physical knowledge plays a central role, with recognition models helping make inference efficient; it does not establish that account as a complete explanation of human vision.
summary.tldr: Galileo combines physical simulation and visual learning to infer object properties and predict events with human-comparable accuracy in its evaluated scenarios.

title: Galileo: Perceiving Physical Object Properties by Integrating a Physics Engine with Deep Learning

abstract: Nonconvex and nonsmooth problems have recently received considerable attention in signal/image processing, statistics and machine learning. However, solving the nonconvex and nonsmooth optimization problems remains a big challenge. Accelerated proximal gradient (APG) is an excellent method for convex programming. However, it is still unknown whether the usual APG can ensure the convergence to a critical point in nonconvex programming. To address this issue, we introduce a monitor-corrector step and extend APG for general nonconvex and nonsmooth programs. Accordingly, we propose a monotone APG and a non-monotone APG. The latter waives the requirement on monotonic reduction of the objective function and needs less computation in each iteration. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to provide APG-type algorithms for general nonconvex and nonsmooth problems ensuring that every accumulation point is a critical point, and the convergence rates remain $O(1/k^2)$ when the problems are convex, in which k is the number of iterations. Numerical results testify to the advantage of our algorithms in speed.

To address this issue, we introduce a monitor-corrector step and extend APG for general nonconvex and nonsmooth programs. Accordingly, we propose a monotone APG and a non-monotone APG. The latter waives the requirement on monotonic reduction of the objective function and needs less computation in each iteration. Numerical results testify to the advantage of our algorithms in speed.

paragraphs: Accelerated proximal gradient methods are effective for convex optimization, but their usual form does not provide an established critical-point convergence guarantee for general nonconvex problems. This paper addresses objectives that can also be nonsmooth, a combination that arises in signal processing, statistics, and machine learning.

The authors introduce a monitor-corrector step and develop two versions of accelerated proximal gradient. One requires the objective to decrease monotonically. The other relaxes that requirement and uses less computation per iteration. This creates two ways to incorporate acceleration while controlling its behavior in the more general optimization setting.

The guarantee is that every accumulation point is a critical point; it does not establish that nonconvex problems reach a global optimum. When the problem is convex, the algorithms retain an O(1/k²) convergence rate. Numerical results also support a speed advantage. Together, these findings extend the reach of accelerated proximal methods while preserving a distinction between the guarantees available for convex and nonconvex objectives.
summary.tldr: A monitor-corrector step extends accelerated proximal gradient methods to nonconvex, nonsmooth problems with critical-point guarantees and retained convex acceleration.

title: Accelerated Proximal Gradient Methods for Nonconvex Programming

abstract: We propose a new approach to designing visual markers (analogous to QR-codes, markers for augmented reality, and robotic fiducial tags) based on the advances in deep generative networks. In our approach, the markers are obtained as color images synthesized by a deep network from input bit strings, whereas another deep network is trained to recover the bit strings back from the photos of these markers. The two networks are trained simultaneously in a joint backpropagation process that takes characteristic photometric and geometric distortions associated with marker fabrication and capture into account. Additionally, a stylization loss based on statistics of activations in a pretrained classification network can be inserted into the learning in order to shift the marker appearance towards some texture prototype. In the experiments, we demonstrate that the markers obtained using our approach are capable of retaining bit strings that are long enough to be practical. The ability to automatically adapt markers according to the usage scenario and the desired capacity as well as the ability to combine information encoding with artistic stylization are the unique properties of our approach. As a byproduct, our approach provides an insight on the structure of patterns that are most suitable for recognition by ConvNets and on their ability to distinguish composite patterns.

paragraphs: Visual markers encode information that must survive being fabricated and photographed. This paper learns both sides of that process: one deep network converts bit strings into color images, and another recovers the bits from photographs of those images. Marker design becomes a joint learning problem between an encoder and a reader.

The networks are trained together using backpropagation while accounting for photometric and geometric distortions associated with production and capture. An optional stylization loss uses activation statistics from a pretrained classification network to move the marker's appearance toward a chosen texture. Information encoding and visual appearance can therefore be shaped within the same training process.

Experiments show that the learned markers retain bit strings long enough to be practically useful. The approach can adapt to a usage scenario and desired capacity while also incorporating artistic stylization. The authors additionally use it to investigate patterns that convolutional networks recognize effectively and their ability to distinguish composite patterns, connecting marker generation with questions about learned visual recognition.
summary.tldr: Jointly trained networks create and read visual markers that can adapt to capture conditions, information capacity, and artistic style.

title: Learnable Visual Markers

abstract: We develop an approach to risk minimization and stochastic optimization that provides a convex surrogate for variance, allowing near-optimal and computationally efficient trading between approximation and estimation error. Our approach builds off of techniques for distributionally robust optimization and Owen's empirical likelihood, and we provide a number of finite-sample and asymptotic results characterizing the theoretical performance of the estimator. In particular, we show that our procedure comes with certificates of optimality, achieving (in some scenarios) faster rates of convergence than empirical risk minimization by virtue of automatically balancing bias and variance. We give corroborating empirical evidence showing that in practice, the estimator indeed trades between variance and absolute performance on a training sample, improving out-of-sample (test) performance over standard empirical risk minimization for a number of classification problems.

paragraphs: Minimizing training error requires balancing how well a model fits observed data against how reliably that fit carries over to new data. This paper develops a convex surrogate for variance that makes this tradeoff computationally efficient. The approach targets risk minimization and stochastic optimization, balancing approximation and estimation error.

The construction draws on distributionally robust optimization and empirical likelihood. The authors establish finite-sample and asymptotic results describing the resulting estimator, including certificates of optimality. In some scenarios, the method converges faster than empirical risk minimization because it automatically balances bias and variance. The faster-rate claim is therefore tied to particular scenarios.

Experiments on several classification problems support the theoretical motivation. The estimator trades some absolute performance on the training sample against variance and achieves better test performance than standard empirical risk minimization. These findings show how incorporating variability into a convex objective can improve generalization in the evaluated problems while retaining an efficiently optimizable formulation.
summary.tldr: A convex variance surrogate efficiently balances fit and variability, with conditional faster-rate guarantees and improved test performance on classification problems.

title: Variance-based Regularization with Convex Objectives

abstract: We study connections between Dykstra's algorithm for projecting onto an intersection of convex sets, the augmented Lagrangian method of multipliers or ADMM, and block coordinate descent. We prove that coordinate descent for a regularized regression problem, in which the penalty is a separable sum of support functions, is exactly equivalent to Dykstra's algorithm applied to the dual problem. ADMM on the dual problem is also seen to be equivalent, in the special case of two sets, with one being a linear subspace. These connections, aside from being interesting in their own right, suggest new ways of analyzing and extending coordinate descent. For example, from existing convergence theory on Dykstra's algorithm over polyhedra, we discern that coordinate descent for the lasso problem converges at an (asymptotically) linear rate. We also develop two parallel versions of coordinate descent, based on the Dykstra and ADMM connections.

The authors show that specific instances of these procedures are exactly equivalent, making their existing analyses useful across formulations.

Coordinate descent for that problem matches Dykstra's algorithm on the corresponding dual problem. This characterizes its eventual convergence behavior. They also develop two parallel coordinate-descent methods from the Dykstra and ADMM connections. The work therefore supplies both a route for transferring theoretical results and a basis for constructing algorithmic extensions.
summary.tldr: Exact connections between coordinate descent, Dykstra's algorithm, and special cases of ADMM yield convergence insights and parallel algorithms.

title: Dykstra's Algorithm, ADMM, and Coordinate Descent: Connections, Insights, and Extensions

abstract: Compression and computational efficiency in deep learning have become a problem of great significance. In this work, we argue that the most principled and effective way to attack this problem is by adopting a Bayesian point of view, where through sparsity inducing priors we prune large parts of the network. We introduce two novelties in this paper: 1) we use hierarchical priors to prune nodes instead of individual weights, and 2) we use the posterior uncertainties to determine the optimal fixed point precision to encode the weights. Both factors significantly contribute to achieving the state of the art in terms of compression rates, while still staying competitive with methods designed to optimize for speed or energy efficiency.

paragraphs: This paper approaches neural network compression through Bayesian modeling. It uses priors that encourage sparsity, allowing large portions of a network to be pruned. The objective is to reduce the resources needed to store and compute with deep networks through a probabilistic account of their parameters.

The first contribution is to organize these priors hierarchically so that pruning acts on entire nodes rather than individual weights. This changes the unit of compression: the method can remove a node together with its associated parameters. The second contribution uses uncertainty in the learned posterior to select the fixed-point precision used to encode weights.

These two choices address different sources of storage cost: how much of the network remains and how precisely its retained weights are represented. The authors report that both contribute substantially to state-of-the-art compression rates. They also report competitiveness with approaches designed around speed or energy efficiency, supporting Bayesian modeling as a way to connect network pruning with numerical representation.
summary.tldr: Bayesian compression combines node-level pruning with uncertainty-guided weight precision to achieve strong compression rates.

title: Bayesian Compression for Deep Learning

abstract: One major obstacle towards AI is the poor ability of models to solve new problems quicker, and without forgetting previously acquired knowledge. To better understand this issue, we study the problem of continual learning, where the model observes, once and one by one, examples concerning a sequence of tasks. First, we propose a set of metrics to evaluate models learning over a continuum of data. These metrics characterize models not only by their test accuracy, but also in terms of their ability to transfer knowledge across tasks. Second, we propose a model for continual learning, called Gradient Episodic Memory (GEM) that alleviates forgetting, while allowing beneficial transfer of knowledge to previous tasks. Our experiments on variants of the MNIST and CIFAR-100 datasets demonstrate the strong performance of GEM when compared to the state-of-the-art.

paragraphs: Continual learning asks a model to acquire new abilities while retaining knowledge from earlier tasks. The paper studies a setting where examples arrive once, one at a time, across a sequence of tasks. This makes the learning process itself central: success depends on what survives and transfers as experience accumulates.

The authors first propose evaluation metrics that go beyond test accuracy. These also characterize knowledge transfer between tasks, allowing evaluation to distinguish successful learning from harmful forgetting and beneficial reuse. That broader perspective matters because two models with similar accuracy can differ in how their experiences affect performance across the task sequence.

The proposed model, Gradient Episodic Memory, alleviates forgetting while permitting beneficial transfer to previous tasks. Later learning can therefore help earlier tasks as well as threaten their retained knowledge. Experiments on variants of MNIST and CIFAR-100 report strong performance relative to the state of the art. The contribution combines a continual-learning method with an evaluation framework that makes cross-task effects explicit.
summary.tldr: Gradient Episodic Memory reduces forgetting while allowing later learning to benefit earlier tasks, alongside metrics for evaluating cross-task transfer.

title: Gradient Episodic Memory for Continual Learning

abstract: As datasets grow richer, an important challenge is to leverage the full features in the data to maximize the number of useful discoveries while controlling for false positives. We address this problem in the context of multiple hypotheses testing, where for each hypothesis, we observe a p-value along with a set of features specific to that hypothesis. For example, in genetic association studies, each hypothesis tests the correlation between a variant and the trait. We have a rich set of features for each variant (e.g. its location, conservation, epigenetics etc.) which could inform how likely the variant is to have a true association. However popular testing approaches, such as Benjamini-Hochberg's procedure (BH) and independent hypothesis weighting (IHW), either ignore these features or assume that the features are categorical. We propose a new algorithm, NeuralFDR, which automatically learns a discovery threshold as a function of all the hypothesis features. We parametrize the discovery threshold as a neural network, which enables flexible handling of multi-dimensional discrete and continuous features as well as efficient end-to-end optimization. We prove that NeuralFDR has strong false discovery rate (FDR) guarantees, and show that it makes substantially more discoveries in synthetic and real datasets. Moreover, we demonstrate that the learned discovery threshold is directly interpretable.

paragraphs: When testing many hypotheses, researchers want to identify useful findings while controlling false discoveries. Each hypothesis may come with more than a p-value: it can also have features that help indicate whether a real association is plausible. In genetic studies, for example, a variant's location and biological characteristics may provide relevant information.

NeuralFDR learns how the discovery threshold should depend on these features. A neural network represents the threshold function, allowing it to use multiple discrete and continuous inputs together. summary.tldr: NeuralFDR learns feature-dependent discovery thresholds with false discovery rate guarantees and reports more discoveries on synthetic and real data.

title: NeuralFDR: Learning Discovery Thresholds from Hypothesis Features

abstract: Abstract The dominant object detection approaches treat the recognition of each region separately and overlook crucial semantic correlations between objects in one scene. This paradigm leads to substantial performance drop when facing heavy long-tail problems, where very few samples are available for rare classes and plenty of confusing categories exists. We exploit diverse human commonsense knowledge for reasoning over large-scale object categories and reaching semantic coherency within one image. Particularly, we present Hybrid Knowledge Routed Modules (HKRM) that incorporates the reasoning routed by two kinds of knowledge forms: an explicit knowledge module for structured constraints that are summarized with linguistic knowledge (e.g. shared attributes, relationships) about concepts; and an implicit knowledge module that depicts some implicit constraints (e.g. common spatial layouts). By functioning over a region-to-region graph, both modules can be individualized and adapted to coordinate with visual patterns in each image, guided by specific knowledge forms. HKRM are light-weight, general-purpose and extensible by easily incorporating multiple knowledge to endow any detection networks the ability of global semantic reasoning. Experiments on large-scale object detection benchmarks show HKRM obtains around 34.5% improvement on VisualGenome (1000 categories) and 30.4% on ADE in terms of mAP.

paragraphs: Recognizing each image region independently can overlook relationships among the objects in a scene. This becomes especially problematic when rare categories have few examples and many categories are easy to confuse. The paper introduces Hybrid Knowledge Routed Modules, or HKRM, to bring semantic relationships into large-scale object detection.

The method uses two forms of knowledge. An explicit module represents structured information expressed through language, such as shared attributes and relationships between concepts. An implicit module captures constraints such as common spatial arrangements. Both operate on a graph connecting image regions, adapting their reasoning to the visual evidence in each image.

Experiments report roughly 34.5% improvement in mAP on VisualGenome with 1,000 categories and 30.4% on ADE. These results support using scene-level semantic reasoning to improve region-level recognition, particularly in the challenging large-category setting that motivates the work.
summary.tldr: HKRM combines explicit semantic knowledge and implicit scene constraints to improve large-scale object detection.

title: Hybrid Knowledge Routed Modules for Large-scale Object Detection

abstract: As an indispensable component, Batch Normalization (BN) has successfully improved the training of deep neural networks (DNNs) with mini-batches, by normalizing the distribution of the internal representation for each hidden layer. However, the effectiveness of BN would diminish with the scenario of micro-batch (e.g. less than 4 samples in a mini-batch), since the estimated statistics in a mini-batch are not reliable with insufficient samples. This limits BN's room in training larger models on segmentation, detection, and video-related problems, which require small batches constrained by memory consumption. In this paper, we present a novel normalization method, called Kalman Normalization (KN), for improving and accelerating the training of DNNs, particularly under the context of micro-batches. Specifically, unlike the existing solutions treating each hidden layer as an isolated system, KN treats all the layers in a network as a whole system, and estimates the statistics of a certain layer by considering the distributions of all its preceding layers, mimicking the merits of Kalman Filtering. On ResNet50 trained in ImageNet, KN has 3.4% lower error than its BN counterpart when using a batch size of 4; Even when using typical batch sizes, KN still maintains an advantage over BN while other BN variants suffer a performance degradation. Moreover, KN can be naturally generalized to many existing normalization variants to obtain gains, e.g. equipping Group Normalization with Group Kalman Normalization (GKN). KN can outperform BN and its variants for large scale object detection and segmentation task in COCO 2017.

paragraphs: Batch Normalization relies on statistics estimated from a mini-batch to normalize a network's internal representations. With very small batches, those estimates can become unreliable. This is especially relevant when memory-intensive tasks such as detection, segmentation, or video processing constrain how many examples can be processed together.

Kalman Normalization treats the network's layers as a connected system. When estimating statistics for one layer, it considers the distributions of preceding layers, drawing on the principle of Kalman filtering. This gives normalization access to information across layers instead of estimating each layer's statistics in isolation. The approach can also extend existing normalization variants, including Group Normalization.

For ResNet50 on ImageNet with batch size four, the abstract reports 3.4% lower error than Batch Normalization. It also reports an advantage at typical batch sizes, where other evaluated Batch Normalization variants degraded. Results on COCO 2017 further show that the method can outperform Batch Normalization and its variants in detection and segmentation. These findings support cross-layer estimation as a practical response to unreliable small-batch statistics.
summary.tldr: Kalman Normalization uses information from preceding layers to estimate normalization statistics, improving reported results especially with small batches.

title: Kalman Normalization: Normalizing Internal Representations Across Network Layers

abstract: In this paper, we propose a novel sampling method, the thermostat-assisted continuously-tempered Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, for the purpose of multimodal Bayesian learning. It simulates a noisy dynamical system by incorporating both a continuously-varying tempering variable and the Nos\'e-Hoover thermostats. A significant benefit is that it is not only able to efficiently generate i.i.d. samples when the underlying posterior distributions are multimodal, but also capable of adaptively neutralising the noise arising from the use of mini-batches. While the properties of the approach have been studied using synthetic datasets, our experiments on three real datasets have also shown its performance gains over several strong baselines for Bayesian learning with various types of neural networks plunged in.
