paragraphs: The paper proposes a sampling method for Bayesian learning when the posterior distribution has multiple modes. Such a posterior contains several distinct regions of high probability, making exploration across those regions central to obtaining useful samples. The method also addresses noise introduced when computations use mini-batches of data.

The sampler simulates a noisy dynamical system that combines a continuously varying tempering variable with Nosé-Hoover thermostats. These components serve the combined aims of sampling a multimodal posterior and adapting to mini-batch noise. The authors state that the method can efficiently generate independent, identically distributed samples in the multimodal setting and adaptively neutralize the noise from mini-batching.

Synthetic datasets are used to study the approach's properties. Experiments on three real datasets, involving several types of neural networks, show performance gains over multiple strong Bayesian-learning baselines. The contribution is a sampling design that addresses multimodality and noisy computation together, with the reported experiments supporting its practical effectiveness across the evaluated neural-network settings.
summary.tldr: A continuously tempered Hamiltonian sampler uses thermostats to support multimodal Bayesian sampling while adapting to mini-batch noise.

title: Thermostat-assisted continuously-tempered Hamiltonian Monte Carlo for Bayesian learning

abstract: Learning to make decisions in an uncertain and dynamic environment is a task of fundamental performance in a number of domains. This paper concerns the problem of learning control policies for an unknown linear dynamical system so as to minimize a quadratic cost function. We present a method, based on convex optimization, that accomplishes this task ‘robustly’, i.e., the worst-case cost, accounting for system uncertainty given the observed data, is minimized. The method balances exploitation and exploration, exciting the system in such a way so as to reduce uncertainty in the model parameters to which the worst-case cost is most sensitive. Numerical simulations and application to a hardware-in-the-loop servo-mechanism are used to demonstrate the approach, with appreciable performance and robustness gains over alternative methods observed in both.

paragraphs: This paper studies learning to control an unknown linear dynamical system while minimizing a quadratic cost. The controller must act using an imperfect model, and its actions also determine what it can learn about the system. The challenge is therefore to balance immediate control performance with collecting information that improves future decisions.

The proposed method uses convex optimization to minimize worst-case cost over system uncertainty supported by the observed data. Exploration is directed toward model parameters whose uncertainty most strongly affects that worst-case cost. The controller excites the system in ways intended to reduce those consequential uncertainties, tying information gathering directly to its control objective.

This approach makes robustness and exploration parts of the same decision problem. Learning about a parameter matters according to its effect on uncertain control performance. The authors demonstrate the method in numerical simulations and a hardware-in-the-loop servo-mechanism application. Both evaluations show appreciable performance and robustness gains over alternative methods, providing evidence for this targeted exploration strategy in the studied linear-quadratic settings.
summary.tldr: A convex-optimization controller explores the uncertainties most consequential for worst-case performance in unknown linear systems.

title: Robust exploration in linear quadratic reinforcement learning

abstract: We consider training over-parameterized two-layer neural networks with Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU) using gradient descent (GD) method. Inspired by a recent line of work, we study the evolutions of network prediction errors across GD iterations, which can be neatly described in a matrix form. When the network is sufficiently over-parameterized, these matrices individually approximate {\em an} integral operator which is determined by the feature vector distribution $\rho$ only. Consequently, GD method can be viewed as {\em approximately} applying the powers of this integral operator on the underlying/target function $f^*$ that generates the responses/labels. We show that if $f^*$ admits a low-rank approximation with respect to the eigenspaces of this integral operator, then the empirical risk decreases to this low rank approximation error at a linear rate which is determined by $f^*$ and $\rho$ only, i.e., the rate is independent of the sample size $n$. Furthermore, if $f^*$ has zero low-rank approximation error, then, as long as the width of the neural network is $\Omega(n\log n)$, the empirical risk decreases to $\Theta(1/\sqrt{n})$. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first result showing the sufficiency of nearly-linear network over-parameterization. We provide an application of our general results to the setting where $\rho$ is the uniform distribution on the spheres and $f^*$ is a polynomial. Throughout this paper, we consider the scenario where the input dimension $d$ is fixed.

paragraphs: This paper analyzes gradient descent for overparameterized, two-layer ReLU networks by tracking how prediction errors evolve. With sufficient width, the matrices describing those updates approximate an integral operator determined by the input distribution. Training can therefore be understood as approximately applying repeated powers of that operator to the target function.

The resulting convergence depends on how well the target function can be approximated using a low-rank collection of the operator's eigenspaces. When such an approximation exists, empirical risk decreases linearly toward its approximation error. The rate is determined by the target function and input distribution, rather than by the number of training samples.

When the low-rank approximation error is zero, a width of order n log n suffices for empirical risk to reach order one over the square root of n. The authors present this as a sufficiency result for nearly linear overparameterization. Their analysis fixes the input dimension and includes an application to polynomial targets with inputs distributed uniformly on spheres.
summary.tldr: An operator-based analysis connects training rates to target-function structure and proves nearly linear network width sufficient under the stated approximation conditions.

title: On Learning Over-parameterized Neural Networks: A Functional Approximation Perspective

abstract: We propose and study a general framework for regularized Markov decision processes (MDPs) where the goal is to find an optimal policy that maximizes the expected discounted total reward plus a policy regularization term. The extant entropy-regularized MDPs can be cast into our framework. Moreover, under our framework, many regularization terms can bring multi-modality and sparsity, which are potentially useful in reinforcement learning. In particular, we present sufficient and necessary conditions that induce a sparse optimal policy. We also conduct a full mathematical analysis of the proposed regularized MDPs, including the optimality condition, performance error, and sparseness control. We provide a generic method to devise regularization forms and propose off-policy actor critic algorithms in complex environment settings. We empirically analyze the numerical properties of optimal policies and compare the performance of different sparse regularization forms in discrete and continuous environments.

paragraphs: The paper studies how adding a regularization term to a reinforcement learning objective changes the optimal policy. The objective combines expected discounted reward with a term that shapes the policy’s action choices. Its framework includes existing entropy regularization methods while also accommodating alternatives that can produce multiple preferred actions and sparsity: some actions receive zero probability.

The central mathematical contribution is a characterization of when sparse optimal policies arise, including necessary and sufficient conditions. The authors also analyze optimality conditions, performance error, and how to control sparsity. This makes the choice of regularizer an explicit design decision whose consequences can be studied, rather than simply an extra term added during training.

The paper connects this analysis to algorithms through a general method for constructing regularizers and off-policy actor-critic methods for complex environments. Experiments examine policy properties and compare sparse regularizers in discrete and continuous settings. The stated contribution is a framework for understanding and constructing these policies; the abstract describes sparsity and multiple modes as potentially useful, without claiming that either always improves learning.
summary.tldr: A general framework characterizes how policy regularization can produce and control sparse optimal policies in reinforcement learning.

title: A Regularized Approach to Sparse Optimal Policy in Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Data augmentation is an essential technique for improving generalization ability of deep learning models. Recently, AutoAugment \cite{cubuk2018autoaugment} has been proposed as an algorithm to automatically search for augmentation policies from a dataset and has significantly enhanced performances on many image recognition tasks. However, its search method requires thousands of GPU hours even for a relatively small dataset. In this paper, we propose an algorithm called Fast AutoAugment that finds effective augmentation policies via a more efficient search strategy based on density matching. In comparison to AutoAugment, the proposed algorithm speeds up the search time by orders of magnitude while achieves comparable performances on image recognition tasks with various models and datasets including CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, SVHN, and ImageNet. title: Fast AutoAugment

abstract: Despite the exciting progress in image captioning, generating diverse captions for a given image remains as an open problem. Existing methods typically apply generative models such as Variational Auto-Encoder to diversify the captions, which however neglect two key factors of diverse expression, i.e., the lexical diversity and the syntactic diversity. To model these two inherent diversities in image captioning, we propose a Variational Structured Semantic Inferring model (termed VSSI-cap) executed in a novel structured encoder-inferer-decoder schema. VSSI-cap mainly innovates in a novel structure, i.e., Variational Multi-modal Inferring tree (termed VarMI-tree). In particular, conditioned on the visual-textual features from the encoder, the VarMI-tree models the lexical and syntactic diversities by inferring their latent variables (with variations) in an approximate posterior inference guided by a visual semantic prior. Then, a reconstruction loss and the posterior-prior KL-divergence are jointly estimated to optimize the VSSI-cap model. Finally, diverse captions are generated upon the visual features and the latent variables from this structured encoder-inferer-decoder model. Experiments on the benchmark dataset show that the proposed VSSI-cap achieves significant improvements over the state-of-the-arts.

VSSI-cap explicitly models lexical and syntactic variation so that diversity is represented within the caption-generation process.

This connects learning to reproduce captions with learning a structured distribution of possible expressions. title: Variational Structured Semantic Inference for Diverse Image Captioning

abstract: The ability to inferring latent psychological traits from human behavior is key to developing personalized human-interacting machine learning systems. Approaches to infer such traits range from surveys to manually-constructed experiments and games. However, these traditional games are limited because they are typically designed based on heuristics. In this paper, we formulate the task of designing behavior diagnostic games that elicit distinguishable behavior as a mutual information maximization problem, which can be solved by optimizing a variational lower bound. Our framework is instantiated by using prospect theory to model varying player traits, and Markov Decision Processes to parameterize the games. We validate our approach empirically, showing that our designed games can successfully distinguish among players with different traits, outperforming manually-designed ones by a large margin.

This paper asks whether the game itself can be optimized to make players with different traits behave more distinguishably.

The authors formulate game design as maximizing mutual information between player traits and observed behavior. They optimize a variational lower bound to make that objective tractable. In their implementation, prospect theory models variation in player traits, while Markov Decision Processes provide a way to parameterize the games being designed.

Empirical results show that the resulting games distinguish players with different traits and outperform manually designed games by a large margin. The finding supports optimizing the situations used to collect behavioral evidence, alongside the task of interpreting that evidence. The demonstrated framework is specifically instantiated with prospect-theory player models and Markov Decision Process games, which gives concrete meaning to the otherwise broad objective of making behavior informative about latent traits.
summary.tldr: Optimizing games for mutual information produces behavior that better distinguishes modeled player traits than manually designed games.

title: Game Design for Eliciting Distinguishable Behavior

abstract: Gradient-based algorithms are effective for many machine learning tasks, but despite ample recent effort and some progress, it often remains unclear why they work in practice in optimising high-dimensional non-convex functions and why they find good minima instead of being trapped in spurious ones.Here we present a quantitative theory explaining this behaviour in a spiked matrix-tensor model.Our framework is based on the Kac-Rice analysis of stationary points and a closed-form analysis of gradient-flow originating from statistical physics. We show that there is a well defined region of parameters where the gradient-flow algorithm finds a good global minimum despite the presence of exponentially many spurious local minima. We show that this is achieved by surfing on saddles that have strong negative direction towards the global minima, a phenomenon that is connected to a BBP-type threshold in the Hessian describing the critical points of the landscapes.

paragraphs: Non-convex objectives can contain many poor local minima, yet gradient-based methods often find good solutions. This paper develops a quantitative explanation in a spiked matrix-tensor model. The question is how the dynamics of optimization interact with the landscape, rather than simply how many undesirable stationary points exist.

The framework combines Kac-Rice analysis of stationary points with a closed-form analysis of gradient flow drawn from statistical physics. The authors identify a well-defined parameter region where gradient flow reaches a good global minimum despite exponentially many spurious local minima. This shows that their abundance alone does not determine the outcome of the analyzed optimization process.

The proposed explanation is that gradient flow moves along saddle points with strong negative-curvature directions leading toward global minima. The authors connect this behavior to a BBP-type threshold in the Hessian, which describes local curvature around critical points. The result provides a model-specific mechanism for successful non-convex optimization: the directions encountered by the dynamics can be favorable even when the overall landscape contains many bad minima.
summary.tldr: In a defined spiked matrix-tensor regime, gradient flow follows favorable saddle directions to a global minimum despite exponentially many spurious minima.

title: Who is Afraid of Big Bad Minima? Analysis of gradient-flow in spiked matrix-tensor models

abstract: We consider classic clustering problems in fully dynamic data streams, where data elements can be both inserted and deleted. In this context, several parameters are of importance: (1) the quality of the solution after each insertion or deletion, (2) the time it takes to update the solution, and (3) how different consecutive solutions are. The question of obtaining efficient algorithms in this context for facility location, $k$-median and $k$-means has been raised in a recent paper by Hubert-Chan et al. [WWW'18] and also appears as a natural follow-up on the online model with recourse studied by Lattanzi and Vassilvitskii [ICML'17] (i.e.: in insertion-only streams). In this paper, we focus on general metric spaces and mainly on the facility location problem. We give an arguably simple algorithm that maintains a constant factor approximation, with $O(n\log n)$ update time, and total recourse $O(n)$. This improves over the naive algorithm which consists in recomputing a solution at each time step and that can take up to $O(n^2)$ update time, and $O(n^2)$ total recourse. These bounds are nearly optimal: in general metric space, inserting a point take $O(n)$ times to describe the distances to other points, and we give a simple lower bound of $O(n)$ for the recourse. Moreover, we generalize this result for the $k$-medians and $k$-means problems: our algorithm maintains a constant factor approximation in time $\widetilde{O}(n+k^2)$. We complement our analysis with experiments showing that the cost of the solution maintained by our algorithm at any time $t$ is very close to the cost of a solution obtained by quickly recomputing a solution from scratch at time $t$ while having a much better running time.

title: Fully Dynamic Consistent Facility Location

abstract: Regularization improves generalization of supervised models to out-of-sample data. Prior works have shown that prediction in the causal direction (effect from cause) results in lower testing error than the anti-causal direction. However, existing regularization methods are agnostic of causality. We introduce Causal Structure Learning (CASTLE) regularization and propose to regularize a neural network by jointly learning the causal relationships between variables. CASTLE learns the causal directed acyclical graph (DAG) as an adjacency matrix embedded in the neural network's input layers, thereby facilitating the discovery of optimal predictors. Furthermore, CASTLE efficiently reconstructs only the features in the causal DAG that have a causal neighbor, whereas reconstruction-based regularizers suboptimally reconstruct all input features. We provide a theoretical generalization bound for our approach and conduct experiments on a plethora of synthetic and real publicly available datasets demonstrating that CASTLE consistently leads to better out-of-sample predictions as compared to other popular benchmark regularizers.

paragraphs: Regularization helps a supervised model make predictions on examples beyond its training data. CASTLE introduces causal structure into this process by jointly learning relationships among variables while training a neural network. The motivation is that the direction of a relationship can matter for prediction, whereas conventional regularizers generally do not account for causality.

The method represents a causal directed acyclic graph through an adjacency matrix embedded in the network’s input layers. Learning this structure becomes an auxiliary part of learning the predictor. CASTLE also uses the graph to determine which input features to reconstruct: it reconstructs features with a causal neighbor, rather than requiring reconstruction of every input feature.

This selective reconstruction ties the regularization objective to the relationships discovered among variables. The paper provides a theoretical generalization bound and evaluates the method on synthetic and publicly available real datasets. CASTLE consistently improves out-of-sample prediction relative to the benchmark regularizers in those experiments. The contribution is therefore a concrete way to incorporate causal graph learning into regularization, supported by both analysis and predictive evaluations.
summary.tldr: CASTLE regularizes neural networks through joint causal graph learning and selective feature reconstruction, improving predictions on the evaluated datasets.

title: CASTLE: Regularization via Auxiliary Causal Graph Discovery

abstract: Despite success on a wide range of problems related to vision, generative adversarial networks (GANs) often suffer from inferior performance due to unstable training, especially for text generation. To solve this issue, we propose a new variational GAN training framework which enjoys superior training stability. Our approach is inspired by a connection of GANs and reinforcement learning under a variational perspective. The connection leads to (1) probability ratio clipping that regularizes generator training to prevent excessively large updates, and (2) a sample re-weighting mechanism that improves discriminator training by downplaying bad-quality fake samples. Moreover, our variational GAN framework can provably overcome the training issue in many GANs that an optimal discriminator cannot provide any informative gradient to training generator. By plugging the training approach in diverse state-of-the-art GAN architectures, we obtain significantly improved performance over a range of tasks, including text generation, text style transfer, and image generation.

paragraphs: Generative adversarial networks can perform poorly when training becomes unstable, particularly in text generation. This paper develops a variational training framework motivated by a connection between GANs and reinforcement learning. The connection leads to changes in how both the generator and discriminator are trained.

For the generator, probability-ratio clipping regularizes training to prevent excessively large updates. For the discriminator, sample reweighting reduces the influence of low-quality generated examples. These mechanisms address different parts of the adversarial learning process: the size of generator updates and the contribution of individual fake samples to discriminator training.

The framework also has a theoretical result concerning a known failure mode: in many GANs, an optimal discriminator provides no informative gradient for improving the generator. The authors show that their framework can overcome this issue. When incorporated into several existing GAN architectures, the method significantly improves reported performance on text generation, text style transfer, and image generation. The evidence supports the training approach across these evaluated tasks and architectures.
summary.tldr: A variational GAN framework stabilizes learning through generator-update clipping and discriminator sample reweighting, improving several text and image tasks.

title: Improving GAN Training with Probability Ratio Clipping and Sample Reweighting

abstract: Pre-trained language models (e.g., BERT (Devlin et al., 2018) and its variants) have achieved remarkable success in varieties of NLP tasks. However, these models usually consist of hundreds of millions of parameters which brings challenges for fine-tuning and online serving in real-life applications due to latency and capacity constraints. In this work, we present a simple and effective approach to compress large Transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017) based pre-trained models, termed as deep self-attention distillation. The small model (student) is trained by deeply mimicking the self-attention module, which plays a vital role in Transformer networks, of the large model (teacher). Specifically, we propose distilling the self-attention module of the last Transformer layer of the teacher, which is effective and flexible for the student. Furthermore, we introduce the scaled dot-product between values in the self-attention module as the new deep self-attention knowledge, in addition to the attention distributions (i.e., the scaled dot-product of queries and keys) that have been used in existing works. Moreover, we show that introducing a teacher assistant (Mirzadeh et al., 2019) also helps the distillation of large pre-trained Transformer models. Experimental results demonstrate that our monolingual model outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in different parameter size of student models. In particular, it retains more than 99% accuracy on SQuAD 2.0 and several GLUE benchmark tasks using 50% of the Transformer parameters and computations of the teacher model. We also obtain competitive results in applying deep self-attention distillation to multilingual pre-trained models.

MiniLM compresses a Transformer by training a smaller student to imitate the self-attention module in the teacher’s final layer. This provides a task-agnostic way to transfer knowledge into the smaller model.

The student learns both the teacher’s attention distributions and relationships expressed by scaled dot-products between value vectors. The latter adds a form of attention-module knowledge beyond the query–key relationships used in existing work. The authors also show that introducing a teacher assistant helps distill large pretrained Transformers.

That figure describes retained teacher performance, not an absolute accuracy of 99%. summary.tldr: MiniLM distills final-layer self-attention relationships into smaller Transformers, retaining over 99% of teacher accuracy on several tasks with half the Transformer resources.

title: MiniLM: Deep Self-Attention Distillation for Task-Agnostic Compression of Pre-Trained Transformers

abstract: Robustness to adversarial attacks is an important concern due to the fragility of deep neural networks to small perturbations, and has received an abundance of attention in recent years. Distributional Robust Optimization (DRO), a particularly promising way of addressing this challenge, studies robustness via divergence-based uncertainty sets and has provided valuable insights into robustification strategies such as regularisation. In the context of machine learning, majority of existing results have chosen $f$-divergences, Wasserstein distances and more recently, the Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) to construct uncertainty sets. We extend this line of work for the purposes of understanding robustness via regularization by studying uncertainty sets constructed with Integral Probability Metrics (IPMs) - a large family of divergences including the MMD, Total Variation and Wasserstein distances. Our main result shows that DRO under \textit{any} choice of IPM corresponds to a family of regularization penalties, which recover and improve upon existing results in the setting of MMD and Wasserstein distances. Due to the generality of our result, we show that other choices of IPMs correspond to other commonly used penalties in machine learning. Furthermore, we extend our results to shed light on adversarial generative modelling via $f$-GANs, constituting the first study of distributional robustness for the $f$-GAN objective. Our results unveil the inductive properties of the discriminator set with regards to robustness, allowing us to give positive comments for a number of existing penalty-based GAN methods such as Wasserstein-, MMD- and Sobolev-GANs. In summary, our results intimately link GANs to distributional robustness, extend previous results on DRO and contribute to our understanding of the link between regularization and robustness at large.

paragraphs: Distributionally robust optimization studies how a model performs across a set of possible data distributions. The way that set is defined determines which changes the model is asked to withstand. This paper examines uncertainty sets built using integral probability metrics, a broad family that includes maximum mean discrepancy, total variation, and Wasserstein distances.

The central result connects distributionally robust optimization under any choice of these metrics to a family of regularization penalties. It recovers and strengthens existing results for maximum mean discrepancy and Wasserstein distances. Other choices within the same framework correspond to additional commonly used penalties, giving a unified account of how regularization relates to robustness.

Their results provide theoretical support for aspects of existing penalty-based methods, including Wasserstein, MMD, and Sobolev GANs. The contribution is a set of mathematical links: choices of distributional uncertainty, training penalties, and discriminator families can be understood together when analyzing robustness.
summary.tldr: The paper links robustness under integral probability metrics to regularization penalties and extends that analysis to GAN objectives and discriminator choices.

title: Distributional Robustness with IPMs and links to Regularization and GANs

abstract: In neural combinatorial optimization (CO), reinforcement learning (RL) can turn a deep neural net into a fast, powerful heuristic solver of NP-hard problems. This approach has a great potential in practical applications because it allows near-optimal solutions to be found without expert guides armed with substantial domain knowledge. We introduce Policy Optimization with Multiple Optima (POMO), an end-to-end approach for building such a heuristic solver. POMO is applicable to a wide range of CO problems. It is designed to exploit the symmetries in the representation of a CO solution. POMO uses a modified REINFORCE algorithm that forces diverse rollouts towards all optimal solutions. Empirically, the low-variance baseline of POMO makes RL training fast and stable, and it is more resistant to local minima compared to previous approaches. We also introduce a new augmentation-based inference method, which accompanies POMO nicely. We demonstrate the effectiveness of POMO by solving three popular NP-hard problems, namely, traveling salesman (TSP), capacitated vehicle routing (CVRP), and 0-1 knapsack (KP). For all three, our solver based on POMO shows a significant improvement in performance over all recent learned heuristics. In particular, we achieve the optimality gap of 0.14% with TSP100 while reducing inference time by more than an order of magnitude.

The authors also introduce an augmentation-based inference procedure that complements the training method when producing solutions.

Experiments cover the traveling salesman problem, capacitated vehicle routing, and zero-one knapsack. POMO improves on the recent learned heuristics compared in all three tasks. For traveling salesman instances with 100 locations, it reports a 0.14% optimality gap while reducing inference time by more than an order of magnitude. These findings show the practical value of exploiting solution symmetry, while the method remains a learned heuristic rather than a guarantee of finding an optimum.
summary.tldr: POMO exploits equivalent optimal solution representations to train faster, more stable reinforcement-learning heuristics for combinatorial optimization.

title: POMO: Policy Optimization with Multiple Optima for Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Despite recent advances, goal-directed generation of structured discrete data remains challenging. For problems such as program synthesis (generating source code) and materials design (generating molecules), finding examples which satisfy desired constraints or exhibit desired properties is difficult. In practice, expensive heuristic search or reinforcement learning algorithms are often employed. In this paper, we investigate the use of conditional generative models which directly attack this inverse problem, by modeling the distribution of discrete structures given properties of interest. Unfortunately, the maximum likelihood training of such models often fails with the samples from the generative model inadequately respecting the input properties. To address this, we introduce a novel approach to directly optimize a reinforcement learning objective, maximizing an expected reward. We avoid high-variance score-function estimators that would otherwise be required by sampling from an approximation to the normalized rewards, allowing simple Monte Carlo estimation of model gradients. We test our methodology on two tasks: generating molecules with user-defined properties and identifying short python expressions which evaluate to a given target value. In both cases, we find improvements over maximum likelihood estimation and other baselines.

paragraphs: Generating a molecule or a program is harder when the result must satisfy particular properties. This paper studies conditional generative models that directly map desired properties to a distribution over discrete structures. The challenge is that ordinary maximum-likelihood training can produce outputs that do not adequately respect the properties supplied as input.

The authors instead optimize an expected-reward objective, aligning training with how well generated structures meet the goal. They estimate model gradients by sampling from an approximation to normalized rewards. This permits simple Monte Carlo estimation while avoiding the high-variance score-function estimators that would otherwise be needed for the chosen reinforcement-learning objective.

The method is evaluated on molecules with user-specified properties and short Python expressions that must evaluate to a target value. It improves over maximum-likelihood training and other compared methods on both tasks. These findings support reward-oriented training as a way to strengthen the connection between a conditioning request and the resulting discrete output, without establishing that every generated structure will satisfy its requested constraints.
summary.tldr: Reward-based training improves conditional generation of molecules and short programs by more directly targeting requested output properties.

title: Goal-directed Generation of Discrete Structures with Conditional Generative Models

abstract: Deep neural networks set the state-of-the-art across many tasks in computer vision, but their generalization ability to simple image distortions is surprisingly fragile. In contrast, the mammalian visual system is robust to a wide range of perturbations. Recent work suggests that this generalization ability can be explained by useful inductive biases encoded in the representations of visual stimuli throughout the visual cortex. Here, we successfully leveraged these inductive biases with a multi-task learning approach: we jointly trained a deep network to perform image classification and to predict neural activity in macaque primary visual cortex (V1) in response to the same natural stimuli. We measured the out-of-distribution generalization abilities of our resulting network by testing its robustness to common image distortions. We found that co-training on monkey V1 data indeed leads to increased robustness despite the absence of those distortions during training. Additionally, we showed that our network's robustness is often very close to that of an Oracle network where parts of the architecture are directly trained on noisy images. Our results also demonstrated that the network's representations become more brain-like as their robustness improves. Using a novel constrained reconstruction analysis, we investigated what makes our brain-regularized network more robust. We found that our monkey co-trained network is more sensitive to content than noise when compared to a Baseline network that we trained for image classification alone. Using DeepGaze-predicted saliency maps for ImageNet images, we found that the monkey co-trained network tends to be more sensitive to salient regions in a scene, reminiscent of existing theories on the role of V1 in the detection of object borders and bottom-up saliency. Overall, our work expands the promising research avenue of transferring inductive biases from biological to artificial neural networks on the representational level, and provides a novel analysis of the effects of our transfer.

paragraphs: Visual neural networks can struggle with simple image distortions that biological vision handles well. The authors also observe that representations become more brain-like as robustness improves, connecting the two outcomes in their experiments.

Analysis using predicted saliency maps also shows greater sensitivity to salient scene regions. Together, these findings support biological neural-response prediction as a useful additional training task and provide evidence about how the resulting representations differ.
summary.tldr: Jointly learning image classification and macaque V1 responses improves robustness to unseen distortions and increases sensitivity to meaningful image content.

title: Towards robust vision by multi-task learning on monkey visual cortex

abstract: When faced with distribution shift at test time, deep neural networks often make inaccurate predictions with unreliable uncertainty estimates.While improving the robustness of neural networks is one promising approach to mitigate this issue, an appealing alternate to robustifying networks against all possible test-time shifts is to instead directly adapt them to unlabeled inputs from the particular distribution shift we encounter at test time.However, this poses a challenging question: in the standard Bayesian model for supervised learning, unlabeled inputs are conditionally independent of model parameters when the labels are unobserved, so what can unlabeled data tell us about the model parameters at test-time? In this paper, we derive a Bayesian model that provides for a well-defined relationship between unlabeled inputs under distributional shift and model parameters, and show how approximate inference in this model can be instantiated with a simple regularized entropy minimization procedure at test-time. We evaluate our method on a variety of distribution shifts for image classification, including image corruptions, natural distribution shifts, and domain adaptation settings, and show that our method improves both accuracy and uncertainty estimation.

paragraphs: When test inputs differ from training inputs, a neural network can become both inaccurate and poorly calibrated about its uncertainty. This paper studies adapting a model directly to the unlabeled inputs encountered at test time. The motivation is to respond to the particular distribution change that occurs, rather than relying entirely on robustness learned beforehand.

A theoretical obstacle arises in the standard Bayesian formulation of supervised learning. Once labels are unobserved, the inputs are conditionally independent of the model parameters, so those inputs alone provide no route for updating the parameters. The authors derive a Bayesian model that explicitly connects shifted, unlabeled inputs to the parameters being adapted.

Approximate inference in this model leads to a practical procedure based on regularized entropy minimization at test time. Evaluations cover image corruptions, natural distribution changes, and domain adaptation for image classification. The reported improvements in both accuracy and uncertainty estimation indicate that adaptation can help predictions and confidence estimates together in these evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian formulation turns adaptation to unlabeled test inputs into regularized entropy minimization, improving accuracy and uncertainty estimates in evaluated image-classification shifts.

title: Bayesian Adaptation for Covariate Shift

abstract: Behavioral cloning has proven to be effective for learning sequential decision-making policies from expert demonstrations. However, behavioral cloning often suffers from the causal confusion problem where a policy relies on the noticeable effect of expert actions due to the strong correlation but not the cause we desire. This paper presents Object-aware REgularizatiOn (OREO), a simple technique that regularizes an imitation policy in an object-aware manner. Our main idea is to encourage a policy to uniformly attend to all semantic objects, in order to prevent the policy from exploiting nuisance variables strongly correlated with expert actions. To this end, we introduce a two-stage approach: (a) we extract semantic objects from images by utilizing discrete codes from a vector-quantized variational autoencoder, and (b) we randomly drop the units that share the same discrete code together, i.e., masking out semantic objects. Our experiments demonstrate that OREO significantly improves the performance of behavioral cloning, outperforming various other regularization and causality-based methods on a variety of Atari environments and a self-driving CARLA environment. We also show that our method even outperforms inverse reinforcement learning methods trained with a considerable amount of environment interaction.

paragraphs: Behavioral cloning learns actions from expert demonstrations, but it can rely on misleading visual correlations. An observable effect of an expert's action may be strongly associated with that action without being the reason it should be chosen. The paper addresses this causal confusion with Object-aware Regularization, or OREO.

OREO encourages a policy to distribute attention across semantic objects rather than exploit a nuisance variable. It first uses discrete codes from a vector-quantized variational autoencoder to extract object-related structure from images. It then randomly drops together the units sharing a code, masking semantic objects as groups. This makes the regularization sensitive to object structure.

Experiments in multiple Atari environments and a CARLA driving environment show substantial behavioral-cloning improvements over other regularization and causality-based methods. The authors also report outperforming inverse reinforcement learning methods trained with considerable environment interaction. These findings support object-aware masking as a practical way to reduce harmful reliance on correlated visual information in the evaluated imitation tasks.
summary.tldr: OREO masks learned semantic objects during training to reduce misleading visual correlations and improve behavioral cloning.

title: Object-Aware Regularization for Addressing Causal Confusion in Imitation Learning

abstract: Given only positive examples and unlabeled examples (from both positive and negative classes), we might hope nevertheless to estimate an accurate positive-versus-negative classifier. Formally, this task is broken down into two subtasks: (i) Mixture Proportion Estimation (MPE)---determining the fraction of positive examples in the unlabeled data; and (ii) PU-learning---given such an estimate, learning the desired positive-versus-negative classifier. Unfortunately, classical methods for both problems break down in high-dimensional settings. Meanwhile, recently proposed heuristics lack theoretical coherence and depend precariously on hyperparameter tuning. In this paper, we propose two simple techniques: Best Bin Estimation (BBE) (for MPE); and Conditional Value Ignoring Risk (CVIR), a simple objective for PU-learning. Both methods dominate previous approaches empirically, and for BBE, we establish formal guarantees that hold whenever we can train a model to cleanly separate out a small subset of positive examples. Our final algorithm (TED)$^n$, alternates between the two procedures, significantly improving both our mixture proportion estimator and classifier

paragraphs: Positive-unlabeled learning starts with labeled positive examples and an unlabeled collection containing both positive and negative cases. The task has two connected parts: estimating how much of the unlabeled collection is positive, and using that estimate to train a classifier. This paper addresses difficulties that earlier approaches encounter in high-dimensional data.

The authors introduce Best Bin Estimation, or BBE, for estimating the positive fraction, and Conditional Value Ignoring Risk, or CVIR, as an objective for classifier training. BBE has formal guarantees when a model can cleanly separate a small subset of positive examples. This is a stated sufficient condition for the guarantee, rather than a claim that all positives must be perfectly separated.

Their final algorithm, called (TED)^n, alternates between estimating the mixture proportion and training the classifier. The authors report that both component methods outperform earlier approaches empirically, and that alternation significantly improves both estimates and classification. The contribution treats prevalence estimation and predictive learning as linked procedures that can improve together, with a conditional theoretical foundation for the estimation component.
summary.tldr: BBE and CVIR jointly improve positive-unlabeled learning, with BBE guarantees when a small positive subset can be cleanly separated.

title: Mixture Proportion Estimation and PU Learning:A Modern Approach

abstract: Quantization is a popular technique that transforms the parameter representation of a neural network from floating-point numbers into lower-precision ones (e.g., 8-bit integers). It reduces the memory footprint and the computational cost at inference, facilitating the deployment of resource-hungry models. However, the parameter perturbations caused by this transformation result in behavioral disparities between the model before and after quantization. For example, a quantized model can misclassify some test-time samples that are otherwise classified correctly. It is not known whether such differences lead to a new security vulnerability. We hypothesize that an adversary may control this disparity to introduce specific behaviors that activate upon quantization. To study this hypothesis, we weaponize quantization-aware training and propose a new training framework to implement adversarial quantization outcomes. Following this framework, we present three attacks we carry out with quantization: (i) an indiscriminate attack for significant accuracy loss; (ii) a targeted attack against specific samples; and (iii) a backdoor attack for controlling the model with an input trigger. We further show that a single compromised model defeats multiple quantization schemes, including robust quantization techniques. Moreover, in a federated learning scenario, we demonstrate that a set of malicious participants who conspire can inject our quantization-activated backdoor. Lastly, we discuss potential counter-measures and show that only re-training consistently removes the attack artifacts. Our code is available at https://github.com/Secure-AI-Systems-Group/Qu-ANTI-zation

paragraphs: Quantization reduces a neural network's memory and inference costs by representing parameters at lower precision. It also changes those parameters and can alter predictions. This paper investigates whether an adversary can deliberately shape that behavioral difference so malicious behavior becomes active when the model is quantized.

The authors adapt quantization-aware training into a framework for creating such outcomes. They demonstrate three forms: broad accuracy degradation, attacks on particular samples, and a backdoor controlled by an input trigger. A single compromised model can affect multiple quantization schemes in their study, including techniques intended to make quantization robust.

The paper also demonstrates a federated-learning scenario in which collaborating malicious participants inject a quantization-activated backdoor. Its countermeasure investigation finds that only retraining consistently removes the attack artifacts among the approaches considered. The findings identify quantization as a transformation whose security implications can extend beyond ordinary accuracy changes, because training can deliberately embed behavior that appears after precision reduction.
summary.tldr: Adversarial training can embed harmful model behavior that activates after quantization, including targeted errors and backdoors.

title: Qu-ANTI-zation: Exploiting Quantization Artifacts for Achieving Adversarial Outcomes

abstract: Existing work on understanding deep learning often employs measures that compress all data-dependent information into a few numbers. In this work, we adopt a perspective based on the role of individual examples. We introduce a measure of the computational difficulty of making a prediction for a given input: the (effective) prediction depth. Our extensive investigation reveals surprising yet simple relationships between the prediction depth of a given input and the model’s uncertainty, confidence, accuracy and speed of learning for that data point. We further categorize difficult examples into three interpretable groups, demonstrate how these groups are processed differently inside deep models and showcase how this understanding allows us to improve prediction accuracy. Insights from our study lead to a coherent view of a number of separately reported phenomena in the literature: early layers generalize while later layers memorize; early layers converge faster and networks learn easy data and simple functions first.

paragraphs: Many attempts to understand deep learning summarize a dataset or a model with a few aggregate measurements. This paper instead studies individual examples and asks how difficult each one is for a network to predict. It introduces effective prediction depth as a measure of the computational difficulty associated with making a prediction for a particular input.

The investigation finds relationships between an example's prediction depth and the model's uncertainty, confidence, accuracy, and speed of learning on that example. The authors also divide difficult examples into three interpretable groups and show that deep models process those groups differently. They demonstrate that using this understanding can improve prediction accuracy.

This perspective connects several observations that had previously been reported separately. These include earlier layers generalizing while later layers memorize, earlier layers converging sooner, and networks learning easy examples and simple functions first. The contribution is an example-level account linking internal computation with learning behavior. The reported relationships come from the authors' investigation; they are not presented as universal laws governing every network or input.
summary.tldr: Effective prediction depth links individual example difficulty to network behavior and helps explain several patterns in deep learning.

title: Deep Learning Through the Lens of Example Difficulty

abstract: Estimating the data uncertainty in regression tasks is often done by learning a quantile function or a prediction interval of the true label conditioned on the input. It is frequently observed that quantile regression---a vanilla algorithm for learning quantiles with asymptotic guarantees---tends to *under-cover* than the desired coverage level in reality. While various fixes have been proposed, a more fundamental understanding of why this under-coverage bias happens in the first place remains elusive.In this paper, we present a rigorous theoretical study on the coverage of uncertainty estimation algorithms in learning quantiles. We prove that quantile regression suffers from an inherent under-coverage bias, in a vanilla setting where we learn a realizable linear quantile function and there is more data than parameters. More quantitatively, for $\alpha>0.5$ and small $d/n$, the $\alpha$-quantile learned by quantile regression roughly achieves coverage $\alpha - (\alpha-1/2)\cdot d/n$ regardless of the noise distribution, where $d$ is the input dimension and $n$ is the number of training data. Our theory reveals that this under-coverage bias stems from a certain high-dimensional parameter estimation error that is not implied by existing theories on quantile regression. Experiments on simulated and real data verify our theory and further illustrate the effect of various factors such as sample size and model capacity on the under-coverage bias in more practical setups.

paragraphs: Quantile regression estimates thresholds that outcomes should fall below at a specified frequency. In practice, the learned thresholds often cover fewer outcomes than intended, despite asymptotic guarantees. This paper investigates the source of that under-coverage, rather than beginning with a correction for its observed effects.

The authors prove an inherent bias in a setting where the true quantile function is linear and realizable, and the number of training examples exceeds the number of parameters. For a target quantile alpha above one-half and a small dimension-to-sample ratio, achieved coverage is approximately alpha minus (alpha minus one-half) times d/n. Here d is input dimension and n is training-set size; the stated approximation is independent of the noise distribution.

The analysis traces the bias to a high-dimensional parameter-estimation error that existing quantile-regression theories do not imply. It therefore identifies a mechanism that can operate even when the model can represent the correct quantile function. Simulated and real-data experiments support the theory and explore how sample size and model capacity influence under-coverage in more practical settings.
summary.tldr: Quantile regression can systematically under-cover even with a realizable linear model, with the analyzed bias scaling approximately with dimension divided by sample size.

title: Understanding the Under-Coverage Bias in Uncertainty Estimation

abstract: Random walks are a fundamental primitive used in many machine learning algorithms with several applications in clustering and semi-supervised learning. Despite their relevance, the first efficient parallel algorithm to compute random walks has been introduced very recently (Łącki et al.). Unfortunately their method has a fundamental shortcoming: their algorithm is non-local in that it heavily relies on computing random walks out of all nodes in the input graph, even though in many practical applications one is interested in computing random walks only from a small subset of nodes in the graph. In this paper, we present a new algorithm that overcomes this limitation by building random walks efficiently and locally at the same time. We show that our technique is both memory and round efficient, and in particular yields an efficient parallel local clustering algorithm. Finally, we complement our theoretical analysis with experimental results showing that our algorithm is significantly more scalable than previous approaches.

paragraphs: Random walks are a basic component of graph-based machine learning, including clustering and semi-supervised learning. Many applications need walks starting from only a small subset of graph nodes. An existing efficient parallel approach nevertheless depends heavily on computing walks from every node, creating a mismatch between the requested computation and the work performed.

This paper introduces a parallel algorithm that constructs random walks efficiently while preserving locality. Its central contribution is to address requests focused on selected starting nodes without the same reliance on walks originating throughout the graph. The theoretical analysis establishes efficiency in both memory use and communication rounds, addressing two separate costs of parallel computation.

The authors also show how the technique yields an efficient parallel algorithm for local clustering. This connects the random-walk primitive to a downstream learning application rather than treating walk generation in isolation. Experiments complement the analysis and show substantially better scalability than previous approaches, supporting the practical value of combining parallel execution with computation focused on the relevant starting nodes.
summary.tldr: A local parallel random-walk algorithm improves memory and round efficiency and supports scalable local clustering.

title: Efficient and Local Parallel Random Walks

abstract: Many reinforcement learning (RL) environments consist of independent entities that interact sparsely. In such environments, RL agents have only limited influence over other entities in any particular situation. Our idea in this work is that learning can be efficiently guided by knowing when and what the agent can influence with its actions. To achieve this, we introduce a measure of situation-dependent causal influence based on conditional mutual information and show that it can reliably detect states of influence. We then propose several ways to integrate this measure into RL algorithms to improve exploration and off-policy learning. All modified algorithms show strong increases in data efficiency on robotic manipulation tasks.

paragraphs: In environments made up of separate entities that interact only occasionally, an agent's actions do not affect everything at every moment. The paper argues that recognizing these opportunities for influence can guide learning. The useful question is situation-dependent: which entities can the agent affect through its actions in the current circumstances?

To answer that question, the authors introduce a causal influence measure based on conditional mutual information. The measure is designed to capture influence in a particular situation rather than assign one fixed level of influence across the environment. They show that it can reliably identify states where influence is present, supplying information that reinforcement learning algorithms can use.

The paper then develops several integrations of this measure into exploration and off-policy learning. Across the modified algorithms, experiments on robotic manipulation tasks show strong improvements in data efficiency. These findings support using detected opportunities for influence to guide how agents learn from interaction, with the reported empirical gains grounded in the manipulation tasks studied.
summary.tldr: A situation-dependent causal influence measure improves the data efficiency of reinforcement learning algorithms on robotic manipulation tasks.

title: Causal Influence Detection for Improving Efficiency in Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Recent research shows that the dynamics of an infinitely wide neural network (NN) trained by gradient descent can be characterized by Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) \citep{jacot2018neural}. Under the squared loss, the infinite-width NN trained by gradient descent with an infinitely small learning rate is equivalent to kernel regression with NTK \citep{arora2019exact}. However, the equivalence is only known for ridge regression currently \citep{arora2019harnessing}, while the equivalence between NN and other kernel machines (KMs), e.g. support vector machine (SVM), remains unknown. Therefore, in this work, we propose to establish the equivalence between NN and SVM, and specifically, the infinitely wide NN trained by soft margin loss and the standard soft margin SVM with NTK trained by subgradient descent. Our main theoretical results include establishing the equivalence between NN and a broad family of $\ell_2$ regularized KMs with finite-width bounds, which cannot be handled by prior work, and showing that every finite-width NN trained by such regularized loss functions is approximately a KM. Furthermore, we demonstrate our theory can enable three practical applications, including (i) \textit{non-vacuous} generalization bound of NN via the corresponding KM; (ii) \textit{nontrivial} robustness certificate for the infinite-width NN (while existing robustness verification methods would provide vacuous bounds); (iii) intrinsically more robust infinite-width NNs than those from previous kernel regression.

However, the equivalence is only known for ridge regression currently \citep{arora2019harnessing}, while the equivalence between NN and other kernel machines (KMs), e.g. support vector machine (SVM), remains unknown. Therefore, in this work, we propose to establish the equivalence between NN and SVM, and specifically, the infinitely wide NN trained by soft margin loss and the standard soft margin SVM with NTK trained by subgradient descent. Our main theoretical results include establishing the equivalence between NN and a broad family of $\ell_2$ regularized KMs with finite-width bounds, which cannot be handled by prior work, and showing that every finite-width NN trained by such regularized loss functions is approximately a KM. paragraphs: The neural tangent kernel connects the training dynamics of infinitely wide neural networks to kernel methods. Earlier equivalence results centered on squared-loss regression. This paper extends the connection to support vector machines and a broader family of kernel machines with ℓ2 regularization, examining how the choice of training loss changes the relationship.

The authors establish an equivalence between an infinitely wide network trained with a soft-margin loss and a standard soft-margin support vector machine using the neural tangent kernel and subgradient descent. Their theory also provides finite-width bounds. For networks trained with the regularized losses covered by the analysis, it gives an approximate kernel-machine characterization at finite width.

The paper demonstrates three uses of this connection: meaningful neural-network generalization bounds through the corresponding kernel machine, nontrivial robustness certificates for infinite-width networks, and improved robustness over the earlier kernel-regression construction. The width and loss conditions matter to interpreting these statements. Exact equivalence concerns the specified infinite-width setting, while finite networks receive an approximate characterization supported by bounds.
summary.tldr: The paper connects suitably trained neural networks to regularized kernel machines, including support vector machines, with implications for generalization and robustness.

title: On the Equivalence between Neural Network and Support Vector Machine

abstract: Linear mixed-effect models provide a natural baseline for estimating disease progression using longitudinal data. They provide interpretable models at the cost of modeling assumptions on the progression profiles and their variability across subjects. A significant improvement is to embed the data in a Riemannian manifold and learn patient-specific trajectories distributed around a central geodesic. A few interpretable parameters characterize subject trajectories at the cost of a prior choice of the metric, which determines the shape of the trajectories. We extend this approach by learning the metric from the data allowing more flexibility while keeping the interpretability. Specifically, we learn the metric as the push-forward of the Euclidean metric by a diffeomorphism. This diffeomorphism is estimated iteratively as the composition of radial basis functions belonging to a reproducible kernel Hilbert space. The metric update allows us to improve the forecasting of imaging and clinical biomarkers in the Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) cohort. Our results compare favorably to the 56 methods benchmarked in the TADPOLE challenge.

paragraphs: Disease progression models must describe both a shared pattern over time and differences between patients. Geometric approaches represent patient trajectories around a central geodesic, a path determined by the geometry of the data space. They offer interpretable trajectory parameters, but choosing the metric in advance constrains the shapes those trajectories can take.

This paper learns that metric from longitudinal data while retaining the interpretable trajectory model. It constructs the metric by transporting Euclidean geometry through a diffeomorphism, a smooth invertible transformation. The transformation is estimated iteratively through compositions of radial basis functions, allowing the geometry itself to adapt to observed progression patterns.

Learning the metric improves forecasts of imaging and clinical biomarkers in the Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative cohort. The authors report results that compare favorably with the 56 methods benchmarked in the TADPOLE challenge. The contribution is therefore a more flexible geometric progression model: patient variation remains described through interpretable parameters, while the underlying trajectory shapes are informed by data rather than fixed entirely by a prior metric choice.
summary.tldr: Learning the geometry underlying patient trajectories improves disease-progression forecasts while preserving an interpretable trajectory model.

title: Learning Riemannian metric for disease progression modeling

abstract: Missing data is an important problem in machine learning practice. Starting from the premise that imputation methods should preserve the causal structure of the data, we develop a regularization scheme that encourages any baseline imputation method to be causally consistent with the underlying data generating mechanism. Our proposal is a causally-aware imputation algorithm (MIRACLE). MIRACLE iteratively refines the imputation of a baseline by simultaneously modeling the missingness generating mechanism, encouraging imputation to be consistent with the causal structure of the data. We conduct extensive experiments on synthetic and a variety of publicly available datasets to show that MIRACLE is able to consistently improve imputation over a variety of benchmark methods across all three missingness scenarios: at random, completely at random, and not at random.

paragraphs: Filling missing entries in a dataset changes the relationships represented by that data. MIRACLE starts from the premise that these replacements should respect the causal structure of the process that generated the observations. Its goal is to improve imputation by considering both the values being filled and the mechanism responsible for their absence.

The method begins with the output of a baseline imputation approach and repeatedly refines it. During refinement, it also models how missingness is generated. A regularization scheme encourages the completed data to remain consistent with the underlying causal mechanism, allowing causal information to guide corrections to an existing imputation.

Experiments on synthetic and publicly available datasets report consistent improvements over a variety of benchmark methods. The evaluations cover data missing completely at random, at random, and not at random. These results support using the missingness mechanism as part of the imputation process across the tested settings. The method encourages causal consistency; the reported evidence establishes empirical improvements rather than an unconditional guarantee that every completed dataset recovers its true causal structure.
summary.tldr: MIRACLE refines existing imputations by modeling missingness and encouraging consistency with the data’s causal structure.

title: MIRACLE: Causally-Aware Imputation via Learning Missing Data Mechanisms

abstract: Binary neural networks (BNNs) represent original full-precision weights and activations into 1-bit with sign function. Since the gradient of the conventional sign function is almost zero everywhere which cannot be used for back-propagation, several attempts have been proposed to alleviate the optimization difficulty by using approximate gradient. However, those approximations corrupt the main direction of factual gradient. To this end, we propose to estimate the gradient of sign function in the Fourier frequency domain using the combination of sine functions for training BNNs, namely frequency domain approximation (FDA). The proposed approach does not affect the low-frequency information of the original sign function which occupies most of the overall energy, and high-frequency coefficients will be ignored to avoid the huge computational overhead. In addition, we embed a noise adaptation module into the training phase to compensate the approximation error. The experiments on several benchmark datasets and neural architectures illustrate that the binary network learned using our method achieves the state-of-the-art accuracy. Code will be available at https://gitee.com/mindspore/models/tree/master/research/cv/FDA-BNN.

paragraphs: Binary neural networks convert weights and activations to one-bit values using a sign function. This makes training difficult because the function's gradient is zero almost everywhere, leaving backpropagation without a useful learning signal. Existing methods substitute approximate gradients, but the paper argues that these approximations can distort the direction of the intended gradient.

The proposed frequency domain approximation represents the sign function through a combination of sine functions and uses that representation to estimate its gradient. It preserves the low-frequency information, which contains most of the function's overall energy, while leaving out high-frequency coefficients to limit computational cost. A noise adaptation module is included during training to compensate for approximation error.

Experiments across several benchmark datasets and network architectures report state-of-the-art accuracy for the resulting binary networks. The contribution is a training method that uses the frequency structure of the binarization function to construct the learning signal. Its reported gains suggest that both the choice of approximation and compensation for its residual error matter for effective binary-network optimization.
summary.tldr: Frequency domain approximation trains binary neural networks with a sine-based gradient estimate and error compensation, achieving reported state-of-the-art accuracy.

title: Learning Frequency Domain Approximation for Binary Neural Networks

abstract: Due to the discrete nature of words, language GANs require to be optimized from rewards provided by discriminator networks, via reinforcement learning methods. This is a much harder setting than for continuous tasks, which enjoy gradient flows from discriminators to generators, usually leading to dramatic learning instabilities. However, we claim that this can be solved by making discriminator and generator networks cooperate to produce output sequences during training. These cooperative outputs, inherently built to obtain higher discrimination scores, not only provide denser rewards for training but also form a more compact artificial set for discriminator training, hence improving its accuracy and stability.In this paper, we show that our SelfGAN framework, built on this cooperative principle, outperforms Teacher Forcing and obtains state-of-the-art results on two challenging tasks, Summarization and Question Generation.

paragraphs: Language GANs face a training difficulty because words are discrete. In the setting described by this paper, the generator learns through reinforcement-learning rewards from a discriminator, rather than direct gradient flow through continuous outputs. This can make learning highly unstable.

The proposed SelfGAN framework has the generator and discriminator cooperate when producing training sequences. Those cooperative sequences are constructed to receive higher discriminator scores. The authors argue that this provides denser rewards to guide generator training. It also produces a more compact artificial training set for the discriminator, improving its accuracy and stability.

The same cooperation thus affects both sides of the training process: the generator receives richer guidance, while the discriminator learns from a more focused set of generated outputs. Experiments report that SelfGAN outperforms teacher forcing and achieves state-of-the-art results on summarization and question generation. These results support cooperative sequence production as a useful approach to the instability encountered in the language-GAN training setting studied.
summary.tldr: SelfGAN makes generators and discriminators cooperate on training sequences, improving learning guidance and reported language-generation results.

title: To Beam Or Not To Beam: That is a Question of Cooperation for Language GANs

abstract: As a research community, we are still lacking a systematic understanding of the progress on adversarial robustness which often makes it hard to identify the most promising ideas in training robust models. A key challenge in benchmarking robustness is that its evaluation is often error-prone leading to robustness overestimation. Our goal is to establish a standardized benchmark of adversarial robustness, which as accurately as possible reflects the robustness of the considered models within a reasonable computational budget. To this end, we start by considering the image classification task and introduce restrictions (possibly loosened in the future) on the allowed models. We evaluate adversarial robustness with AutoAttack, an ensemble of white- and black-box attacks, which was recently shown in a large-scale study to improve almost all robustness evaluations compared to the original publications. To prevent overadaptation of new defenses to AutoAttack, we welcome external evaluations based on adaptive attacks, especially where AutoAttack flags a potential overestimation of robustness. Our leaderboard, hosted at https://robustbench.github.io/, contains evaluations of 120+ models and aims at reflecting the current state of the art in image classification on a set of well-defined tasks in $\ell_\infty$- and $\ell_2$-threat models and on common corruptions, with possible extensions in the future. Additionally, we open-source the library https://github.com/RobustBench/robustbench that provides unified access to 80+ robust models to facilitate their downstream applications. Finally, based on the collected models, we analyze the impact of robustness on the performance on distribution shifts, calibration, out-of-distribution detection, fairness, privacy leakage, smoothness, and transferability.

paragraphs: RobustBench addresses a measurement problem in adversarial robustness: flawed evaluation can make models appear more resistant to attacks than they are. The project aims to provide standardized assessments that are as accurate as possible within a reasonable computational budget. Its initial focus is image classification, with restrictions on eligible models to support that evaluation.

The benchmark uses AutoAttack, which combines attacks with and without access to internal model information. It also welcomes external adaptive attacks to reduce the risk that defenses become overly specialized to AutoAttack, particularly when the evaluation flags possible overestimation. The leaderboard contains more than 120 models across defined perturbation settings and common image corruptions.

An accompanying library gives unified access to more than 80 robust models for further use. The authors also examine how robustness relates to distribution shifts, calibration, detection of unfamiliar inputs, fairness, privacy leakage, smoothness, and transferability. These analyses broaden the resource beyond rankings, while the explicit evaluation scope keeps robustness claims tied to the tested conditions.
summary.tldr: RobustBench standardizes adversarial evaluation, shares robust models, and invites adaptive testing to help detect overstated robustness.

title: RobustBench: a standardized adversarial robustness benchmark

abstract: We consider the fundamental problem of fairly and efficiently allocating $T$ indivisible items among $n$ agents with additive preferences. The items become available over a sequence of rounds, and every item must be allocated immediately and irrevocably before the next one arrives. Previous work shows that when the agents' valuations for the items are drawn from known distributions, it is possible (under mild technical assumptions) to find allocations that are envy-free with high probability and Pareto efficient ex-post. We study a \emph{partial-information} setting, where it is possible to elicit ordinal but not cardinal information. When a new item arrives, the algorithm can query each agent for the relative rank of this item with respect to a subset of the past items. When values are drawn from i.i.d.\ distributions, we give an algorithm that is envy-free and $(1-\epsilon)$-welfare-maximizing with high probability. We provide similar guarantees (envy-freeness and a constant approximation to welfare with high probability) even with minimally expressive queries that ask for a comparison to a single previous item. For independent but non-identical agents, we obtain envy-freeness and a constant approximation to Pareto efficiency with high probability. We prove that all our results are asymptotically tight.
