paragraphs: This paper studies fair allocation when indivisible items arrive sequentially and each must be assigned immediately and permanently. Agents have additive preferences, but the algorithm cannot ask for numerical values. Instead, it can ask how an arriving item ranks relative to selected earlier items, giving it ordinal information about preferences.

When values come from independent, identically distributed draws, the authors give an algorithm that achieves envy-freeness and welfare within a factor of 1−ε of the maximum, with high probability. They also study especially limited queries that compare the new item with only one earlier item. Even with this restricted feedback, they obtain envy-freeness and a constant-factor welfare approximation with high probability.

For independent agents with non-identical distributions, the guarantees become envy-freeness and a constant approximation to Pareto efficiency, again with high probability. The paper proves its results asymptotically tight. These findings show that, under the respective distributional assumptions, useful fairness and efficiency guarantees can survive both irrevocable decisions and the absence of numerical preference reports.
summary.tldr: Under specified distributional assumptions, ordinal comparisons suffice for high-probability fairness and efficiency guarantees in irrevocable online allocation.

title: Dynamic Fair Division with Partial Information

abstract: Pre-training on time series poses a unique challenge due to the potential mismatch between pre-training and target domains, such as shifts in temporal dynamics, fast-evolving trends, and long-range and short-cyclic effects, which can lead to poor downstream performance. While domain adaptation methods can mitigate these shifts, most methods need examples directly from the target domain, making them suboptimal for pre-training. To address this challenge, methods need to accommodate target domains with different temporal dynamics and be capable of doing so without seeing any target examples during pre-training. Relative to other modalities, in time series, we expect that time-based and frequency-based representations of the same example are located close together in the time-frequency space. To this end, we posit that time-frequency consistency (TF-C) --- embedding a time-based neighborhood of an example close to its frequency-based neighborhood --- is desirable for pre-training. Motivated by TF-C, we define a decomposable pre-training model, where the self-supervised signal is provided by the distance between time and frequency components, each individually trained by contrastive estimation. We evaluate the new method on eight datasets, including electrodiagnostic testing, human activity recognition, mechanical fault detection, and physical status monitoring. Experiments against eight state-of-the-art methods show that TF-C outperforms baselines by 15.4% (F1 score) on average in one-to-one settings (e.g., fine-tuning an EEG-pretrained model on EMG data) and by 8.4% (precision) in challenging one-to-many settings (e.g., fine-tuning an EEG-pretrained model for either hand-gesture recognition or mechanical fault prediction), reflecting the breadth of scenarios that arise in real-world applications. The source code and datasets are available at https://github.com/mims-harvard/TFC-pretraining.

paragraphs: Time-series pretraining can transfer poorly when the target domain has different dynamics, trends, or cycles. Domain adaptation often needs examples from the target, which may be unavailable during pretraining. This paper proposes time-frequency consistency as a way to learn representations intended to accommodate unseen target domains with different temporal behavior.

The idea is to place the time-based neighborhood of an example near its frequency-based neighborhood in the learned representation space. The model has separate time and frequency components, each trained through contrastive estimation. Distances between the components provide an additional self-supervised signal, encouraging the two views of a signal to remain consistent.

Evaluation covers eight datasets spanning electrodiagnostic testing, activity recognition, mechanical faults, and physical status monitoring. Against eight state-of-the-art methods, the authors report average improvements of 15.4% in F1 for one-to-one transfer and 8.4% in precision for one-to-many transfer. These results support the approach across varied tested transfers, including using a shared pretraining source for substantially different downstream tasks.
summary.tldr: Aligning time-based and frequency-based representations improves time-series pretraining transfer across the evaluated downstream domains.

title: Self-Supervised Contrastive Pre-Training For Time Series via Time-Frequency Consistency

abstract: Recent advances in face forgery techniques produce nearly visually untraceable deepfake videos, which could be leveraged with malicious intentions. As a result, researchers have been devoted to deepfake detection. Previous studies have identified the importance of local low-level cues and temporal information in pursuit to generalize well across deepfake methods, however, they still suffer from robustness problem against post-processings. In this work, we propose the Local- & Temporal-aware Transformer-based Deepfake Detection (LTTD) framework, which adopts a local-to-global learning protocol with a particular focus on the valuable temporal information within local sequences. Specifically, we propose a Local Sequence Transformer (LST), which models the temporal consistency on sequences of restricted spatial regions, where low-level information is hierarchically enhanced with shallow layers of learned 3D filters. Based on the local temporal embeddings, we then achieve the final classification in a global contrastive way. Extensive experiments on popular datasets validate that our approach effectively spots local forgery cues and achieves state-of-the-art performance.

paragraphs: The paper investigates deepfake detection through local image details and how those details change over time. Earlier work had identified both as useful for generalizing across forgery methods, while still experiencing robustness problems after videos undergo post-processing. The proposed LTTD framework emphasizes temporal information within small spatial regions before forming a global decision.

Its Local Sequence Transformer models temporal consistency in sequences restricted to particular image regions. Shallow layers of learned three-dimensional filters progressively enhance low-level information in those sequences. This produces local temporal embeddings: representations that combine information about a small region with information about its behavior across time.

The framework then uses those embeddings for final classification through a global contrastive approach. This local-to-global organization lets the detector build its overall judgment from localized temporal evidence. Extensive experiments on popular datasets show that the method identifies local forgery cues and achieves state-of-the-art performance. The stated findings support focusing temporal modeling on restricted regions as a useful design choice for deepfake detection.
summary.tldr: LTTD detects deepfakes by modeling temporal consistency within local video regions and combining those representations into a global classification.

title: Delving into Sequential Patches for Deepfake Detection

abstract: Coordinate networks like Multiplicative Filter Networks (MFNs) and BACON offer some control over the frequency spectrum used to represent continuous signals such as images or 3D volumes. Yet, they are not readily applicable to problems for which coarse-to-fine estimation is required, including various inverse problems in which coarse-to-fine optimization plays a key role in avoiding poor local minima. We introduce a new coordinate network architecture and training scheme that enables coarse-to-fine optimization with fine-grained control over the frequency support of learned reconstructions. This is achieved with two key innovations. First, we incorporate skip connections so that structure at one scale is preserved when fitting finer-scale structure. Second, we propose a novel initialization scheme to provide control over the model frequency spectrum at each stage of optimization. We demonstrate how these modifications enable multiscale optimization for coarse-to-fine fitting to natural images. We then evaluate our model on synthetically generated datasets for the the problem of single-particle cryo-EM reconstruction. We learn high resolution multiscale structures, on par with the state-of-the art. Project webpage: https://shekshaa.github.io/ResidualMFN/.

paragraphs: Reconstructing an image or volume can benefit from first fitting broad structure and then adding finer detail. Existing coordinate networks offer some control over represented frequencies, but are not readily suited to this coarse-to-fine optimization. This paper introduces an architecture and training scheme that provide finer control over which frequencies participate at each stage.

Two changes make the approach work. Skip connections preserve structure learned at one scale while the network fits finer-scale content. A new initialization scheme controls the model's frequency spectrum during successive optimization stages. Together, these changes support multiscale fitting, which matters in inverse problems where coarse-to-fine optimization helps avoid poor local minima.

The authors first demonstrate the method by fitting natural images from coarse to fine. They then evaluate single-particle cryo-EM reconstruction using synthetically generated datasets. The model learns high-resolution structures at multiple scales with results reported as comparable to the state of the art. The evidence connects architectural frequency control with practical multiscale reconstruction in these settings.
summary.tldr: Skip connections and frequency-controlled initialization enable coordinate networks to reconstruct images and volumes progressively from coarse to fine.

title: Residual Multiplicative Filter Networks for Multiscale Reconstruction

abstract: Vision Transformers (ViTs) yield impressive performance across various vision tasks. However, heavy computation and memory footprint make them inaccessible for edge devices. Previous works apply importance criteria determined independently by each individual component to prune ViTs. Considering that heterogeneous components in ViTs play distinct roles, these approaches lead to suboptimal performance. In this paper, we introduce joint importance, which integrates essential structural-aware interactions between components for the first time, to perform collaborative pruning. Based on the theoretical analysis, we construct a Taylor-based approximation to evaluate the joint importance. This guides pruning toward a more balanced reduction across all components. To further reduce the algorithm complexity, we incorporate the interactions into the optimization function under some mild assumptions. Moreover, the proposed method can be seamlessly applied to various tasks including object detection. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our method. Notably, the proposed approach outperforms the existing state-of-the-art approaches on ImageNet, increasing accuracy by 0.7% over the DeiT-Base baseline while saving 50% FLOPs. abstract: It is widely believed that the success of deep networks lies in their ability to learn a meaningful representation of the features of the data. Yet, understanding when and how this feature learning improves performance remains a challenge: for example, it is beneficial for modern architectures trained to classify images, whereas it is detrimental for fully-connected networks trained for the same task on the same data. Here we propose an explanation for this puzzle, by showing that feature learning can perform worse than lazy training (via random feature kernel or the NTK) as the former can lead to a sparser neural representation. Although sparsity is known to be essential for learning anisotropic data, it is detrimental when the target function is constant or smooth along certain directions of input space. We illustrate this phenomenon in two settings: (i) regression of Gaussian random functions on the $d$-dimensional unit sphere and (ii) classification of benchmark datasets of images. For (i), we compute the scaling of the generalization error with number of training points, and show that methods that do not learn features generalize better, even when the dimension of the input space is large. For (ii), we show empirically that learning features can indeed lead to sparse and thereby less smooth representations of the image predictors. This fact is plausibly responsible for deteriorating the performance, which is known to be correlated with smoothness along diffeomorphisms.

paragraphs: The paper asks why learning features can help some image-classification architectures yet hurt fully connected networks on the same task. Its proposed explanation centers on sparsity. Feature learning can produce a sparser representation, and that representation can generalize worse than approaches based on random features or the neural tangent kernel.

The effect depends on the structure of the target function. Sparsity can be useful for anisotropic data, but the authors show that it can be harmful when the target stays constant or changes smoothly along some input directions. They investigate regression of Gaussian random functions on a multidimensional sphere and calculate how generalization error scales with the number of training examples. In that setting, methods without feature learning generalize better, even in high dimensions.

Experiments on image-classification benchmarks also show that feature learning can create sparse, less smooth predictors. The authors describe this as a plausible explanation for poorer performance, rather than a settled causal account of every case. The findings identify a specific reason representation learning may fail: the learned representation can sacrifice smoothness that the prediction task benefits from preserving.
summary.tldr: Feature learning can hurt generalization when the sparse representations it produces fail to preserve useful smoothness.

title: Learning sparse features can lead to overfitting in neural networks

abstract: Denoising diffusion models (DDMs) have shown promising results in 3D point cloud synthesis. To advance 3D DDMs and make them useful for digital artists, we require (i) high generation quality, (ii) flexibility for manipulation and applications such as conditional synthesis and shape interpolation, and (iii) the ability to output smooth surfaces or meshes. To this end, we introduce the hierarchical Latent Point Diffusion Model (LION) for 3D shape generation. LION is set up as a variational autoencoder (VAE) with a hierarchical latent space that combines a global shape latent representation with a point-structured latent space. For generation, we train two hierarchical DDMs in these latent spaces. The hierarchical VAE approach boosts performance compared to DDMs that operate on point clouds directly, while the point-structured latents are still ideally suited for DDM-based modeling. Experimentally, LION achieves state-of-the-art generation performance on multiple ShapeNet benchmarks. Furthermore, our VAE framework allows us to easily use LION for different relevant tasks: LION excels at multimodal shape denoising and voxel-conditioned synthesis, and it can be adapted for text- and image-driven 3D generation. We also demonstrate shape autoencoding and latent shape interpolation, and we augment LION with modern surface reconstruction techniques to generate smooth 3D meshes. We hope that LION provides a powerful tool for artists working with 3D shapes due to its high-quality generation, flexibility, and surface reconstruction. Project page and code: https://nv-tlabs.github.io/LION.

paragraphs: Generating useful 3D shapes requires more than producing plausible point clouds. The paper also targets flexible manipulation and the ability to produce smooth surfaces or meshes. LION addresses these needs through a hierarchical variational autoencoder whose latent representation combines a global description of a shape with a representation organized as points.

Two hierarchical diffusion models learn to generate within these latent spaces. The authors report that this arrangement improves performance over diffusion directly on point clouds, while retaining a point-structured representation suited to diffusion modeling. The autoencoder framework also supports encoding existing shapes and interpolating between their latent representations.

The authors also describe adaptation to text- and image-driven generation. Adding surface reconstruction techniques produces smooth meshes. Together, these capabilities connect shape generation with editing, conditioning, and surface output, addressing several distinct requirements of tools intended for artists working with 3D content.
summary.tldr: LION generates 3D shapes through hierarchical latent diffusion and supports conditioning, interpolation, denoising, and smooth mesh reconstruction.

title: LION: Latent Point Diffusion Models for 3D Shape Generation

abstract: We give uniform concentration inequality for random tensors acting on rank-1 Kronecker structured signals, which parallels a Gordon-type inequality for this class of tensor structured data. Two variants of the random embedding are considered, where the embedding dimension depends on explicit quantities characterizing the complexity of the signal. As applications of the tools developed herein, we illustrate with examples from signal recovery and optimization.
originalAbstract: We give uniform concentration inequality for random tensors acting on rank-1 Kronecker structured signals, which parallels a Gordon-type inequality for this class of tensor structured data. Two variants of the random embedding are considered, where the embedding dimension depends on explicit quantities characterizing the complexity of the signal. As applications of the tools developed herein, we illustrate with examples from signal recovery and optimization.

paragraphs: This paper studies random embeddings for signals with rank-one Kronecker structure. Such signals have a tensor organization built from component factors, and the analysis explicitly uses that structure. The question concerns near-isometric behavior: how a random embedding can preserve the geometric size of signals in the class being considered.

The main result is a uniform concentration inequality for random tensors acting on these structured signals. Uniformity makes the result concern the signal class collectively, rather than only a single selected signal. The authors describe the inequality as a counterpart to a Gordon-type inequality for this tensor-structured setting, connecting the analysis to an established kind of geometric probability bound.

The paper considers two variants of the random embedding. Their embedding dimensions depend on explicit quantities describing signal complexity, making that complexity central to the dimension requirements. Examples from signal recovery and optimization illustrate applications of the developed tools. The contribution is therefore a theoretical framework for structured embeddings, accompanied by examples showing where its guarantees can be used.
summary.tldr: Uniform concentration bounds connect random tensor embedding dimensions to the complexity of rank-one Kronecker-structured signals.

title: Near-Isometric Properties of Kronecker-Structured Random Tensor Embeddings

abstract: Multi-agent reinforcement learning has drawn increasing attention in practice, e.g., robotics and automatic driving, as it can explore optimal policies using samples generated by interacting with the environment. However, high reward uncertainty still remains a problem when we want to train a satisfactory model, because obtaining high-quality reward feedback is usually expensive and even infeasible. To handle this issue, previous methods mainly focus on passive reward correction. At the same time, recent active reward estimation methods have proven to be a recipe for reducing the effect of reward uncertainty. In this paper, we propose a novel Distributional Reward Estimation framework for effective Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (DRE-MARL). Our main idea is to design the multi-action-branch reward estimation and policy-weighted reward aggregation for stabilized training. Specifically, we design the multi-action-branch reward estimation to model reward distributions on all action branches. Then we utilize reward aggregation to obtain stable updating signals during training. Our intuition is that consideration of all possible consequences of actions could be useful for learning policies. The superiority of the DRE-MARL is demonstrated using benchmark multi-agent scenarios, compared with the SOTA baselines in terms of both effectiveness and robustness.

paragraphs: Multi-agent reinforcement learning depends on reward feedback to improve the decisions of interacting agents. Reliable feedback can be expensive or unavailable, leaving substantial uncertainty in the training signal. This paper addresses that problem with DRE-MARL, a framework that actively estimates reward distributions to support more effective and stable policy learning.

The method has two main components. Multi-action-branch reward estimation models reward distributions across all action branches, keeping track of possible outcomes associated with different choices. Policy-weighted aggregation then combines reward information into signals used to update the learner. The motivation is that considering the range of possible action consequences could help policy learning when observed rewards are uncertain.

These findings support the combination of distributional estimation and aggregation as a way to manage uncertain rewards. The reported gains concern those evaluated scenarios, while the broader contribution is a training framework built around richer reward estimates.
summary.tldr: DRE-MARL estimates reward distributions across action branches and aggregates them to improve multi-agent learning under reward uncertainty.

title: Distributional Reward Estimation for Effective Multi-agent Deep Reinforcement Learning

abstract: For a $d$-dimensional log-concave distribution $\pi(\theta) \propto e^{-f(\theta)}$ constrained to a convex body $K$, the problem of outputting samples from a distribution $\nu$ which is $\varepsilon$-close in infinity-distance $\sup_{\theta \in K} |\log \frac{\nu(\theta)}{\pi(\theta)}|$ to $\pi$ arises in differentially private optimization. While sampling within total-variation distance $\varepsilon$ of $\pi$ can be done by algorithms whose runtime depends polylogarithmically on $\frac{1}{\varepsilon}$, prior algorithms for sampling in $\varepsilon$ infinity distance have runtime bounds that depend polynomially on $\frac{1}{\varepsilon}$. We bridge this gap by presenting an algorithm that outputs a point $\varepsilon$-close to $\pi$ in infinity distance that requires at most $\mathrm{poly}(\log \frac{1}{\varepsilon}, d)$ calls to a membership oracle for $K$ and evaluation oracle for $f$, when $f$ is Lipschitz. Our approach departs from prior works that construct Markov chains on a $\frac{1}{\varepsilon^2}$-discretization of $K$ to achieve a sample with $\varepsilon$ infinity-distance error, and present a method to directly convert continuous samples from $K$ with total-variation bounds to samples with infinity bounds. This approach also allows us to obtain an improvement on the dimension $d$ in the running time for the problem of sampling from a log-concave distribution on polytopes $K$ with infinity distance $\varepsilon$, by plugging in TV-distance running time bounds for the Dikin Walk Markov chain.

paragraphs: Some differentially private optimization problems require sampling distributions that closely match a target at every point. This paper studies that requirement for log-concave distributions constrained to a convex body. Its infinity-distance criterion bounds the largest absolute log density ratio, imposing pointwise control beyond what a total-variation guarantee alone provides.

Previous infinity-distance sampling bounds depended polynomially on inverse error, whereas total-variation sampling could achieve polylogarithmic dependence. When the target's negative log density is Lipschitz, the proposed algorithm obtains infinity-distance error at most epsilon using a number of membership and function-evaluation oracle calls polynomial in dimension and log inverse error. This substantially improves the stated dependence on requested accuracy.

The method converts continuous samples with total-variation guarantees into samples with infinity-distance guarantees, departing from approaches based on fine discretizations of the domain. For convex bodies that are polytopes, combining this conversion with Dikin Walk bounds also improves dimension dependence. The contribution links a more accessible sampling guarantee to the stronger guarantee needed by the motivating applications.
summary.tldr: A continuous-sample conversion achieves infinity-distance guarantees with polylogarithmic inverse-error oracle complexity under the stated Lipschitz assumption.

title: Sampling from Log-Concave Distributions with Infinity-Distance Guarantees

abstract: We develop a variant of the Monteiro-Svaiter (MS) acceleration framework that removes the need to solve an expensive implicit equation at every iteration. Consequently, for any $p\ge 2$ we improve the complexity of convex optimization with Lipschitz $p$th derivative by a logarithmic factor, matching a lower bound. We also introduce an MS subproblem solver that requires no knowledge of problem parameters, and implement it as either a second- or first-order method by solving linear systems or applying MinRes, respectively. On logistic regression problems our method outperforms previous accelerated second-order methods, but under-performs Newton's method; simply iterating our first-order adaptive subproblem solver is competitive with L-BFGS.

paragraphs: Acceleration frameworks aim to reduce the work needed to solve optimization problems, but the steps they require can themselves be costly. This paper modifies Monteiro-Svaiter acceleration to remove an expensive implicit equation that otherwise must be solved at every iteration. The change directly targets overhead within the acceleration procedure.

For convex optimization with a Lipschitz pth derivative, for any p of at least two, the variant improves complexity by a logarithmic factor and matches a lower bound. The authors also introduce an adaptive subproblem solver that needs no knowledge of problem parameters. It can be implemented as a second-order method using linear-system solves or as a first-order method using MinRes.

The practical comparisons are mixed in an informative way. On logistic regression problems, the method outperforms previous accelerated second-order methods but falls behind Newton's method. Simply repeating the adaptive first-order subproblem solver is competitive with L-BFGS. Thus, the paper combines an optimal theoretical complexity result with empirical evidence that depends on which competing method is considered.
summary.tldr: A revised Monteiro-Svaiter framework removes costly implicit solves, matches a convex-optimization lower bound, and introduces a parameter-adaptive subproblem solver.

title: Optimal and Adaptive Monteiro-Svaiter Acceleration

abstract: The NP-hard problem of optimizing a shallow ReLU network can be characterized as a combinatorial search over each training example’s activation pattern followed by a constrained convex problem given a fixed set of activation patterns. We explore the implications of this combinatorial aspect of ReLU optimization in this work. We show that it can be naturally modeled via a geometric and combinatoric object known as a zonotope with its vertex set isomorphic to the set of feasible activation patterns. This assists in analysis and provides a foundation for further research. We demonstrate its usefulness when we explore the sensitivity of the optimal loss to perturbations of the training data. Later we discuss methods of zonotope vertex selection and its relevance to optimization. Overparameterization assists in training by making a randomly chosen vertex more likely to contain a good solution. We then introduce a novel polynomial-time vertex selection procedure that provably picks a vertex containing the global optimum using only double the minimum number of parameters required to fit the data. We further introduce a local greedy search heuristic over zonotope vertices and demonstrate that it outperforms gradient descent on underparameterized problems.

paragraphs: Training a shallow ReLU network involves deciding which neurons activate on which training examples. The paper separates this difficult optimization problem into a combinatorial search over activation patterns and a constrained convex problem once those patterns are fixed. This makes the discrete choices inside network training explicit.

The authors represent feasible activation patterns using a geometric object called a zonotope. Its vertices correspond to the possible activation configurations, providing a way to analyze training through geometry. They use this connection to study how changes in the training data affect the best achievable loss and to examine strategies for selecting promising vertices.

This perspective also explains a benefit of overparameterization: a randomly selected vertex becomes more likely to contain a good solution. The paper introduces a polynomial-time vertex-selection procedure that provably includes the global optimum when using twice the minimum parameter count needed to fit the data. It also reports that a greedy local search over vertices outperforms gradient descent on underparameterized problems.
summary.tldr: A geometric view of ReLU activation patterns yields new optimization guarantees and a greedy search method that improves training on underparameterized problems.

title: A Combinatorial Perspective on the Optimization of Shallow ReLU Networks

abstract: Continual Learning (CL) sequentially learns new tasks like human beings, with the goal to achieve better Stability (S, remembering past tasks) and Plasticity (P, adapting to new tasks). Due to the fact that past training data is not available, it is valuable to explore the influence difference on S and P among training examples, which may improve the learning pattern towards better SP. Inspired by Influence Function (IF), we first study example influence via adding perturbation to example weight and computing the influence derivation. To avoid the storage and calculation burden of Hessian inverse in neural networks, we propose a simple yet effective MetaSP algorithm to simulate the two key steps in the computation of IF and obtain the S- and P-aware example influence. Moreover, we propose to fuse two kinds of example influence by solving a dual-objective optimization problem, and obtain a fused influence towards SP Pareto optimality. The fused influence can be used to control the update of model and optimize the storage of rehearsal. Empirical results show that our algorithm significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods on both task- and class-incremental benchmark CL datasets.

paragraphs: Continual learning must balance remembering earlier tasks with adapting to new ones. The paper calls these goals stability and plasticity. When past training data is no longer available in full, deciding how much influence individual examples should have becomes especially valuable: an example's contribution to new learning may differ from its contribution to retaining earlier knowledge.

The authors study these contributions by slightly changing an example's weight and examining the resulting influence. Conventional influence-function calculations involve an inverse Hessian, which is burdensome for neural networks. Their MetaSP algorithm simulates two key steps of that calculation to estimate influence separately for stability and plasticity without that storage and computation burden.

MetaSP then combines the two influence estimates through a dual-objective optimization aimed toward Pareto optimality, balancing the competing goals. The combined influence guides both model updates and the selection of examples stored for rehearsal. Experiments report significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods on task-incremental and class-incremental benchmarks, supporting example influence as a useful control signal for continual learning.
summary.tldr: MetaSP estimates how examples affect remembering and adaptation, then combines those estimates to guide continual learning and rehearsal.

title: Exploring Example Influence in Continual Learning

abstract: In this work, we propose a universal and adaptive second-order method for minimization of second-order smooth, convex functions. Precisely, our algorithm achieves $O(\sigma / \sqrt{T})$ when the oracle feedback is stochastic with variance $\sigma$, and obtains the improved $O( 1 / T^3)$ convergence with deterministic oracles. Our method achieves this rate interpolation without knowing the nature of the oracle a priori, which was enabled by a parameter-free step-size that is oblivious to the knowledge of smoothness modulus, variance bounds and the diameter of the constrained set. To our knowledge, this is the first universal algorithm that achieves the aforementioned global guarantees within second-order convex optimization literature.
originalAbstract: In this work, we propose a universal and adaptive second-order method for minimization of second-order smooth, convex functions. Precisely, our algorithm achieves $O(\sigma / \sqrt{T})$ when the oracle feedback is stochastic with variance $\sigma$, and obtains the improved $O( 1 / T^3)$ convergence with deterministic oracles. Our method achieves this rate interpolation without knowing the nature of the oracle a priori, which was enabled by a parameter-free step-size that is oblivious to the knowledge of smoothness modulus, variance bounds and the diameter of the constrained set. To our knowledge, this is the first universal algorithm that achieves the aforementioned global guarantees within second-order convex optimization literature.

paragraphs: Optimization methods may receive exact information about an objective or noisy information from a stochastic source. Extra-Newton is designed to adapt between these situations when minimizing convex functions with second-order smoothness. As a second-order method, it uses information about curvature, and its central contribution is a convergence guarantee that changes with the feedback without requiring its nature in advance.

For stochastic oracle feedback with variance denoted by sigma in the abstract, the algorithm achieves a rate of O(sigma / sqrt(T)). With a deterministic oracle, it achieves the faster rate O(1 / T^3). Here T represents the number of optimization steps. The same method interpolates between these guarantees rather than requiring the user to select a separate algorithm for each setting.

The enabling mechanism is a parameter-free step size that does not require the smoothness modulus, variance bounds, or diameter of the constrained set. This removes several pieces of advance information from algorithm tuning. Within second-order convex optimization, the authors identify the combination of these global guarantees and automatic adaptation as the first such result to their knowledge.
summary.tldr: Extra-Newton automatically adapts its convergence rate to stochastic or deterministic feedback without prior knowledge of key optimization parameters.

title: Extra-Newton: A First Approach to Noise-Adaptive Accelerated Second-Order Methods

abstract: The generation of 3D molecules requires simultaneously deciding the categorical features (atom types) and continuous features (atom coordinates). Deep generative models, especially Diffusion Models (DMs), have demonstrated effectiveness in generating feature-rich geometries. However, existing DMs typically suffer from unstable probability dynamics with inefficient sampling speed. In this paper, we introduce geometric flow matching, which enjoys the advantages of both equivariant modeling and stabilized probability dynamics. More specifically, we propose a hybrid probability path where the coordinates probability path is regularized by an equivariant optimal transport, and the information between different modalities is aligned. Experimentally, the proposed method could consistently achieve better performance on multiple molecule generation benchmarks with 4.75$\times$ speed up of sampling on average.

paragraphs: Generating a three-dimensional molecule requires deciding both which atom types to use and where to place them. These are different kinds of variables: atom identities are categorical, while coordinates vary continuously. The paper addresses their joint generation, focusing on unstable probability dynamics and slow sampling identified in existing diffusion approaches.

The proposed geometric flow matching method combines equivariant modeling with a hybrid probability path. Its coordinate path is regularized using equivariant optimal transport, while information across the categorical and continuous parts is aligned. This design connects the evolution of atom identities and positions while preserving the geometric structure represented by the model's equivariance.

Experiments report consistently better performance across multiple molecule-generation benchmarks, together with an average sampling speedup of 4.75 times. The result matters because it couples improved generation performance with reduced sampling time in the evaluated settings. The contribution is therefore both a geometric formulation of the generation process and empirical evidence that coordinating the two feature types can make that process more effective and efficient.
summary.tldr: Geometric flow matching jointly generates atom types and coordinates, improving benchmark performance with a reported average 4.75-fold sampling speedup.

title: Equivariant Flow Matching with Hybrid Probability Transport for 3D Molecule Generation

abstract: Forecasting human motion of multiple persons is very challenging. It requires to model the interactions between humans and the interactions with objects and the environment. For example, a person might want to make a coffee, but if the coffee machine is already occupied the person will haveto wait. These complex relations between scene geometry and persons ariseconstantly in our daily lives, and models that wish to accurately forecasthuman behavior will have to take them into consideration. To facilitate research in this direction, we propose Humans in Kitchens, alarge-scale multi-person human motion dataset with annotated 3D human poses, scene geometry and activities per person and frame.Our dataset consists of over 7.3h recorded data of up to 16 persons at the same time in four kitchen scenes, with more than 4M annotated human poses, represented by a parametric 3D body model. In addition, dynamic scene geometry and objects like chair or cupboard are annotated per frame. As first benchmarks, we propose two protocols for short-term and long-term human motion forecasting.

It includes over four million annotated human poses represented through a parametric three-dimensional body model. Scene geometry and each person’s activities are annotated per frame, alongside changing scene geometry and objects such as chairs and cupboards.

These annotations connect movement to the surrounding people and physical environment, providing information needed to investigate context-aware forecasting. The paper also introduces two evaluation protocols covering short-term and long-term prediction. Its contribution is therefore both a detailed record of multiperson activity and a framework for evaluating forecasts over different time horizons, rather than a reported improvement from a particular forecasting model.
summary.tldr: Humans in Kitchens supplies detailed multiperson motion and scene annotations, plus protocols for short- and long-term forecasting.

title: Humans in Kitchens: A Dataset for Multi-Person Human Motion Forecasting with Scene Context

abstract: Generative models capable of precisely capturing nuanced clinical features in medical images hold great promise for facilitating clinical data sharing, enhancing rare disease datasets, and efficiently synthesizing (annotated) medical images at scale. Despite their potential, assessing the quality of synthetic medical images remains a challenge. While modern generative models can synthesize visually-realistic medical images, the clinical plausibility of these images may be called into question. Domain-agnostic scores, such as FID score, precision, and recall, cannot incorporate clinical knowledge and are, therefore, not suitable for assessing clinical sensibility. Additionally, there are numerous unpredictable ways in which generative models may fail to synthesize clinically plausible images, making it challenging to anticipate potential failures and design automated scores for their detection. To address these challenges, this paper introduces a pathologist-in-the-loop framework for generating clinically-plausible synthetic medical images. Our framework comprises three steps: (1) pretraining a conditional diffusion model to generate medical images conditioned on a clinical concept, (2) expert pathologist evaluation of the generated images to assess whether they satisfy clinical desiderata, and (3) training a reward model that predicts human feedback on new samples, which we use to incorporate expert knowledge into the finetuning objective of the diffusion model. Our results show that human feedback significantly improves the quality of synthetic images in terms of fidelity, diversity, utility in downstream applications, and plausibility as evaluated by experts. We also demonstrate that human feedback can teach the model new clinical concepts not annotated in the original training data. Our results demonstrate the value of incorporating human feedback in clinical applications where generative models may struggle to capture extensive domain knowledge from raw data alone.

title: Aligning Synthetic Medical Images with Clinical Knowledge using Human Feedback

abstract: The replicability crisis in the social, behavioral, and data sciences has led to the formulation of algorithm frameworks for replicability --- i.e., a requirement that an algorithm produce identical outputs (with high probability) when run on two different samples from the same underlying distribution. While still in its infancy, provably replicable algorithms have been developed for many fundamental tasks in machine learning and statistics, including statistical query learning, the heavy hitters problem, and distribution testing. In this work we initiate the study of replicable reinforcement learning, providing a provably replicable algorithm for parallel value iteration, and a provably replicable version of R-Max in the episodic setting. These are the first formal replicability results for control problems, which present different challenges for replication than batch learning settings.

paragraphs: Replicability asks whether an algorithm gives the same output when it receives different samples from the same underlying distribution. The formal requirement studied here is that the outputs be identical with high probability. This is a stronger target than obtaining similar performance across runs, because it concerns agreement in the algorithm's actual result.

The paper brings that requirement into reinforcement learning, where an algorithm learns to make decisions in a control problem. The authors provide a provably replicable algorithm for parallel value iteration and a provably replicable version of R-Max in the episodic setting. These two constructions establish formal replicability results for specific reinforcement-learning procedures.

The contribution extends an emerging line of work on replicable algorithms beyond statistical and batch-learning tasks into control. The abstract emphasizes that control creates different replication challenges from learning on a fixed batch of examples. By supplying proofs for these reinforcement-learning algorithms, the paper establishes that high-probability output agreement can be made an explicit algorithmic guarantee in the studied control settings.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes formal replicability guarantees for parallel value iteration and episodic R-Max.

title: Replicable Reinforcement Learning

abstract: We study multi-product inventory control problems where a manager makes sequential replenishment decisions based on partial historical information in order to minimize its cumulative losses. Our motivation is to consider general demands, losses and dynamics to go beyond standard models which usually rely on newsvendor-type losses, fixed dynamics, and unrealistic i.i.d. demand assumptions. We propose MaxCOSD, an online algorithm that has provable guarantees even for problems with non-i.i.d. demands and stateful dynamics, including for instance perishability. We consider what we call non-degeneracy assumptions on the demand process, and argue that they are necessary to allow learning.

We propose MaxCOSD, an online algorithm that has provable guarantees even for problems with non-i.i.d. demands and stateful dynamics, including for instance perishability. paragraphs: The paper studies how to replenish multiple products over time when a manager has only partial historical information. The objective is to minimize cumulative losses across the sequence of decisions. Its motivation is to move beyond inventory models built around a standard loss form, fixed dynamics, and independent demands drawn from an unchanged distribution.

The authors propose MaxCOSD, an online algorithm with provable guarantees for more general inventory problems. The covered settings include non-independent or changing demand and stateful dynamics, where the inventory situation carries consequences forward. Perishability is one stated example. Through online convex optimization, the work brings these sequential features into the learning problem.

The guarantees are accompanied by what the authors call non-degeneracy assumptions on the demand process. They argue that such assumptions are necessary to make learning possible. The contribution therefore broadens the demand and inventory behavior that can be handled while retaining explicit conditions on the environment. Its central finding is that useful guarantees can extend beyond the usual independent-demand formulation.
summary.tldr: MaxCOSD provides online inventory-control guarantees beyond independent-demand models, including stateful dynamics, under demand non-degeneracy assumptions.

title: Online Inventory Problems: Beyond the i.i.d. Setting with Online Convex Optimization

abstract: Diffusion models (DMs) have recently been introduced in image deblurring and exhibited promising performance, particularly in terms of details reconstruction. However, the diffusion model requires a large number of inference iterations to recover the clean image from pure Gaussian noise, which consumes massive computational resources. Moreover, the distribution synthesized by the diffusion model is often misaligned with the target results, leading to restrictions in distortion-based metrics. To address the above issues, we propose the Hierarchical Integration Diffusion Model (HI-Diff), for realistic image deblurring. Specifically, we perform the DM in a highly compacted latent space to generate the prior feature for the deblurring process. The deblurring process is implemented by a regression-based method to obtain better distortion accuracy. Meanwhile, the highly compact latent space ensures the efficiency of the DM. Furthermore, we design the hierarchical integration module to fuse the prior into the regression-based model from multiple scales, enabling better generalization in complex blurry scenarios. Comprehensive experiments on synthetic and real-world blur datasets demonstrate that our HI-Diff outperforms state-of-the-art methods. Code and trained models are available at https://github.com/zhengchen1999/HI-Diff.

paragraphs: Diffusion models can reconstruct image details during deblurring, but generating a clean image through many denoising iterations is computationally expensive. Their generated results can also differ from the target in ways that hurt distortion-based measurements. HI-Diff addresses both issues by assigning diffusion and direct image restoration different roles.

The diffusion model operates in a highly compressed latent space and generates a prior feature to guide restoration. A regression-based model performs the actual deblurring, supporting better distortion accuracy. Working in the compact latent space makes the diffusion component efficient, while its output still contributes information to the reconstruction process.

A hierarchical integration module inserts this prior into the regression model at multiple scales. The design aims to improve generalization across complicated blur conditions by making the generated information available throughout the restoration hierarchy. Experiments on synthetic and real-world blur datasets report performance above state-of-the-art methods. The contribution is a combined design that uses diffusion-derived guidance alongside regression-based reconstruction.
summary.tldr: HI-Diff uses compact latent diffusion to guide a multiscale regression model for efficient, accurate image deblurring.

title: Hierarchical Integration Diffusion Model for Realistic Image Deblurring

abstract: Bayesian neural networks often approximate the weight-posterior with a Gaussian distribution. However, practical posteriors are often, even locally, highly non-Gaussian, and empirical performance deteriorates. We propose a simple parametric approximate posterior that adapts to the shape of the true posterior through a Riemannian metric that is determined by the log-posterior gradient. We develop a Riemannian Laplace approximation where samples naturally fall into weight-regions with low negative log-posterior. We show that these samples can be drawn by solving a system of ordinary differential equations, which can be done efficiently by leveraging the structure of the Riemannian metric and automatic differentiation. Empirically, we demonstrate that our approach consistently improves over the conventional Laplace approximation across tasks. We further show that, unlike the conventional Laplace approximation, our method is not overly sensitive to the choice of prior, which alleviates a practical pitfall of current approaches.

paragraphs: Bayesian neural networks often use a Gaussian distribution to approximate uncertainty over their weights. Actual weight posteriors can depart strongly from a Gaussian shape even locally, weakening empirical performance. This paper proposes an approximate posterior that adapts its shape using a Riemannian metric determined by the gradient of the log posterior.

The resulting Riemannian Laplace approximation directs samples toward weight regions with low negative log posterior. Sampling is implemented by solving a system of ordinary differential equations. The authors use the structure of the metric together with automatic differentiation to make this computation efficient. The approach therefore changes the geometry used by the approximation while retaining a concrete procedure for drawing samples.

Across the evaluated tasks, the method consistently improves on conventional Laplace approximation. The authors also find that it is not overly sensitive to the choice of prior, addressing a practical weakness of the conventional approach. These empirical findings support adapting posterior geometry as a way to improve Bayesian neural-network approximation.
summary.tldr: A Riemannian Laplace approximation adapts to posterior shape and empirically improves Bayesian neural-network inference with less prior sensitivity.

title: Riemannian Laplace approximations for Bayesian neural networks

abstract: Real-world datasets are often highly class-imbalanced, which can adversely impact the performance of deep learning models. The majority of research on training neural networks under class imbalance has focused on specialized loss functions and sampling techniques. Notably, we demonstrate that simply tuning existing components of standard deep learning pipelines, such as the batch size, data augmentation, architecture size, pre-training, optimizer, and label smoothing, can achieve state-of-the-art performance without any specialized loss functions or samplers. We also provide key prescriptions and considerations for training under class imbalance, and an understanding of why imbalance methods succeed or fail.

Notably, we demonstrate that simply tuning existing components of standard deep learning pipelines, such as the batch size, data augmentation, architecture size, pre-training, optimizer, and label smoothing, can achieve state-of-the-art performance without any specialized loss functions or samplers. We also provide key prescriptions and considerations for training under class imbalance, and an understanding of why imbalance methods succeed or fail.

paragraphs: Class imbalance occurs when some categories have far more training examples than others, and it can hurt neural network performance. Much work addresses this through specialized loss functions or sampling rules. This paper investigates how far ordinary training components can go when they are tuned for the imbalanced setting.

The study considers batch size, data augmentation, network size, pretraining, optimizer choice, and label smoothing. The authors demonstrate that tuning these existing components can achieve state-of-the-art performance without specialized losses or samplers. The result highlights the importance of the overall training configuration when judging what is needed to learn effectively from unequal class frequencies.

The paper also offers training prescriptions and considerations, together with an account of why methods for imbalance succeed or fail. Its practical contribution is evidence that strong performance can come from configuring familiar pipeline elements appropriately. This supports treating those choices as a substantial part of the imbalance problem, while the stated result is that they can achieve leading performance, rather than that every imbalanced dataset needs the same configuration.
summary.tldr: Tuning standard training components can achieve state-of-the-art performance under class imbalance without specialized losses or samplers.

title: Simplifying Neural Network Training Under Class Imbalance

abstract: Visual object tracking (VOT) is one of the most fundamental tasks in computer vision community. State-of-the-art VOT trackers extract positive and negative examples that are used to guide the tracker to distinguish the object from the background. In this paper, we show that this characteristic can be exploited to introduce new threats and hence propose a simple yet effective poison-only backdoor attack. To be specific, we poison a small part of the training data by attaching a predefined trigger pattern to the background region of each video frame, so that the trigger appears almost exclusively in the extracted negative examples. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work that reveals the threat of poison-only backdoor attack on VOT trackers. We experimentally show that our backdoor attack can significantly degrade the performance of both two-stream Siamese and one-stream Transformer trackers on the poisoned data while gaining comparable performance with the benign trackers on the clean data.

paragraphs: Visual object trackers distinguish a target object from its surrounding background as video progresses. The paper examines a vulnerability in trackers that extract positive and negative examples to learn that distinction. Its central finding is that poisoning a small portion of training data can introduce a backdoor through this example-selection process.

BadTrack places a predefined trigger in the background regions of training video frames. Because of where it appears, the trigger occurs almost exclusively among extracted negative examples. The attack therefore exploits the relationship between spatial placement and the training examples produced by the tracker. The proposed threat requires poisoning data rather than modifying the tracker through another intervention.

Experiments cover both two-stream Siamese trackers and one-stream Transformer trackers. The attack substantially reduces performance on poisoned data while leaving performance on clean data comparable to benign trackers. That combination matters because clean-data quality alone would not reveal the reported degradation. The authors present this as, to their knowledge, the first demonstration of a poison-only backdoor threat against visual object tracking.
summary.tldr: BadTrack poisons a small amount of tracking data to create a backdoor that degrades poisoned-data performance while preserving clean-data performance.

title: BadTrack: A Poison-Only Backdoor Attack on Visual Object Tracking

abstract: We present new information-theoretic generalization guarantees through the a novel construction of the "neighboring-hypothesis" matrix and a new family of stability notions termed sample-conditioned hypothesis (SCH) stability. Our approach yields sharper bounds that improve upon previous information-theoretic bounds in various learning scenarios. Notably, these bounds address the limitations of existing information-theoretic bounds in the context of stochastic convex optimization (SCO) problems, as explored in the recent work by Haghifam et al. (2023).
originalAbstract: We present new information-theoretic generalization guarantees through the a novel construction of the "neighboring-hypothesis" matrix and a new family of stability notions termed sample-conditioned hypothesis (SCH) stability. Our approach yields sharper bounds that improve upon previous information-theoretic bounds in various learning scenarios. Notably, these bounds address the limitations of existing information-theoretic bounds in the context of stochastic convex optimization (SCO) problems, as explored in the recent work by Haghifam et al. (2023).

paragraphs: Generalization guarantees describe how learning from a sample relates to performance beyond that sample. Information-theoretic bounds provide one way to formalize this relationship, but their usefulness depends on how tightly they capture the learning situation. This paper develops a new framework for obtaining sharper guarantees in several settings.

The construction centers on a neighboring-hypothesis matrix and a family of notions called sample-conditioned hypothesis stability. These provide a new way to organize the hypotheses considered in the analysis and express stability with reference to the sample. Together, they form the basis for the paper’s improved information-theoretic bounds.

The authors report improvements over previous bounds in various learning scenarios, with particular attention to stochastic convex optimization. In that setting, their guarantees address limitations identified in earlier information-theoretic analyses. The stated advance is therefore about the strength of the mathematical account of generalization: a more informative stability formulation leads to tighter guarantees in the scenarios analyzed. The abstract does not claim a universal improvement across every learning problem.
summary.tldr: A neighboring-hypothesis matrix and sample-conditioned stability yield sharper information-theoretic generalization bounds, including for stochastic convex optimization.

title: Sample-Conditioned Hypothesis Stability Sharpens Information-Theoretic Generalization Bounds

abstract: In recent years, prompt tuning has sparked a research surge in adapting pre-trained models. Unlike the unified pre-training strategy employed in the language field, the graph field exhibits diverse pre-training strategies, posing challenges in designing appropriate prompt-based tuning methods for graph neural networks. While some pioneering work has devised specialized prompting functions for models that employ edge prediction as their pre-training tasks, these methods are limited to specific pre-trained GNN models and lack broader applicability. In this paper, we introduce a universal prompt-based tuning method called Graph Prompt Feature (GPF) for pre-trained GNN models under any pre-training strategy. GPF operates on the input graph's feature space and can theoretically achieve an equivalent effect to any form of prompting function. Consequently, we no longer need to illustrate the prompting function corresponding to each pre-training strategy explicitly. Instead, we employ GPF to obtain the prompted graph for the downstream task in an adaptive manner. We provide rigorous derivations to demonstrate the universality of GPF and make guarantee of its effectiveness. The experimental results under various pre-training strategies indicate that our method performs better than fine-tuning, with an average improvement of about 1.4% in full-shot scenarios and about 3.2% in few-shot scenarios. Moreover, our method significantly outperforms existing specialized prompt-based tuning methods when applied to models utilizing the pre-training strategy they specialize in. These numerous advantages position our method as a compelling alternative to fine-tuning for downstream adaptations.

Existing specialized approaches can depend on a particular pretraining task, such as edge prediction. Graph Prompt Feature, or GPF, addresses this fragmentation by applying prompts in the input graph’s feature space.

These results support a common feature-space mechanism as a useful alternative to adapting each pretrained graph model through a separately designed prompt.
summary.tldr: GPF prompts graph input features to provide a theoretically universal adaptation method with reported gains over fine-tuning and specialized prompts.

title: Universal Prompt Tuning for Graph Neural Networks

abstract: Machine learning approaches often require training and evaluation datasets with a clear separation between positive and negative examples. This requirement overly simplifies the natural subjectivity present in many tasks, and obscures the inherent diversity in human perceptions and opinions about many content items. Preserving the variance in content and diversity in human perceptions in datasets is often quite expensive and laborious. This is especially troubling when building safety datasets for conversational AI systems, as safety is socio-culturally situated in this context. To demonstrate this crucial aspect of conversational AI safety, and to facilitate in-depth model performance analyses, we introduce the DICES (Diversity In Conversational AI Evaluation for Safety) dataset that contains fine-grained demographics information about raters, high replication of ratings per item to ensure statistical power for analyses, and encodes rater votes as distributions across different demographics to allow for in-depth explorations of different aggregation strategies. The DICES dataset enables the observation and measurement of variance, ambiguity, and diversity in the context of safety for conversational AI. We further describe a set of metrics that show how rater diversity influences safety perception across different geographic regions, ethnicity groups, age groups, and genders. The goal of the DICES dataset is to be used as a shared resource and benchmark that respects diverse perspectives during safety evaluation of conversational AI systems.

paragraphs: People can disagree about whether a conversational AI response is safe, and those judgments can depend on social and cultural context. Reducing every example to a single positive or negative label can hide that disagreement. DICES is a dataset designed to make differences in safety perception visible and measurable.

The dataset combines detailed demographic information about raters with many ratings for each item. It represents votes as distributions across demographic groups, preserving how judgments vary instead of retaining only an aggregate verdict. The repeated ratings provide statistical support for analysis, while the distributions let researchers examine different ways of combining individual opinions.

The authors also describe metrics showing how rater diversity affects safety judgments across geographic regions, ethnicities, ages, and genders. This makes DICES useful for examining ambiguity and differences that a single overall score can obscure. Its contribution is a shared evaluation resource that supports analysis of multiple perspectives, helping researchers assess conversational AI safety while retaining the diversity of the people making those assessments.
summary.tldr: DICES preserves demographic variation and disagreement in human ratings so conversational AI safety can be evaluated across diverse perspectives.

title: DICES Dataset: Diversity in Conversational AI Evaluation for Safety

abstract: Neural radiance fields (NeRFs) are able to synthesize realistic novel views from multi-view images captured from distinct positions and perspectives. In NeRF's rendering pipeline, neural networks are used to represent a scene independently or transform queried learnable feature vector of a point to the expected color or density. With the aid of geometry guides either in the form of occupancy grids or proposal networks, the number of color neural network evaluations can be reduced from hundreds to dozens in the standard volume rendering framework. However, many evaluations of the color neural network are still a bottleneck for fast NeRF reconstruction. This paper revisits volume feature rendering (VFR) for the purpose of fast NeRF reconstruction. The VFR integrates the queried feature vectors of a ray into one feature vector, which is then transformed to the final pixel color by a color neural network. This fundamental change to the standard volume rendering framework requires only one single color neural network evaluation to render a pixel, which substantially lowers the high computational complexity of the rendering framework attributed to a large number of color neural network evaluations. Consequently, we can use a comparably larger color neural network to achieve a better rendering quality while maintaining the same training and rendering time costs. This approach achieves the state-of-the-art rendering quality on both synthetic and real-world datasets while requiring less training time compared with existing methods.

abstract: Bases have become an integral part of modern deep learning-based models for time series forecasting due to their ability to act as feature extractors or future references. To be effective, a basis must be tailored to the specific set of time series data and exhibit distinct correlation with each time series within the set. However, current state-of-the-art methods are limited in their ability to satisfy both of these requirements simultaneously. To address this challenge, we propose BasisFormer, an end-to-end time series forecasting architecture that leverages learnable and interpretable bases. This architecture comprises three components: First, we acquire bases through adaptive self-supervised learning, which treats the historical and future sections of the time series as two distinct views and employs contrastive learning. Next, we design a Coef module that calculates the similarity coefficients between the time series and bases in the historical view via bidirectional cross-attention. Finally, we present a Forecast module that selects and consolidates the bases in the future view based on the similarity coefficients, resulting in accurate future predictions. Through extensive experiments on six datasets, we demonstrate that BasisFormer outperforms previous state-of-the-art methods by 11.04% and 15.78% respectively for univariate and multivariate forecasting tasks. Code isavailable at: https://github.com/nzl5116190/Basisformer.

paragraphs: BasisFormer forecasts time series using learned bases: patterns that help represent observations and provide references for future behavior. The paper argues that useful bases must both fit the dataset and have distinct relationships with individual series. Its architecture learns these patterns and how to combine them within one forecasting system.

The method first learns bases through a self-supervised contrastive procedure that treats historical and future sections as two views. A Coef module then uses bidirectional cross-attention to measure similarity between a series and the historical parts of the bases. A Forecast module uses those coefficients to select and combine the future parts, turning relationships found in the observed history into predictions.

Experiments on six datasets report improvements over previous state-of-the-art methods of 11.04% for univariate forecasting and 15.78% for multivariate forecasting. The approach matters because its learned bases connect historical matching with future construction. That structure also provides an interpretable organization for the forecast: predictions are assembled from bases according to their measured relevance.
summary.tldr: BasisFormer learns interpretable time-series bases and uses attention-derived similarities to combine their future patterns into forecasts.

title: BasisFormer: Attention-based Time Series Forecasting with Learnable and Interpretable Basis

abstract: Recent studies have shown promising results on utilizing large pre-trained image-language models for video question answering. While these image-language models can efficiently bootstrap the representation learning of video-language models, they typically concatenate uniformly sampled video frames as visual inputs without explicit language-aware, temporal modeling. When only a portion of a video input is relevant to the language query, such uniform frame sampling can often lead to missing important visual cues. Although humans often find a video moment to focus on and rewind the moment to answer questions, training a query-aware video moment localizer often requires expensive annotations and high computational costs. To address this issue, we propose Self-Chained Video Localization-Answering (SeViLA), a novel framework that leverages a single image-language model (BLIP- 2) to tackle both temporal keyframe localization and question answering on videos. SeViLA framework consists of two modules: Localizer and Answerer, where both are parameter-efficiently fine-tuned from BLIP-2. We propose two ways of chaining these modules for cascaded inference and self-refinement. First, in the forward chain, the Localizer finds multiple language-aware keyframes in a video, which the Answerer uses to predict the answer. Second, in the reverse chain, the Answerer generates keyframe pseudo-labels to refine the Localizer, alleviating the need for expensive video moment localization annotations. Our SeViLA framework outperforms several strong baselines/previous works on five challenging video question answering and event prediction benchmarks, and achieves the state-of-the-art in both fine-tuning (NExT-QA and STAR) and zero-shot (NExT-QA, STAR, How2QA, and VLEP) settings. We show a comprehensive analysis of our framework, including the impact of Localizer, comparisons of Localizer with other temporal localization models, pre-training/self-refinement of Localizer, and varying the number of keyframes.

title: Self-Chained Image-Language Model for Video Localization and Question Answering

abstract: Recent work on pruning large language models (LLMs) has shown that one can eliminate a large number of parameters without compromising performance, making pruning a promising strategy to reduce LLM model size. Existing LLM pruning strategies typically assign uniform pruning ratios across layers, limiting overall pruning ability; and recent work on layerwise pruning of LLMs is often based on heuristics that can easily lead to suboptimal performance. In this paper, we leverage Heavy-Tailed Self-Regularization (HT-SR) Theory, in particular the shape of empirical spectral densities (ESDs) of weight matrices, to design improved layerwise pruning ratios for LLMs. Our analysis reveals a wide variability in how well-trained, and thus relatedly how prunable, different layers of an LLM are. Based on this, we propose AlphaPruning, which uses shape metrics to allocate layerwise sparsity ratios in a more theoretically-principled manner. AlphaPruning can be used in conjunction with multiple existing LLM pruning methods. Our empirical results show that AlphaPruning prunes LLaMA-7B to 80% sparsity while maintaining reasonable perplexity, marking a first in the literature on LLMs.

paragraphs: Pruning reduces a language model's size by removing parameters. A central decision is how much to remove from each layer. Assigning every layer the same pruning ratio overlooks differences between layers, while heuristic allocations can produce suboptimal results. AlphaPruning addresses this allocation problem using information contained in the model's weight matrices.

The method draws on Heavy-Tailed Self-Regularization theory and examines the shapes of empirical spectral densities of those matrices. The authors' analysis finds substantial variation in how well different layers are trained and, relatedly, how amenable they are to pruning. AlphaPruning uses these shape measurements to assign different sparsity ratios across layers. It can be combined with multiple existing pruning methods.

In the reported experiments, AlphaPruning brings LLaMA-7B to 80% sparsity while retaining what the authors describe as reasonable perplexity. That result supports the value of distributing pruning unevenly according to layer properties. The claim concerns maintaining a useful language-modeling measure at high sparsity; it does not state that removing this many parameters preserves every aspect of model performance.
summary.tldr: AlphaPruning uses weight-matrix spectral shapes to allocate pruning across layers, reaching 80% sparsity in LLaMA-7B with reasonable perplexity.

title: AlphaPruning: Using Heavy-Tailed Self Regularization Theory for Improved Layer-wise Pruning of Large Language Models

abstract: The benefit of transformers in large-scale 3D point cloud perception tasks, such as 3D object detection, is limited by their quadratic computation cost when modeling long-range relationships. In contrast, linear RNNs have low computational complexity and are suitable for long-range modeling. Toward this goal, we propose a simple and effective window-based framework built on Linear group RNN (i.e., perform linear RNN for grouped features) for accurate 3D object detection, called LION. The key property is to allow sufficient feature interaction in a much larger group than transformer-based methods. However, effectively applying linear group RNN to 3D object detection in highly sparse point clouds is not trivial due to its limitation in handling spatial modeling. To tackle this problem, we simply introduce a 3D spatial feature descriptor and integrate it into the linear group RNN operators to enhance their spatial features rather than blindly increasing the number of scanning orders for voxel features. To further address the challenge in highly sparse point clouds, we propose a 3D voxel generation strategy to densify foreground features thanks to linear group RNN as a natural property of auto-regressive models. Extensive experiments verify the effectiveness of the proposed components and the generalization of our LION on different linear group RNN operators including Mamba, RWKV, and RetNet. Furthermore, it is worth mentioning that our LION-Mamba achieves state-of-the-art on Waymo, nuScenes, Argoverse V2, and ONCE datasets. Last but not least, our method supports kinds of advanced linear RNN operators (e.g., RetNet, RWKV, Mamba, xLSTM and TTT) on small but popular KITTI dataset for a quick experience with our linear RNN-based framework.

paragraphs: LION applies linear recurrent neural networks to 3D object detection in point clouds. Its motivation is the quadratic computation associated with transformer-based long-range interactions. By running linear RNNs over grouped features within a window-based framework, LION allows feature interaction across much larger groups than the transformer-based methods discussed in the paper.
