paragraphs: Graph-based nearest-neighbor methods connect dataset items and search those connections for points close to a query. Popular systems use beam search to maintain promising candidates during exploration. This paper focuses on when that exploration should stop, replacing a commonly used beam-width-based stopping condition with one based on distances.

The resulting Adaptive Beam Search has a theoretical guarantee under a stated condition: the search graph must be navigable. When that condition holds, the method approximately solves the nearest-neighbor problem. This establishes a connection between a graph's navigability and the accuracy of search, giving the stopping rule a formal foundation.

The authors also test the rule on navigable graphs and on approximately navigable structures used in practice, including HNSW and Vamana. Across the evaluated recall levels, datasets, graph constructions, and requested neighbor counts, it outperforms standard beam search. The practical results extend beyond the exact theoretical setting, while the formal guarantee remains conditional on graph navigability.
summary.tldr: A distance-based stopping rule improves graph nearest-neighbor search empirically and guarantees approximate accuracy when the graph is navigable.

title: Distance Adaptive Beam Search for Provably Accurate Graph-Based Nearest Neighbor Search

abstract: Network pruning reduces computational requirements of large neural networks, with N:M sparsity—retaining only N out of every M consecutive weights—offering a compelling balance between compressed model quality and hardware acceleration. However, N:M sparsity only accelerates forward-pass computations, as N:M patterns are not preserved during matrix transposition, limiting efficiency during training where both passes are computationally intensive. While transposable N:M sparsity has been proposed to address this limitation, existing methods for finding transposable N:M sparse masks either fail to scale to large models or are restricted to M=4 which results in suboptimal compression-accuracy trade-off. We introduce an efficient solver for transposable N:M masks that scales to billion-parameter models. We formulate mask generation as optimal transport problems and solve through entropy regularization and Dykstra's algorithm, followed by a rounding procedure. Our tensor-based implementation exploits GPU parallelism, achieving up to 100× speedup with only 1-10\% error compared to existing methods. Our approach can be integrated with layer-wise N:M pruning frameworks including Wanda, SparseGPT and ALPS to produce transposable N:M sparse models with arbitrary N:M values. Experiments show that LLaMA3.2-8B with transposable 16:32 sparsity maintains performance close to its standard N:M counterpart and outperforms standard 2:4 sparse model, showing the practical value of our approach. Our code is available at https://github.com/mazumder-lab/TSENOR.

TSENOR addresses the construction of masks that satisfy the sparsity structure in both orientations and scale to billion-parameter models.

summary.tldr: TSENOR efficiently constructs transposable N:M pruning masks at billion-parameter scale, enabling flexible sparsity patterns with promising model-quality results.

title: TSENOR: Highly-Efficient Algorithm for Finding Transposable N:M Sparse Masks

abstract: We prove that, given a mean-field location-scale variational family, black-box variational inference (BBVI) with the reparametrization gradient converges at a rate that is nearly independent of explicit dimension dependence. Specifically, for a $d$-dimensional strongly log-concave and log-smooth target, the number of iterations for BBVI with a sub-Gaussian family to obtain a solution $\epsilon$-close to the global optimum has a dimension dependence of $\mathrm{O}(\log d)$. This is a significant improvement over the $\mathrm{O}(d)$ dependence of full-rank location-scale families. For heavy-tailed families, we prove a weaker $\mathrm{O}(d^{2/k})$ dependence, where $k$ is the number of finite moments of the family. Additionally, if the Hessian of the target log-density is constant, the complexity is free of any explicit dimension dependence. We also prove that our bound on the gradient variance, which is key to our result, cannot be improved using only spectral bounds on the Hessian of the target log-density.

paragraphs: Black-box variational inference fits an approximating probability distribution by optimizing its parameters. This paper studies how the required number of optimization iterations grows with dimension when using a mean-field location-scale family and the reparameterization gradient. Its central result concerns convergence to the global optimum of that optimization problem.

For a strongly log-concave, log-smooth target and a sub-Gaussian variational family, the explicit dimension dependence is O(log d). This improves on the O(d) dependence associated with full-rank location-scale families. For heavy-tailed families, the authors establish the weaker dependence O(d^(2/k)), where k counts the family's finite moments.

The result becomes stronger when the target log-density has a constant Hessian: the complexity then has no explicit dimension dependence. These are conditional mathematical guarantees, with the target's curvature and the family's tail behavior determining the applicable result. The proof relies on a gradient-variance bound, which the authors also show cannot be improved using only spectral bounds on that Hessian. This identifies both a favorable convergence regime and a limit of the available curvature information.
summary.tldr: Under stated curvature and distributional assumptions, mean-field BBVI has logarithmic or even no explicit dimension dependence in its iteration complexity.

title: Nearly Dimension-Independent Convergence of Mean-Field Black-Box Variational Inference

abstract: Advanced reasoning models with agentic capabilities (AI agents) are deployed to interact with humans and to solve sequential decision‑making problems under (often approximate) utility functions and internal models. When such problems have resource or failure constraints where action sequences may be forcibly terminated once resources are exhausted, agents face implicit trade‑offs that reshape their utility-driven (rational) behaviour. Additionally, since these agents are typically commissioned by a human principal to act on their behalf, asymmetries in constraint exposure can give rise to previously unanticipated misalignment between human objectives and agent incentives. We formalise this setting through a survival bandit framework, provide theoretical and empirical results that quantify the impact of survival‑driven preference shifts, identify conditions under which misalignment emerges and propose mechanisms to mitigate the emergence of risk-seeking or risk-averse behaviours. As a result, this work aims to increase understanding and interpretability of emergent behaviours of AI agents operating under such survival pressure, and offer guidelines for safely deploying such AI systems in critical resource‑limited environments.

paragraphs: An agent pursuing a utility function may change its behavior when running out of resources can terminate its action sequence. The possibility of termination introduces implicit trade-offs into otherwise rational decision-making. This paper studies how such pressure can shift an agent's preferences toward or away from risk, even when it is acting on behalf of a human.

The authors formalize the problem using a survival bandit framework. Their analysis focuses on how constraints affect sequential choices and how differences between the human's and agent's exposure to those constraints can create misalignment. The central issue is that pursuing utility under survival pressure can produce incentives that differ from the objectives of the person commissioning the agent.

The paper provides theoretical and empirical results quantifying these preference shifts, identifies conditions under which misalignment emerges, and proposes mechanisms to mitigate risk-seeking or risk-averse behavior. Its contribution is a framework for interpreting constraint-driven behavior and informing deployment in resource-limited environments. The stated results concern conditions for these effects, rather than asserting that all constrained agents become misaligned.
summary.tldr: A survival bandit framework explains how resource constraints can shift rational agents' risk preferences and create conditional misalignment with human objectives.

title: Emergent Risk Awareness in Rational Agents under Resource Constraints

abstract: Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) or drones, are increasingly used in search and rescue missions to detect human presence. Existing systems primarily leverage vision-based methods which are prone to fail under low-visibility or occlusion. Drone-based audio perception offers promise but suffers from extreme ego-noise that masks sounds indicating human presence. Existing datasets are either limited in diversity or synthetic, lacking real acoustic interactions, and there are no standardized setups for drone audition. To this end, we present DroneAudioset (The dataset is publicly available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/ahlab-drone-project/DroneAudioSet/ under the MIT license), a comprehensive drone audition dataset featuring 23.5 hours of annotated recordings, covering a wide range of signal-to-noise ratios (SNRs) from -57.2 dB to -2.5 dB, across various drone types, throttles, microphone configurations as well as environments. The dataset enables development and systematic evaluation of noise suppression and classification methods for human-presence detection under challenging conditions, while also informing practical design considerations for drone audition systems, such as microphone placement trade-offs, and development of drone noise-aware audio processing. This dataset is an important step towards enabling design and deployment of drone-audition systems.

paragraphs: DroneAudioset addresses a practical obstacle to using sound in drone-based search and rescue: the drone itself produces intense noise that can mask evidence of human presence. Audio could complement vision when visibility is poor or people are occluded, but developing useful systems requires recordings that capture the actual acoustic conditions around operating drones.

The dataset contains 23.5 hours of annotated recordings spanning different drone types, throttle settings, microphone configurations, and environments. Its signal-to-noise ratios range from −57.2 dB to −2.5 dB, covering challenging conditions in which the desired sound is weaker than the noise. This variation supports evaluation across a range of recording setups rather than a single fixed configuration.

The contribution is a resource for developing and systematically testing noise suppression and human-presence classification methods. It also supports investigation of practical design choices, including microphone placement and processing that accounts for drone noise. By providing real acoustic recordings with broad variation, the dataset advances the evidence base needed to design drone audition systems.
summary.tldr: DroneAudioset provides 23.5 hours of annotated audio for studying human-presence detection amid severe drone noise.

title: DroneAudioset: An Audio Dataset for Drone-based Search and Rescue

abstract: World models aim to capture the dynamics of the environment, enabling agents to predict and plan for future states. In most scenarios of interest, the dynamics are highly centered on interactions among objects within the environment. This motivates the development of world models that operate on object-centric rather than monolithic representations, with the goal of more effectively capturing environment dynamics and enhancing compositional generalization. However, the development of object-centric world models has largely been explored in environments with limited visual complexity (such as basic geometries). It remains underexplored whether such models can be effective in more challenging settings. In this paper, we fill this gap by introducing Dyn-O, an enhanced structured world model built upon object-centric representations. Compared to prior work in object-centric representations, Dyn-O improves in both learning representations and modeling dynamics. On the challenging Procgen games, we demonstrate that our method can learn object-centric world models directly from pixel observations, outperforming DreamerV3 in rollout prediction accuracy. Furthermore, by decoupling object centric features into dynamic-agnostic and dynamic-aware components, we enable finer-grained manipulation of these features and generate more diverse imagined trajectories. The code of Dyn-O can be found at: https://github.com/wangzizhao/dyn-O.

It remains underexplored whether such models can be effective in more challenging settings. In this paper, we fill this gap by introducing Dyn-O, an enhanced structured world model built upon object-centric representations. Compared to prior work in object-centric representations, Dyn-O improves in both learning representations and modeling dynamics. On the challenging Procgen games, we demonstrate that our method can learn object-centric world models directly from pixel observations, outperforming DreamerV3 in rollout prediction accuracy. Furthermore, by decoupling object centric features into dynamic-agnostic and dynamic-aware components, we enable finer-grained manipulation of these features and generate more diverse imagined trajectories. The code of Dyn-O can be found at: https://github.com/wangzizhao/dyn-O.

paragraphs: Dyn-O builds world models that represent an environment through its objects. The motivation is that many changes in an environment arise from interactions among objects, so a structured representation may help model those changes. Earlier object-centric world models were largely explored in visually simple settings, leaving their effectiveness in richer scenes less established.

The proposed system improves both the learning of object-centric representations and the prediction of their dynamics. It learns directly from pixel observations in the Procgen games, providing a test in more challenging visual environments. The paper reports higher rollout prediction accuracy than DreamerV3, meaning its predicted sequences more accurately capture subsequent observations in that evaluation.

Dyn-O also separates object features into components that are dynamic-agnostic and dynamic-aware. This separation supports more precise manipulation of the representation and enables more varied imagined trajectories. The stated findings demonstrate stronger prediction and controllable imagination in the tested environments. Compositional generalization motivates the object-centric approach, while rollout accuracy and trajectory diversity are the specific outcomes highlighted in the abstract.
summary.tldr: Dyn-O learns object-centric world models from pixels, improving Procgen rollout prediction and enabling finer control over imagined trajectories.

title: Dyn-O: Building Structured World Models with Object-Centric Representations

abstract: Numerous studies have demonstrated that the Transformer architecture possesses the capability for in-context learning (ICL). In scenarios involving function approximation, context can serve as a control parameter for the model, endowing it with the universal approximation property (UAP). In practice, context is represented by tokens from a finite set, referred to as a vocabulary, which is the case considered in this paper, i.e., vocabulary in-context learning (VICL). We demonstrate that VICL in single-layer Transformers, without positional encoding, does not possess the UAP; however, it is possible to achieve the UAP when positional encoding is included. Several sufficient conditions for the positional encoding are provided. Our findings reveal the benefits of positional encoding from an approximation theory perspective in the context of in-context learning.

paragraphs: In-context learning lets a model change its behavior through the context it receives. For function approximation, that context can act as a control input. This paper studies the practical restriction that context consists of tokens selected from a finite vocabulary, calling the resulting setting vocabulary in-context learning.

The authors ask whether single-layer Transformers in this setting have the universal approximation property: the ability to approximate functions arbitrarily closely in the theoretical setting under consideration. They show that, without positional encoding, vocabulary in-context learning lacks this property. This identifies an expressive limitation of the architecture when context is restricted to finite-vocabulary tokens.

Adding positional encoding makes universal approximation possible, and the paper gives several sufficient conditions on the encoding. The result does not say that every positional encoding works; the conditions establish ways to obtain the property. The contribution gives an approximation-theoretic explanation for the value of position information in in-context learning, connecting an architectural choice to what a shallow Transformer can represent.
summary.tldr: Suitable positional encodings enable universal approximation through finite-vocabulary context in single-layer Transformers, where it is impossible without them.

title: Vocabulary In-Context Learning in Transformers: Benefits of Positional Encoding

abstract: Recent advances in reasoning techniques have substantially improved the performance of large language models (LLMs), raising expectations for their ability to provide accurate, truthful, and reliable information. However, emerging evidence suggests that iterative reasoning may foster belief entrenchment and confirmation bias, rather than enhancing truth-seeking behavior. In this study, we propose a systematic evaluation framework for *belief entrenchment* in LLM reasoning by leveraging the Martingale property from Bayesian statistics. This property implies that, under rational belief updating, the expected value of future beliefs should remain equal to the current belief, i.e., belief updates are unpredictable from the current belief. We propose the unsupervised, regression-based *Martingale Score* to measure violations of this property, which signal deviation from the Bayesian ability of updating on new evidence. In open-ended problem domains including event forecasting, value-laden questions, and academic paper review, we find such violations to be widespread across models and setups, where the current belief positively predicts future belief updates, a phenomenon which we term *belief entrenchment*. We identify the models, reasoning techniques, and domains more prone to belief entrenchment. Finally, we validate the Martingale Score by showing that it predicts ground-truth accuracy on problem domains where ground truth labels are available. This indicates that, while designed as an unsupervised metric that operates even in domains without access to ground truth, the Martingale Score is a useful proxy of the truth-seeking ability of a reasoning process.

It builds an evaluation framework around the Bayesian martingale property: under rational updating, the expected future belief equals the current belief. In this sense, the current belief should not predict the direction of later updates.

The proposed Martingale Score uses regression to measure departures from that property without needing correct-answer labels. This matters because some open-ended domains lack readily available correct answers. The findings position the score as a proxy for truth-seeking behavior in a reasoning process, supported by its observed relationship with accuracy where that relationship can be checked.
summary.tldr: The Martingale Score measures predictable belief reinforcement during LLM reasoning without requiring ground-truth answers.

title: Martingale Score: An Unsupervised Metric for Bayesian Rationality in LLM Reasoning

abstract: The integration of big data, physical laws, and machine learning algorithms has shown potential to improve the estimation and understanding of complex real-world systems. However, effectively incorporating physical laws with uncertainties into machine learning algorithms remains understudied. In this work, we bridge this gap by developing the Partial Physics Informed Diffusion Model (PPIDM), a novel framework that integrates known physical principles through a physics operator while reducing the impact of unknown dynamics by minimizing related discrepancies. We showcase PPIDM’s capabilities using ocean surface chlorophyll concentration data, which are influenced by both physical and biological processes, while the latter is poorly constrained. Experimental results reveal that PPIDM achieves substantially improved prediction accuracy and stability, significantly outperforming baseline methods that either neglect physics entirely or impose incomplete physical constraints under the assumption of completeness.

paragraphs: Physical knowledge can help reconstruct complex environmental signals, but available laws may describe only part of what drives the observations. Ocean surface chlorophyll concentration illustrates this problem: both physical and biological processes influence it, while the biological contribution is poorly constrained. Treating the known physics as a complete description can therefore misrepresent the system.

The proposed Partial Physics Informed Diffusion Model incorporates known principles through a physics operator. It also minimizes discrepancies associated with unknown dynamics to reduce their impact. This design explicitly accommodates incomplete physical knowledge, allowing the model to use the constraints that are available without assuming they account for all observed behavior.

The authors demonstrate the framework on ocean surface chlorophyll data. Experiments report substantially improved prediction accuracy and stability relative to methods that ignore physics and methods that impose incomplete constraints as though they were complete. The findings support incorporating partial physical knowledge in a way that acknowledges unresolved dynamics, making the treatment of uncertainty in the physical description central to the approach.
summary.tldr: PPIDM improves ocean chlorophyll reconstruction by incorporating known physics while accounting for incompletely understood dynamics.

title: Partial Physics Informed Diffusion Model for Ocean Chlorophyll Concentration Reconstruction

abstract: We introduce Neural Hamiltonian Diffusion, a unified framework for learning stochastic Hamiltonian dynamics on differentiable manifolds. While Hamiltonian Neural Networks (HNNs) model conservative systems in flat Euclidean space, they fail to account for geometric structure and intrinsic stochasticity. Conversely, diffusion models on Riemannian manifolds offer geometry-aware stochastic modeling but lack physical inductive biases. Our method parameterizes a Hamiltonian with a neural network and defines its dynamics as a stochastic differential equation on a (pseudo-)Riemannian manifold equipped with a Poisson structure. This enables physically consistent modeling of dynamics on curved, periodic, or causally structured spaces. We demonstrate that the proposed geometric dynamics generalizes existing approaches and applies to systems ranging from molecular dynamics to relativistic n-body problems.

paragraphs: Learning physical dynamics can require representing both randomness and the geometry of the space in which a system evolves. The paper identifies a gap between two approaches: Hamiltonian neural networks model conservative dynamics in flat space, while manifold diffusion models account for geometry and randomness but lack the same physical inductive structure.

Neural Hamiltonian Diffusion combines these ingredients in one framework. A neural network represents the Hamiltonian, and a stochastic differential equation defines motion on a differentiable manifold. The space has a Riemannian or pseudo-Riemannian geometry together with a Poisson structure, providing the mathematical ingredients for connecting the learned Hamiltonian to dynamics that respect the space’s organization.

This formulation supports physically consistent modeling in curved, periodic, and causally structured spaces. The authors demonstrate that the proposed dynamics generalize existing approaches and apply to systems ranging from molecular dynamics to relativistic many-body problems. The contribution is a unified modeling framework that accommodates geometric structure, Hamiltonian organization, and stochastic behavior within the same description of a system’s evolution.
summary.tldr: Neural Hamiltonian Diffusion combines learned Hamiltonians, stochastic dynamics, and manifold geometry to model physically structured systems.

title: Neural Hamiltonian Diffusions for Modeling Structured Geometric Dynamics

abstract: Fine-tuning foundation models has emerged as a powerful approach for generating objects with specific desired properties. Reinforcement learning (RL) provides an effective framework for this purpose, enabling models to generate outputs that maximize a given reward function. However, in many applications such as text generation and drug discovery, it can be suboptimal to optimize using a single reward signal, as multiple evaluation criteria are often necessary. This paper proposes a novel reinforcement learning-based method for fine-tuning foundation models using multiple reward signals. By employing an iterative fine-tuning strategy across these rewards, our approach generalizes state-of-the-art RL-based methods. We further provide a theoretical analysis that offers insights into the performance of multi-reward RL fine-tuning. Experimental results across diverse domains including text, biological sequence, and small molecule generation, demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm compared to state-of-the-art baselines.

paragraphs: Foundation models are often adapted to generate outputs with particular desired properties. Reinforcement learning can do this by rewarding outputs that meet a chosen criterion. The paper addresses applications where a single reward is insufficient because several evaluation criteria matter, including text generation and the design of biological sequences or small molecules.

The proposed method uses an iterative fine-tuning strategy across multiple reward signals. This extends state-of-the-art reinforcement learning approaches to settings with more than one criterion for evaluating generated objects. The authors also provide a theoretical analysis offering insight into the performance of this multi-reward training procedure, connecting the algorithmic proposal with an examination of its behavior.

Experiments span text, biological sequence, and small molecule generation, reporting effectiveness relative to state-of-the-art baselines. The range of domains matters because the motivating issue is shared across different types of generated outputs: one criterion may not adequately capture what makes an output useful. The findings support iterative multi-reward fine-tuning as a general approach for incorporating several desired properties into model adaptation.
summary.tldr: An iterative reinforcement learning method fine-tunes foundation models across multiple rewards, with theoretical analysis and evaluations in text and molecular generation.

title: Iterative Foundation Model Fine-Tuning on Multiple Rewards

abstract: While language models have shown remarkable performance across diverse tasks, they still encounter challenges in complex reasoning scenarios. Recent research suggests that language models trained on linearized search traces toward solutions, rather than solely on the final solutions, exhibit improved generalization, despite the search traces being potentially noisy or suboptimal. However, relying on such imperfect traces can result in inefficient use of test-time compute. To address this, we propose guided reinforced self-training (Guided-ReST), a fine-tuning algorithm designed to improve the model’s capability for effective search during inference. The key insight behind Guided-ReST is that optimal solutions can serve as valuable step-by-step landmarks to guide the model’s search process. Based on this insight, we introduce a novel data generation method that seamlessly incorporates optimal solutions into the model’s search procedure, enabling the generation of high-quality search traces. By fine-tuning the model on these search traces, we effectively distill improved search strategies into the model. Our method significantly enhances the search capabilities of language models on arithmetic reasoning and code self-repair tasks, including Countdown, CodeContests, and CodeForces. We release the source code at https://github.com/snu-mllab/guided-rest.

paragraphs: Training a language model on sequences that describe a search for a solution can improve reasoning generalization. However, noisy or suboptimal search traces can also teach inefficient behavior, wasting computation during inference. Guided Reinforced Self-Training, or Guided-ReST, aims to improve the search strategies learned from those traces.

Its key idea is to use optimal solutions as step-by-step landmarks during the model’s search. The data-generation procedure incorporates these solutions into the search process to produce higher-quality traces. Fine-tuning on the resulting traces then distills the improved search behavior into the model. The role of the known solutions is therefore to guide production of training trajectories, not merely to supply final-answer targets.

The authors report significant improvements in search capability on arithmetic reasoning and code self-repair tasks, including Countdown, CodeContests, and CodeForces. These findings indicate that the quality and guidance of search-trace generation matter for teaching effective inference-time search. The approach connects supervision from optimal solutions with training on the process used to reach them.
summary.tldr: Guided-ReST uses optimal solutions to guide training-trace generation and teach language models more effective inference-time search.

title: Learning to Better Search with Language Models via Guided Reinforced Self-Training

abstract: In multimodal learning, dominant modalities often overshadow others, limiting generalization. We propose Modality-Aware Sharpness-Aware Minimization (M-SAM), a model-agnostic framework that applies to many modalities and supports early and late fusion scenarios. In every iteration, M-SAM in three steps optimizes learning. \textbf{First, it identifies the dominant modality} based on modalities' contribution in the accuracy using Shapley. \textbf{Second, it decomposes the loss landscape}, or in another language, it modulates the loss to prioritize the robustness of the model in favor of the dominant modality, and \textbf{third, M-SAM updates the weights} by backpropagation of modulated gradients. This ensures robust learning for the dominant modality while enhancing contributions from others, allowing the model to explore and exploit complementary features that strengthen overall performance. Extensive experiments on four diverse datasets show that M-SAM outperforms the latest state-of-the-art optimization and gradient manipulation methods and significantly balances and improves multimodal learning. The code will be released.

paragraphs: When a model learns from several modalities, one source can dominate training and leave complementary information underused. This imbalance can limit generalization. Modality-Aware Sharpness-Aware Minimization, or M-SAM, addresses the problem through the optimization procedure. The framework is model-agnostic and supports both early and late fusion across multiple modalities.

Each iteration begins by estimating modalities' contributions to accuracy using Shapley values and identifying the dominant modality. M-SAM then modulates the loss to prioritize robustness with respect to that modality. Finally, it updates model weights by backpropagating the modified gradients. The intended effect is robust learning for the dominant source together with stronger contributions from the others.

Across four diverse datasets, the authors report improvements over the compared state-of-the-art optimization and gradient-manipulation methods. The results indicate better modality balance alongside better overall performance. The approach matters because it treats imbalance as something the training dynamics can address, using measured modality contributions to guide how the model learns complementary features.
summary.tldr: M-SAM adjusts gradients according to modality contributions to improve robustness, balance, and multimodal performance.

title: Modality-Aware SAM: Sharpness-Aware-Minimization Driven Gradient Modulation for Harmonized Multimodal Learning

abstract: Modern foundation models are trained on diverse datasets to enhance generalization across tasks and domains. A central challenge in this process is determining how to effectively mix and sample data from multiple sources. This naturally leads to a multi-task learning (MTL) perspective. While prior work in MTL has emphasized mitigating gradient conflicts, we observe that large-scale pretraining scenarios—such as multilingual or multi-domain training—often exhibit little to no gradient conflict. Motivated by this observation, we propose $\textbf{PiKE}$ ($\textbf{P}$ositive gradient $\textbf{i}$nteraction-based $\textbf{K}$-task weights $\textbf{E}$stimator), an adaptive data mixing algorithm that dynamically adjusts sampling weights during training. PiKE exploits non-conflicting gradient interactions to minimize a near-tight upper bound on the average loss decrease at each step, while incurring negligible computational overhead. We provide theoretical convergence guarantees and show that PiKE outperforms static and non-adaptive mixing baselines. Furthermore, we extend PiKE to promote balanced learning across tasks. Extensive experiments on large-scale language model pretraining confirm that PiKE achieves faster convergence and improved downstream performance compared to existing approaches.

paragraphs: Training a foundation model on several datasets requires deciding how often to sample each source. PiKE approaches that choice as a multitask learning problem. Its motivation is the observation that large multilingual or multidomain pretraining often exhibits little gradient conflict, meaning updates associated with different tasks do not strongly oppose one another.

Rather than keeping sampling proportions fixed, PiKE adjusts them throughout training using these non-conflicting gradient interactions. Its weighting rule is derived from a near-tight bound governing the average loss change at each step. The authors report negligible computational overhead, making the adaptation intended to fit within large-scale training rather than becoming a substantial additional workload.

The paper provides convergence guarantees and extends the method to encourage more balanced learning across tasks. In large-scale language-model pretraining experiments, PiKE converges faster and improves downstream performance compared with existing approaches, including static and non-adaptive mixtures. The findings support adapting data allocation to useful interactions between tasks in the low-conflict setting that motivates the method.
summary.tldr: PiKE dynamically adjusts training-data mixtures using non-conflicting gradient interactions, improving convergence and downstream results in large-scale pretraining experiments.

title: PiKE: Adaptive Data Mixing for Large-Scale Multi-Task Learning Under Low Gradient Conflicts

abstract: The lack of training data is a common challenge in many machine learning problems, which is often tackled by semi-supervised learning methods or transfer learning methods. The former requires unlabeled images from the same distribution as the labeled ones and the latter leverages labeled images from related homogenous tasks. However, these restrictions often cannot be satisfied. To address this, we propose a novel robust and discriminative self-taught learning approach to utilize any unlabeled data without the above restrictions. Our new approach employs a robust loss function to learn the dictionary, and enforces the structured sparse regularization to automatically select the optimal dictionary basis vectors and incorporate the supervision information contained in the labeled data. We derive an efficient iterative algorithm to solve the optimization problem and rigorously prove its convergence. Promising results in extensive experiments have validated the proposed approach.

paragraphs: When labeled training data are scarce, additional data can help, but familiar approaches impose restrictions on where those data come from. The abstract contrasts same-distribution unlabeled images in semi-supervised learning with labeled images from related homogeneous tasks in transfer learning. The proposed self-taught approach is designed to use unlabeled data without those source restrictions.

The method learns a dictionary using a robust loss function. Dictionary basis vectors provide components for representing examples, and structured sparse regularization selects useful components while incorporating supervision from the labeled data. This connects the representation learned from unlabeled examples to the distinctions relevant to the supervised task.

The authors derive an efficient iterative optimization algorithm and rigorously prove its convergence. Extensive experiments produce results described as promising. The contribution combines flexibility in the source of unlabeled data with a mechanism for selecting task-relevant dictionary elements. Its convergence result supports the optimization procedure, while the experimental results support the usefulness of the overall learning approach in the examined settings.
summary.tldr: Robust dictionary learning and structured sparsity use unrestricted-source unlabeled data to build task-relevant representations.

title: Robust and Discriminative Self-Taught Learning

abstract: The paper studies the problem of recovering a spectrally sparse object from a small number of time domain samples. Specifically, the object of interest with ambient dimension n is assumed to be a mixture of r complex multi-dimensional sinusoids, while the underlying frequencies can assume any value in the unit disk. Conventional compressed sensing paradigms suffer from the \em basis mismatch issue when imposing a discrete dictionary on the Fourier representation. To address this problem, we develop a novel nonparametric algorithm, called enhanced matrix completion (EMaC), based on structured matrix completion. The algorithm starts by converting the data into a low-rank enhanced form with multi-fold Hankel structure, then attempts recovery via nuclear norm minimization. Under mild incoherence conditions, EMaC allows perfect recovery as soon as the number of samples exceeds the order of \mathcalO(r\log^2 n). We also show that, in many instances, accurate completion of a low-rank multi-fold Hankel matrix is possible when the number of observed entries is proportional to the information theoretical limits (except for a logarithmic gap). The robustness of EMaC against bounded noise and its applicability to super resolution are further demonstrated by numerical experiments.

Their underlying frequencies can vary continuously within the unit disk. A fixed discrete Fourier dictionary can therefore mismatch the true frequencies, creating a difficulty for conventional compressed sensing approaches.

Enhanced matrix completion, or EMaC, addresses this through a structured matrix representation. It converts the data into a low-rank matrix with multi-fold Hankel structure and attempts recovery by minimizing the nuclear norm. The representation uses the signal's sinusoidal structure without requiring frequencies to match a predetermined discrete dictionary.

summary.tldr: EMaC recovers spectrally sparse signals through structured low-rank matrix completion, with exact-recovery guarantees under incoherence conditions.

title: Spectral Compressed Sensing via Structured Matrix Completion

abstract: Direct policy search methods offer the promise of automatically learning controllers for complex, high-dimensional tasks. However, prior applications of policy search often required specialized, low-dimensional policy classes, limiting their generality. In this work, we introduce a policy search algorithm that can directly learn high-dimensional, general-purpose policies, represented by neural networks. We formulate the policy search problem as an optimization over trajectory distributions, alternating between optimizing the policy to match the trajectories, and optimizing the trajectories to match the policy and minimize expected cost. Our method can learn policies for complex tasks such as bipedal push recovery and walking on uneven terrain, while outperforming prior methods.

We formulate the policy search problem as an optimization over trajectory distributions, alternating between optimizing the policy to match the trajectories, and optimizing the trajectories to match the policy and minimize expected cost. paragraphs: Direct policy search aims to learn controllers automatically, including for tasks with many dimensions. Earlier applications often relied on specialized policy classes with relatively few parameters, restricting their generality. This paper introduces an algorithm for learning more general, high-dimensional policies represented by neural networks.

The method formulates learning as optimization over distributions of trajectories. It alternates between two linked steps: adjusting the policy to match the trajectories, then adjusting the trajectories to match the policy while reducing expected cost. This creates a coupled learning process in which the desired behavior and the controller are repeatedly brought into closer agreement.

The authors report learning policies for difficult control tasks, including recovering from pushes during bipedal movement and walking over uneven terrain, while outperforming prior methods. These results support the use of trajectory optimization to train expressive neural network controllers. The main significance is that the algorithm connects trajectory-level optimization with policy learning in a form capable of handling the complex tasks demonstrated.
summary.tldr: Alternating optimization of trajectories and neural network policies learns controllers for complex tasks such as bipedal push recovery and uneven-terrain walking.

title: Learning Complex Neural Network Policies with Trajectory Optimization

abstract: We propose a state-based variant of the classical online learning problem of tracking the best expert. In our setting, the actions of the algorithm and experts correspond to local moves through a continuous and bounded state space. At each step, Nature chooses payoffs as a function of each player’s current position and action. Our model therefore integrates the problem of prediction with expert advice with the stateful formalisms of reinforcement learning. Traditional no-regret learning approaches no longer apply, but we propose a simple algorithm that provably achieves no-regret when the state space is any convex Euclidean region. Our algorithm combines techniques from online learning with results from the literature on pursuit-evasion games. We describe a quantitative trading application in which the convex region captures inventory risk constraints, and local moves limit market impact. Using historical market data, we show experimentally that our algorithm has a strong advantage over classic no-regret approaches.

summary.tldr: A pursuit-evasion-inspired algorithm achieves no regret for stateful expert tracking in convex regions and shows advantages on historical trading data.

title: Pursuit-Evasion Without Regret, with an Application to Trading

abstract: We consider the matrix completion problem of recovering a structured matrix from noisy and partial measurements. Recent works have proposed tractable estimators with strong statistical guarantees for the case where the underlying matrix is low–rank, and the measurements consist of a subset, either of the exact individual entries, or of the entries perturbed by additive Gaussian noise, which is thus implicitly suited for thin–tailed continuous data. Arguably, common applications of matrix completion require estimators for (a) heterogeneous data–types, such as skewed–continuous, count, binary, etc., (b) for heterogeneous noise models (beyond Gaussian), which capture varied uncertainty in the measurements, and (c) heterogeneous structural constraints beyond low–rank, such as block–sparsity, or a superposition structure of low–rank plus elementwise sparseness, among others. In this paper, we provide a vastly unified framework for generalized matrix completion by considering a matrix completion setting wherein the matrix entries are sampled from any member of the rich family of \textitexponential family distributions; and impose general structural constraints on the underlying matrix, as captured by a general regularizer \mathcalR(.). We propose a simple convex regularized M–estimator for the generalized framework, and provide a unified and novel statistical analysis for this general class of estimators. We finally corroborate our theoretical results on simulated datasets.

paragraphs: Matrix completion reconstructs a matrix from incomplete observations. This paper addresses settings where the observations are noisy and their statistical behavior extends beyond exact entries or additive Gaussian noise. It also considers structural information beyond low rank, motivated by data such as counts, binary measurements, and skewed continuous values.

The framework models observed entries using exponential-family distributions and expresses matrix structure through a general regularizer. This creates a common formulation for different observation models and constraints, including block sparsity and combinations of low-rank and elementwise sparse structure. Both the distribution of the measurements and the organization of the underlying matrix become explicit parts of the estimation problem.

The authors propose a convex regularized M-estimator and provide a unified statistical analysis for this class of estimators. Simulated datasets corroborate the theoretical results. The contribution is a broader framework in which varied matrix completion problems can be formulated and analyzed together. Its scope is defined by the exponential-family observation setting and the structural constraints represented by the regularizer.
summary.tldr: A convex estimation framework extends matrix completion to exponential-family observations and structural constraints beyond low rank.

title: Exponential Family Matrix Completion under Structural Constraints

abstract: This paper presents a novel unifying framework of anytime sparse Gaussian process regression (SGPR) models that can produce good predictive performance fast and improve their predictive performance over time. Our proposed unifying framework reverses the variational inference procedure to theoretically construct a non-trivial, concave functional that is maximized at the predictive distribution of any SGPR model of our choice. As a result, a stochastic natural gradient ascent method can be derived that involves iteratively following the stochastic natural gradient of the functional to improve its estimate of the predictive distribution of the chosen SGPR model and is guaranteed to achieve asymptotic convergence to it. Interestingly, we show that if the predictive distribution of the chosen SGPR model satisfies certain decomposability conditions, then the stochastic natural gradient is an unbiased estimator of the exact natural gradient and can be computed in constant time (i.e., independent of data size) at each iteration. We empirically evaluate the trade-off between the predictive performance vs. time efficiency of the anytime SGPR models on two real-world million-sized datasets.

paragraphs: This paper develops a common framework for sparse Gaussian process regression models that can provide useful predictions quickly and refine them as computation continues. This anytime behavior makes prediction quality a function of the time available, while keeping a chosen sparse model’s predictive distribution as the eventual target.

The authors reverse the usual variational construction: they start from the desired predictive distribution and build a concave objective whose maximum occurs there. They then derive stochastic natural gradient updates that improve the current distribution estimate. The framework guarantees asymptotic convergence to the predictive distribution of the selected sparse Gaussian process model.

A further efficiency result depends on specific decomposability conditions. When the chosen predictive distribution satisfies them, each stochastic gradient is unbiased and can be computed in time independent of dataset size. This is a per-iteration result, rather than a claim about total convergence time. Experiments on two real datasets containing millions of observations examine the resulting trade-off between prediction quality and computation time.
summary.tldr: An anytime framework incrementally approaches a chosen sparse Gaussian process predictor, with constant-time stochastic gradient computation under decomposability conditions.

title: A Unifying Framework of Anytime Sparse Gaussian Process Regression Models with Stochastic Variational Inference for Big Data

abstract: There are many edge-aware filters varying in their construction forms and filtering properties. It seems impossible to uniformly represent and accelerate them in a single framework. We made the attempt to learn a big and important family of edge-aware operators from data. Our method is based on a deep convolutional neural network with a gradient domain training procedure, which gives rise to a powerful tool to approximate various filters without knowing the original models and implementation details. The only difference among these operators in our system becomes merely the learned parameters. Our system enables fast approximation for complex edge-aware filters and achieves up to 200x acceleration, regardless of their originally very different implementation. Fast speed can also be achieved when creating new effects using spatially varying filter or filter combination, bearing out the effectiveness of our deep edge-aware filters.

paragraphs: Edge-aware image filters have many different mathematical forms and implementations, making a common acceleration strategy difficult. This paper learns an important family of these operators from data. Its goal is to approximate their behavior through a shared neural-network framework, so that different filtering effects can use the same computational approach.

The method uses a deep convolutional neural network trained in the gradient domain, focusing training on image changes represented by gradients. It can approximate filters without needing their original mathematical models or implementation details. Within this framework, the learned parameters distinguish one operator from another, allowing a common architecture to represent varied filtering behavior.

The authors report acceleration of up to 200 times for complex edge-aware filters. This is a reported maximum, rather than a speedup promised for every operator. The framework also achieves fast processing for effects built from spatially varying filters or combinations of filters, showing that its usefulness extends to composing new image effects.
summary.tldr: A shared convolutional network learns to approximate varied edge-aware filters, with reported acceleration of up to 200 times.

title: Deep Edge-Aware Filters

abstract: Mastering the game of Go has remained a long-standing challenge to the field of AI. Modern computer Go programs rely on processing millions of possible future positions to play well, but intuitively a stronger and more ’humanlike’ way to play the game would be to rely on pattern recognition rather than brute force computation. Following this sentiment, we train deep convolutional neural networks to play Go by training them to predict the moves made by expert Go players. To solve this problem we introduce a number of novel techniques, including a method of tying weights in the network to ’hard code’ symmetries that are expected to exist in the target function, and demonstrate in an ablation study they considerably improve performance. Our final networks are able to achieve move prediction accuracies of 41.1% and 44.4% on two different Go datasets, surpassing previous state of the art on this task by significant margins. Additionally, while previous move prediction systems have not yielded strong Go playing programs, we show that the networks trained in this work acquired high levels of skill. Our convolutional neural networks can consistently defeat the well known Go program GNU Go and win some games against state of the art Go playing program Fuego while using a fraction of the play time.

paragraphs: This paper trains deep convolutional networks to predict moves made by expert Go players. The motivation is to build playing strength through recognizing board patterns, given that strong computer Go programs commonly examine millions of future positions. Expert move prediction supplies the training task for learning useful patterns.

The authors introduce several techniques, including tying network weights to encode symmetries expected in the target function. An ablation study shows that the introduced techniques considerably improve performance. The final networks reach move-prediction accuracies of 41.1 percent and 44.4 percent on two datasets, exceeding the previous state of the art on that task.

These results show that the learned predictors acquire substantial playing skill, with the reported strength against Fuego remaining qualified.
summary.tldr: Convolutional networks trained on expert Go moves achieve strong prediction results and substantial playing skill with comparatively little play time.

title: Training Deep Convolutional Neural Networks to Play Go

abstract: The benefit of exploiting label dependence in multi-label classification is known to be closely dependent on the type of loss to be minimized. In this paper, we show that the subsets of labels that appear as irreducible factors in the factorization of the conditional distribution of the label set given the input features play a pivotal role for multi-label classification in the context of subset Zero-One loss minimization, as they divide the learning task into simpler independent multi-class problems. We establish theoretical results to characterize and identify these irreducible label factors for any given probability distribution satisfying the Composition property. The analysis lays the foundation for generic multi-label classification and optimal feature subset selection procedures under this subclass of distributions. Our conclusions are supported by carefully designed experiments on synthetic and benchmark data.

paragraphs: Multi-label classification predicts several labels for each input. Under subset zero-one loss, the prediction is assessed as a whole label set, making the structure of label dependence particularly relevant. This paper asks which groups of labels must be handled together to minimize that loss, rather than treating all label relationships as equally important.

The authors identify irreducible factors of the conditional label distribution as the key units. These are subsets that remain together when the distribution is factored given the input features. The factorization divides the original learning task into independent multiclass problems, each covering the joint possibilities within one label group.

The theoretical results characterize and identify these groups for distributions satisfying the Composition property. Within that subclass, the analysis provides a foundation for general multi-label classification procedures and optimal feature-subset selection. Experiments on synthetic and benchmark data support the conclusions. The result connects a precise distributional property to a simpler organization of prediction, while keeping the optimality claims tied to the stated loss and distribution family.
summary.tldr: For distributions satisfying Composition, irreducible label factors reduce subset-zero-one classification to independent multiclass problems.

title: On the Optimality of Multi-Label Classification under Subset Zero-One Loss for Distributions Satisfying the Composition Property

abstract: Reinforcement learning can acquire complex behaviors from high-level specifications. However, defining a cost function that can be optimized effectively and encodes the correct task is challenging in practice. We explore how inverse optimal control (IOC) can be used to learn behaviors from demonstrations, with applications to torque control of high-dimensional robotic systems. Our method addresses two key challenges in inverse optimal control: first, the need for informative features and effective regularization to impose structure on the cost, and second, the difficulty of learning the cost function under unknown dynamics for high-dimensional continuous systems. To address the former challenge, we present an algorithm capable of learning arbitrary nonlinear cost functions, such as neural networks, without meticulous feature engineering. To address the latter challenge, we formulate an efficient sample-based approximation for MaxEnt IOC. We evaluate our method on a series of simulated tasks and real-world robotic manipulation problems, demonstrating substantial improvement over prior methods both in terms of task complexity and sample efficiency.

paragraphs: A reinforcement learning system needs a cost function that expresses the intended behavior and can be optimized effectively. Designing that function is difficult for complex robots. This paper studies inverse optimal control, which learns costs from demonstrations, with particular attention to torque control in robotic systems with many continuous dimensions.

The method tackles two connected obstacles. One is representing the cost without relying on meticulous manual feature design; the authors develop an algorithm capable of learning arbitrary nonlinear cost functions, including neural networks. The other is learning when the system dynamics are unknown. They address this through an efficient sample-based approximation to maximum-entropy inverse optimal control.

The work is evaluated on simulated tasks and real robotic manipulation problems. The authors report substantial improvements over prior methods in the complexity of tasks handled and in sample efficiency. These findings support the combination of flexible cost learning and sample-based inference for learning behavior from demonstrations. The reported gains concern the evaluated tasks, while unknown dynamics and high-dimensional continuous control define the challenges the method addresses.
summary.tldr: Guided cost learning learns nonlinear costs from demonstrations under unknown dynamics, improving task complexity and sample efficiency in robotic evaluations.

title: Guided Cost Learning: Deep Inverse Optimal Control via Policy Optimization

abstract: We study the problem of supervised learning for both binary and multiclass classification from a unified geometric perspective. In particular, we propose a geometric regularization technique to find the submanifold corresponding to an estimator of the class probability P(y|\vec x). The regularization term measures the volume of this submanifold, based on the intuition that overfitting produces rapid local oscillations and hence large volume of the estimator. This technique can be applied to regularize any classification function that satisfies two requirements: firstly, an estimator of the class probability can be obtained; secondly, first and second derivatives of the class probability estimator can be calculated. In experiments, we apply our regularization technique to standard loss functions for classification, our RBF-based implementation compares favorably to widely used regularization methods for both binary and multiclass classification.

The regularization term measures the volume of this submanifold, based on the intuition that overfitting produces rapid local oscillations and hence large volume of the estimator. paragraphs: This paper treats binary and multiclass classification through the geometry of predicted class probabilities. A classifier assigns probabilities to labels as its input changes. The authors view that probability estimator as defining a geometric surface, or submanifold, and propose controlling its complexity by penalizing the surface’s volume.

The motivating intuition is that overfitting creates rapid local fluctuations in predicted probabilities. Those fluctuations enlarge the associated surface, so a volume penalty discourages this kind of behavior. The regularizer thus connects the shape of the probability function to a measure of model complexity. It supplies a common geometric perspective for classification with either two classes or several.

The approach applies to classification functions that meet two explicit requirements: class probabilities must be available, and their first and second derivatives must be calculable. The authors combine the regularizer with standard classification losses. In experiments, their radial-basis-function implementation compares favorably with widely used regularization methods on both binary and multiclass tasks, providing empirical support for the geometric approach.
summary.tldr: Penalizing the geometric volume of a classifier’s probability surface provides a regularizer that performs favorably in binary and multiclass experiments.

title: Differential Geometric Regularization for Supervised Learning of Classifiers

abstract: Sparsity is a basic property of real vectors that is exploited in a wide variety of machine learning applications. In this work, we describe property testing algorithms for sparsity that observe a low-dimensional projec- tion of the input. We consider two settings. In the first setting, we test sparsity with respect to an unknown basis: given input vectors $y_1 ,...,y_p \in R^d$ whose concatenation as columns forms $Y \in R^{d \times p}$ , does $Y = AX$ for matrices $A \in R^{d\times m}$ and $X \in R^{m \times p}$ such that each column of $X$ is $k$-sparse, or is $Y$ “far” from having such a decomposition? In the second setting, we test sparsity with respect to a known basis: for a fixed design ma- trix $A \in R^{d \times m}$ , given input vector $y \in R^d$ , is $y = Ax$ for some $k$-sparse vector $x$ or is $y$ “far” from having such a decomposition? We analyze our algorithms using tools from high-dimensional geometry and probability.

paragraphs: Sparsity means that a representation uses only a small number of nonzero coefficients. This paper studies how to test for that property while observing only a low-dimensional projection of the input. The task is to distinguish inputs that have a sparse representation from those that are far from having one.

In the unknown-basis setting, the input contains several vectors. The question is whether they can all be expressed through a shared matrix, with each vector using at most k nonzero coefficients. Both that shared matrix and the coefficients are unspecified. This tests whether the collection admits a common sparse description.

In the known-basis setting, the representation matrix is fixed and the input is a single vector. The algorithm tests whether that vector can be produced using a k-sparse coefficient vector, or is far from such a representation. The authors analyze both settings using high-dimensional geometry and probability. Their contribution concerns testing the existence of sparse structure from compressed observations, with the known and unknown representation settings treated separately.
summary.tldr: The paper develops algorithms that test for sparse representations from low-dimensional projections, with either known or unknown bases.

title: Testing Sparsity over Known and Unknown Bases

abstract: Modeling agent behavior is central to understanding the emergence of complex phenomena in multiagent systems. Prior work in agent modeling has largely been task-specific and driven by hand-engineering domain-specific prior knowledge. We propose a general learning framework for modeling agent behavior in any multiagent system using only a handful of interaction data. Our framework casts agent modeling as a representation learning problem. Consequently, we construct a novel objective inspired by imitation learning and agent identification and design an algorithm for unsupervised learning of representations of agent policies. We demonstrate empirically the utility of the proposed framework in (i) a challenging high-dimensional competitive environment for continuous control and (ii) a cooperative environment for communication, on supervised predictive tasks, unsupervised clustering, and policy optimization using deep reinforcement learning.

Prior work in agent modeling has largely been task-specific and driven by hand-engineering domain-specific prior knowledge. We propose a general learning framework for modeling agent behavior in any multiagent system using only a handful of interaction data. Our framework casts agent modeling as a representation learning problem. Consequently, we construct a novel objective inspired by imitation learning and agent identification and design an algorithm for unsupervised learning of representations of agent policies. We demonstrate empirically the utility of the proposed framework in (i) a challenging high-dimensional competitive environment for continuous control and (ii) a cooperative environment for communication, on supervised predictive tasks, unsupervised clustering, and policy optimization using deep reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: Understanding a multiagent system requires a useful description of how its participants behave. Earlier modeling approaches often depend on task-specific knowledge designed by hand. This paper instead proposes learning representations of agents' policies from a small amount of interaction data, with the aim of providing a general framework for agent modeling.

The learning objective draws on both imitation learning and agent identification. These inspirations connect describing what an agent does with distinguishing its behavior from that of other agents. The resulting algorithm learns policy representations without supervision. Treating behavior as a representation-learning problem makes those learned descriptions available for several subsequent uses rather than tying them to one prediction task.

The authors evaluate the framework in a high-dimensional competitive continuous-control environment and a cooperative communication environment. They demonstrate utility for supervised prediction, unsupervised clustering, and policy optimization with deep reinforcement learning. This variety of uses supports the value of learned policy representations in the tested settings, while the empirical evidence comes from those two types of multiagent environment.
summary.tldr: An unsupervised framework learns policy representations from limited interactions and supports prediction, clustering, and reinforcement learning in multiagent experiments.

title: Learning Policy Representations in Multiagent Systems

abstract: Faced with distribution shift between training and test set, we wish to detect and quantify the shift, and to correct our classifiers without test set labels. Motivated by medical diagnosis, where diseases (targets), cause symptoms (observations), we focus on label shift, where the label marginal p(y) changes but the conditional p(x| y) does not. We propose Black Box Shift Estimation (BBSE) to estimate the test distribution p(y). BBSE exploits arbitrary black box predictors to reduce dimensionality prior to shift correction. While better predictors give tighter estimates, BBSE works even when predictors are biased, inaccurate, or uncalibrated, so long as their confusion matrices are invertible. We prove BBSE’s consistency, bound its error, and introduce a statistical test that uses BBSE to detect shift. We also leverage BBSE to correct classifiers. Experiments demonstrate accurate estimates and improved prediction, even on high-dimensional datasets of natural images.

Motivated by medical diagnosis, where diseases (targets), cause symptoms (observations), we focus on label shift, where the label marginal p(y) changes but the conditional p(x| y) does not. We propose Black Box Shift Estimation (BBSE) to estimate the test distribution p(y). BBSE exploits arbitrary black box predictors to reduce dimensionality prior to shift correction. paragraphs: This paper addresses label shift: class frequencies change between training and deployment, while the distribution of observations within each class stays fixed. The goal is to detect and measure that change, then adjust a classifier without needing labels for the test data. This separates a specific kind of distribution shift from changes in how classes themselves appear.

Black Box Shift Estimation uses a predictor’s outputs to reduce the dimensionality of the estimation problem. The predictor can be biased, inaccurate, or uncalibrated, provided its confusion matrix is invertible. Better predictors yield tighter estimates, but perfect prediction is not required for the approach to work.

The authors prove consistency, give error bounds, and develop a statistical test for detecting shift. They also use the estimated class frequencies to correct classifiers. Experiments report accurate estimates and improved predictions, including on high-dimensional natural images. These results support using an existing predictor as a tool for adaptation under the stated label-shift and invertibility conditions.
summary.tldr: BBSE detects and estimates label shift without test labels using black-box predictors whose confusion matrices are invertible.

title: Detecting and Correcting for Label Shift with Black Box Predictors

abstract: This paper proposes Self-Imitation Learning (SIL), a simple off-policy actor-critic algorithm that learns to reproduce the agent’s past good decisions. This algorithm is designed to verify our hypothesis that exploiting past good experiences can indirectly drive deep exploration. Our empirical results show that SIL significantly improves advantage actor-critic (A2C) on several hard exploration Atari games and is competitive to the state-of-the-art count-based exploration methods. We also show that SIL improves proximal policy optimization (PPO) on MuJoCo tasks.

This algorithm is designed to verify our hypothesis that exploiting past good experiences can indirectly drive deep exploration. Our empirical results show that SIL significantly improves advantage actor-critic (A2C) on several hard exploration Atari games and is competitive to the state-of-the-art count-based exploration methods. We also show that SIL improves proximal policy optimization (PPO) on MuJoCo tasks.

paragraphs: Self-Imitation Learning asks whether an agent can improve exploration by learning to repeat its own past good decisions. The motivating hypothesis is that exploiting successful experiences can indirectly encourage deeper exploration. The paper turns that idea into a simple off-policy actor-critic algorithm, allowing learning to draw on experience from earlier behavior.

The method's central learning target is the agent's own record of good decisions. Reproducing those decisions gives past successes a continuing role in training. This makes the connection between exploitation and exploration the key question: the authors investigate whether strengthening behavior that has already worked can help an agent make progress on tasks where exploration is difficult.

Experiments show that SIL substantially improves advantage actor-critic on several hard-exploration Atari games and is competitive with leading count-based exploration methods. The authors also report improvements to proximal policy optimization on MuJoCo tasks. These results support the proposed strategy in the tested settings and show benefits with both learning algorithms, while the broader mechanism remains framed as the motivating hypothesis.
summary.tldr: Self-Imitation Learning reuses an agent's past good decisions and improves tested actor-critic methods on Atari and MuJoCo tasks.

title: Self-Imitation Learning

abstract: Recently, a unified model for image-to-image translation tasks within adversarial learning framework has aroused widespread research interests in computer vision practitioners. Their reported empirical success however lacks solid theoretical interpretations for its inherent mechanism. In this paper, we reformulate their model from a brand-new geometrical perspective and have eventually reached a full interpretation on some interesting but unclear empirical phenomenons from their experiments. Furthermore, by extending the definition of generalization for generative adversarial nets to a broader sense, we have derived a condition to control the generalization capability of their model. According to our derived condition, several practical suggestions have also been proposed on model design and dataset construction as a guidance for further empirical researches.

Such a model transforms images between settings, and its observed behavior had lacked a solid account of the underlying mechanism. The authors reformulate the model geometrically to analyze how it operates.

The geometric perspective provides an interpretation of several previously unclear phenomena in the model’s experiments. This makes the reformulation useful as an explanatory tool: it connects aspects of observed behavior with the model’s structure. The paper’s emphasis is on understanding an existing translation framework and extracting consequences from that understanding.

The authors also broaden the definition of generalization for generative adversarial networks and derive a condition for controlling the translation model’s generalization capability. They use that condition to develop practical suggestions for model design and dataset construction. The result links theory to decisions about both the model and its training data, offering guidance for subsequent empirical work within the analyzed framework.
summary.tldr: A geometric analysis explains observed adversarial image-translation behavior and yields a condition guiding generalization, model design, and data construction.

title: Theoretical Analysis of Image-to-Image Translation with Adversarial Learning

abstract: To assess the difference between real and synthetic data, Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) are trained using a distribution discrepancy measure. Three widely employed measures are information-theoretic divergences, integral probability metrics, and Hilbert space discrepancy metrics. We elucidate the theoretical connections between these three popular GAN training criteria and propose a novel procedure, called $\chi^2$ (Chi-square) GAN, that is conceptually simple, stable at training and resistant to mode collapse. Our procedure naturally generalizes to address the problem of simultaneous matching of multiple distributions. Further, we propose a resampling strategy that significantly improves sample quality, by repurposing the trained critic function via an importance weighting mechanism. Experiments show that the proposed procedure improves stability and convergence, and yields state-of-art results on a wide range of generative modeling tasks.

paragraphs: Training a generative adversarial network requires a way to measure the difference between generated and real data distributions. The paper studies connections among three families of such measures: information-theoretic divergences, integral probability metrics, and Hilbert-space discrepancies. Understanding their relationships provides the theoretical foundation for a new training procedure called Chi-square GAN.

The proposed procedure is described as conceptually simple, stable during training, and resistant to mode collapse, the loss of diversity in generated outputs. Its formulation also extends naturally to matching several distributions simultaneously. This broadens the role of the method beyond a single comparison between one real distribution and one synthetic distribution.

The authors additionally reuse the trained critic through an importance-weighted resampling strategy that significantly improves sample quality. Thus, the critic contributes both to training and to the subsequent selection of samples. Across a range of generative-modeling tasks, experiments show improved stability and convergence alongside state-of-the-art results. Resistance to mode collapse is the stated claim, rather than a guarantee that collapse can never occur.
summary.tldr: Chi-square GAN connects several distribution-matching criteria and combines stable training with critic-based resampling to improve generated samples.

title: Chi-square Generative Adversarial Network

abstract: In distributed statistical learning, $N$ samples are split across $m$ machines and a learner wishes to use minimal communication to learn as well as if the examples were on a single machine. This model has received substantial interest in machine learning due to its scalability and potential for parallel speedup. However, in high-dimensional settings, where the number examples is smaller than the number of features (‘"dimension"), the speedup afforded by distributed learning may be overshadowed by the cost of communicating a single example. This paper investigates the following question: When is it possible to learn a $d$-dimensional model in the distributed setting with total communication sublinear in $d$? Starting with a negative result, we observe that for learning $\ell_1$-bounded or sparse linear models, no algorithm can obtain optimal error until communication is linear in dimension. Our main result is that by slightly relaxing the standard boundedness assumptions for linear models, we can obtain distributed algorithms that enjoy optimal error with communication logarithmic in dimension. This result is based on a family of algorithms that combine mirror descent with randomized sparsification/quantization of iterates, and extends to the general stochastic convex optimization model.
