paragraphs: Distributed learning aims to use data spread across machines while matching the accuracy available if all examples were together. In high dimensions, even transmitting one example can be costly enough to undermine parallel speedups. The paper asks when total communication can grow more slowly than the model’s dimension.

It first establishes a negative result for learning L1-bounded or sparse linear models: achieving optimal error requires communication at least linear in dimension. This shows that sparsity or an L1 bound alone does not provide the desired communication savings under the conditions considered.

The positive result changes the boundedness assumptions slightly. Under the relaxed assumptions, the authors construct distributed algorithms with optimal error and communication that depends only logarithmically on dimension. Their methods combine mirror descent with randomized sparsification or quantization of iterates, and the result extends to stochastic convex optimization. The contrast between the lower bound and the construction makes the assumptions consequential: a modest change in the model conditions can substantially change the achievable dependence on dimension.
summary.tldr: Slightly relaxed boundedness assumptions enable optimal distributed learning with logarithmic dependence on dimension in communication.

title: Distributed Learning with Sublinear Communication

abstract: The formation of a real-world graph typically arises from the highly complex interaction of many latent factors. The existing deep learning methods for graph-structured data neglect the entanglement of the latent factors, rendering the learned representations non-robust and hardly explainable. However, learning representations that disentangle the latent factors poses great challenges and remains largely unexplored in the literature of graph neural networks. In this paper, we introduce the disentangled graph convolutional network (DisenGCN) to learn disentangled node representations. In particular, we propose a novel neighborhood routing mechanism, which is capable of dynamically identifying the latent factor that may have caused the edge between a node and one of its neighbors, and accordingly assigning the neighbor to a channel that extracts and convolutes features specific to that factor. We theoretically prove the convergence properties of the routing mechanism. Empirical results show that our proposed model can achieve significant performance gains, especially when the data demonstrate the existence of many entangled factors.

Empirical results show that our proposed model can achieve significant performance gains, especially when the data demonstrate the existence of many entangled factors.

paragraphs: A graph can contain connections arising from several interacting latent factors. When a representation mixes these factors together, it can be difficult to explain and may lack robustness. DisenGCN addresses this problem by learning node representations that separate the different factors associated with their neighborhoods.

Its key mechanism routes neighbors into distinct feature-processing channels. For each connection, the mechanism dynamically identifies a latent factor that may explain the edge and assigns the neighbor to a channel devoted to that factor. This gives the graph convolution a way to process different kinds of neighborhood information separately. The inferred assignment concerns a possible explanation of the connection, rather than an established causal account.

The authors prove convergence properties for the routing mechanism and report significant empirical performance gains. The improvements are especially pronounced when the data exhibit many entangled factors. Together, these results support factor-specific neighborhood processing as a useful way to construct graph representations, with theoretical support for the routing procedure and experimental support for the resulting model.
summary.tldr: DisenGCN routes neighbors into latent-factor channels to learn separated node representations, with convergence analysis and reported empirical gains.

title: Disentangled Graph Convolutional Networks

abstract: Model inference, such as model comparison, model checking, and model selection, is an important part of model development. Leave-one-out cross-validation (LOO) is a general approach for assessing the generalizability of a model, but unfortunately, LOO does not scale well to large datasets. We propose a combination of using approximate inference techniques and probability-proportional-to-size-sampling (PPS) for fast LOO model evaluation for large datasets. We provide both theoretical and empirical results showing good properties for large data.

We provide both theoretical and empirical results showing good properties for large data.

paragraphs: Leave-one-out cross-validation assesses how well a model generalizes by considering predictions for observations excluded from fitting. This makes it useful during model comparison, checking, and selection. Its difficulty is computational: evaluating a large dataset in this way can make an otherwise useful model-development procedure expensive.

The paper proposes combining approximate inference with probability-proportional-to-size sampling to accelerate Bayesian leave-one-out evaluation. These ingredients address the workload from two directions. Approximate inference provides a less expensive route to the model calculations, while the sampling scheme selects observations using unequal probabilities tied to a measure of size. Together, they provide an approach to evaluation intended for large datasets.

The authors supply both theoretical and empirical results supporting the approach's properties in the large-data setting. The contribution concerns evaluating models efficiently, making generalization assessment more practical as datasets grow. This matters because model development requires comparing and checking fitted models as well as producing them, and the cost of evaluation can itself become a bottleneck.
summary.tldr: Combining approximate inference with probability-proportional-to-size sampling makes Bayesian leave-one-out model evaluation more practical for large datasets.

title: Bayesian leave-one-out cross-validation for large data

abstract: In this work we analyse quantitatively the interplay between the loss landscape and performance of descent algorithms in a prototypical inference problem, the spiked matrix-tensor model. We study a loss function that is the negative log-likelihood of the model. We analyse the number of local minima at a fixed distance from the signal/spike with the Kac-Rice formula, and locate trivialization of the landscape at large signal-to-noise ratios. We evaluate analytically the performance of a gradient flow algorithm using integro-differential PDEs as developed in physics of disordered systems for the Langevin dynamics. We analyze the performance of an approximate message passing algorithm estimating the maximum likelihood configuration via its state evolution. We conclude by comparing the above results: while we observe a drastic slow down of the gradient flow dynamics even in the region where the landscape is trivial, both the analyzed algorithms are shown to perform well even in the part of the region of parameters where spurious local minima are present.

paragraphs: The paper investigates how the geometry of an optimization objective relates to the behavior of algorithms trying to recover a hidden signal. Its setting is the spiked matrix-tensor model, using negative log-likelihood as the loss. The question is whether the presence or absence of spurious local minima explains algorithmic performance.

The authors use the Kac-Rice formula to analyze how many local minima occur at specified distances from the signal and locate landscape trivialization at high signal-to-noise ratios. They separately analyze gradient-flow dynamics through integro-differential equations and approximate message passing through state evolution. These tools allow a quantitative comparison between landscape structure and recovery behavior.

The comparison reveals that gradient flow can slow dramatically even where the landscape is trivial. Conversely, both analyzed algorithms perform well in part of the parameter region containing spurious minima. These findings show that the mere existence of undesirable minima does not fully determine performance in this model: dynamics can remain slow without them or succeed despite their presence.
summary.tldr: In a spiked matrix-tensor model, algorithms can succeed despite spurious minima, while gradient flow can slow even in a trivial landscape.

title: Passed & Spurious: Descent Algorithms and Local Minima in Spiked Matrix-Tensor Models

abstract: We present a neural network architecture that is fully equivariant with respect to transformations under the Lorentz group, a fundamental symmetry of space and time in physics. The architecture is based on the theory of the finite-dimensional representations of the Lorentz group and the equivariant nonlinearity involves the tensor product. For classification tasks in particle physics, we show that such an equivariant architecture leads to drastically simpler models that have relatively few learnable parameters and are much more physically interpretable than leading approaches that use CNNs and point cloud approaches. The performance of the network is tested on a public classification dataset [https://zenodo.org/record/2603256] for tagging top quark decays given energy-momenta of jet constituents produced in proton-proton collisions.

paragraphs: This paper builds a neural network around Lorentz symmetry, a fundamental symmetry of space and time. The architecture is fully equivariant: its representations transform consistently when the inputs undergo Lorentz transformations. Embedding this relationship into the architecture gives the model an explicit connection to the physical structure of its inputs.

The construction uses finite-dimensional representations of the Lorentz group. Its nonlinear operations involve tensor products while preserving equivariance. This makes the symmetry a property of the network's computations, rather than merely a pattern the model might discover from training data. The authors show that this approach yields substantially simpler models for particle-physics classification.

The resulting networks have relatively few learnable parameters and are more physically interpretable than leading convolutional and point-cloud approaches. Performance is tested on a public task that identifies top-quark decays from the energy-momenta of jet constituents in proton-proton collisions. The stated contribution emphasizes architectural simplicity and interpretability alongside this classification evaluation, without claiming a specific accuracy improvement.
summary.tldr: A Lorentz-equivariant architecture produces simpler, more physically interpretable neural models for particle-physics classification.

title: Lorentz Group Equivariant Neural Network for Particle Physics

abstract: Incremental gradient (IG) methods, such as stochastic gradient descent and its variants are commonly used for large scale optimization in machine learning. Despite the sustained effort to make IG methods more data-efficient, it remains an open question how to select a training data subset that can theoretically and practically perform on par with the full dataset. Here we develop CRAIG, a method to select a weighted subset (or coreset) of training data that closely estimates the full gradient by maximizing a submodular function. We prove that applying IG to this subset is guaranteed to converge to the (near)optimal solution with the same convergence rate as that of IG for convex optimization. As a result, CRAIG achieves a speedup that is inversely proportional to the size of the subset. To our knowledge, this is the first rigorous method for data-efficient training of general machine learning models. Our extensive set of experiments show that CRAIG, while achieving practically the same solution, speeds up various IG methods by up to 6x for logistic regression and 3x for training deep neural networks.

paragraphs: Training on a smaller dataset saves work only if the selected examples still support a good solution. This paper introduces CRAIG, which chooses a weighted subset of training examples, called a coreset. Its selection criterion aims to make the subset closely approximate the gradient of the full dataset, preserving the information used to update the model.

CRAIG constructs this subset by maximizing a submodular function. For convex optimization, the authors prove that incremental gradient methods applied to the subset converge to an optimal or near-optimal solution at the same convergence rate as the corresponding full-data method. The convex convergence theorem and the neural-network experiments provide distinct forms of support for the approach.
summary.tldr: CRAIG selects weighted training subsets that approximate full-data gradients, offering convex convergence guarantees and substantial measured training speedups.

title: Coresets for Data-efficient Training of Machine Learning Models

abstract: We build a Bayesian contextual classification model using an optimistic score ratio for robust binary classification when there is limited information on the class-conditional, or contextual, distribution. The optimistic score searches for the distribution that is most plausible to explain the observed outcomes in the testing sample among all distributions belonging to the contextual ambiguity set which is prescribed using a limited structural constraint on the mean vector and the covariance matrix of the underlying contextual distribution. We show that the Bayesian classifier using the optimistic score ratio is conceptually attractive, delivers solid statistical guarantees and is computationally tractable. We showcase the power of the proposed optimistic score ratio classifier on both synthetic and empirical data.

The optimistic score searches for the distribution that is most plausible to explain the observed outcomes in the testing sample among all distributions belonging to the contextual ambiguity set which is prescribed using a limited structural constraint on the mean vector and the covariance matrix of the underlying contextual distribution. We show that the Bayesian classifier using the optimistic score ratio is conceptually attractive, delivers solid statistical guarantees and is computationally tractable. paragraphs: The paper studies binary classification when information about the distribution associated with each class is limited. A Bayesian classifier needs a way to compare how plausibly the classes explain a test observation. Here, uncertainty about the class-conditional distributions is incorporated into that comparison through sets of possible distributions.

The authors define these ambiguity sets using limited structural constraints on the mean vector and covariance matrix. For each contextual distribution, an optimistic score searches the allowed set for the distribution that most plausibly explains the observed test outcomes. A ratio of these scores then supplies the basis for classification, using the available distributional information without specifying a single fully known distribution.

The authors establish statistical guarantees and show that the resulting classifier is computationally tractable. They also demonstrate it on synthetic and empirical data. The contribution connects a specific treatment of distributional uncertainty with an implementable decision rule, providing a robust classification approach for the limited-information setting described by its ambiguity sets.
summary.tldr: An optimistic score ratio enables robust binary classification using distributional ambiguity sets constrained by means and covariances.

title: Robust Bayesian Classification Using An Optimistic Score Ratio

abstract: Few-shot dataset generalization is a challenging variant of the well-studied few-shot classification problem where a diverse training set of several datasets is given, for the purpose of training an adaptable model that can then learn classes from \emph{new datasets} using only a few examples. To this end, we propose to utilize the diverse training set to construct a \emph{universal template}: a partial model that can define a wide array of dataset-specialized models, by plugging in appropriate components. For each new few-shot classification problem, our approach therefore only requires inferring a small number of parameters to insert into the universal template. We design a separate network that produces an initialization of those parameters for each given task, and we then fine-tune its proposed initialization via a few steps of gradient descent. Our approach is more parameter-efficient, scalable and adaptable compared to previous methods, and achieves the state-of-the-art on the challenging Meta-Dataset benchmark.

paragraphs: Few-shot dataset generalization requires learning new classes from only a few examples in datasets not encountered during training. Training therefore draws on several diverse datasets to prepare a model for later adaptation. The challenge includes changes between datasets as well as the limited number of examples for each new classification task.

The paper proposes a universal template: a partially specified model that becomes specialized when suitable components are inserted. For a new task, adaptation only requires inferring a small number of parameters for those components. A separate network supplies an initial parameter setting based on the task, and a few gradient descent steps refine that initialization.

This design concentrates task-specific adaptation into a compact part of the model while using the diverse training collection to learn the shared template. The authors report greater parameter efficiency, scalability, and adaptability than previous methods, together with state-of-the-art results on Meta-Dataset. The findings support combining a reusable model structure with lightweight, task-dependent specialization.
summary.tldr: A universal model template adapts to new few-shot datasets by initializing and refining only a small set of task-specific parameters.

title: Learning a Universal Template for Few-shot Dataset Generalization

abstract: This paper investigates how to weight imperfect expert demonstrations for generative adversarial imitation learning (GAIL). The agent is expected to perform behaviors demonstrated by experts. But in many applications, experts could also make mistakes and their demonstrations would mislead or slow the learning process of the agent. Recently, existing methods for imitation learning from imperfect demonstrations mostly focus on using the preference or confidence scores to distinguish imperfect demonstrations. However, these auxiliary information needs to be collected with the help of an oracle, which is usually hard and expensive to afford in practice. In contrast, this paper proposes a method of learning to weight imperfect demonstrations in GAIL without imposing extensive prior information. We provide a rigorous mathematical analysis, presenting that the weights of demonstrations can be exactly determined by combining the discriminator and agent policy in GAIL. Theoretical analysis suggests that with the estimated weights the agent can learn a better policy beyond those plain expert demonstrations. Experiments in the Mujoco and Atari environments demonstrate that the proposed algorithm outperforms baseline methods in handling imperfect expert demonstrations.

paragraphs: Imitation learning can be hindered when demonstrations contain expert mistakes. Treating every example as equally useful may mislead an agent or slow its learning. This paper studies that problem within generative adversarial imitation learning, where earlier approaches often relied on additional preference judgments or confidence scores supplied by an oracle.

The proposed method learns how to weight imperfect demonstrations without imposing extensive prior information. Its mathematical analysis shows that the weights can be determined exactly by combining the discriminator and the agent policy already present in the adversarial imitation framework. This ties the assessment of demonstration quality to components of the learning process, reducing reliance on separately collected judgments.

The theoretical analysis suggests that using estimated weights can allow the agent to learn a policy better than straightforward imitation of the demonstrations. Experiments in MuJoCo and Atari show that the proposed algorithm outperforms baseline methods when handling imperfect demonstrations. These findings support weighting as a way to extract useful behavior from flawed examples while avoiding the assumption that every expert action deserves equal influence.
summary.tldr: The method uses a GAIL discriminator and agent policy to weight imperfect demonstrations and improve imitation without extensive prior quality information.

title: Learning to Weight Imperfect Demonstrations

abstract: The Transformer architecture has gained growing attention in graph representation learning recently, as it naturally overcomes several limitations of graph neural networks (GNNs) by avoiding their strict structural inductive biases and instead only encoding the graph structure via positional encoding. Here, we show that the node representations generated by the Transformer with positional encoding do not necessarily capture structural similarity between them. To address this issue, we propose the Structure-Aware Transformer, a class of simple and flexible graph Transformers built upon a new self-attention mechanism. This new self-attention incorporates structural information into the original self-attention by extracting a subgraph representation rooted at each node before computing the attention. We propose several methods for automatically generating the subgraph representation and show theoretically that the resulting representations are at least as expressive as the subgraph representations. Empirically, our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on five graph prediction benchmarks. Our structure-aware framework can leverage any existing GNN to extract the subgraph representation, and we show that it systematically improves performance relative to the base GNN model, successfully combining the advantages of GNNs and Transformers. Our code is available at https://github.com/BorgwardtLab/SAT.

paragraphs: Graph Transformers can encode graph structure through positional information while avoiding the strict structural biases of conventional graph neural networks. The paper shows that positional encoding alone does not necessarily make node representations reflect structural similarity. Nodes' surrounding graph patterns therefore need a more direct role in attention.

The Structure-Aware Transformer first extracts a representation of a subgraph rooted at each node. It incorporates these representations into self-attention, so attention uses information about local structure. The authors propose several ways to generate the subgraph representations and prove that the resulting representations are at least as expressive as those supplied to the attention mechanism.

The framework can use an existing graph neural network as its subgraph extractor. Experiments report state-of-the-art results on five graph prediction benchmarks and systematic improvements over the corresponding base graph neural network. The approach thus provides a way to combine structural representations produced by graph networks with Transformer attention. Its theoretical guarantee preserves the extractor's expressive strength, while the reported empirical results show benefits from the combined architecture.
summary.tldr: Structure-Aware Transformers incorporate node-rooted subgraph representations into attention and improve graph prediction in the reported benchmarks.

title: Structure-Aware Transformer for Graph Representation Learning

abstract: Nesterov’s Accelerated Gradient (NAG) for optimization has better performance than its continuous time limit (noiseless kinetic Langevin) when a finite step-size is employed (Shi et al., 2021). This work explores the sampling counterpart of this phenonemon and proposes a diffusion process, whose discretizations can yield accelerated gradient-based MCMC methods. More precisely, we reformulate the optimizer of NAG for strongly convex functions (NAG-SC) as a Hessian-Free High-Resolution ODE, change its high-resolution coefficient to a hyperparameter, inject appropriate noise, and discretize the resulting diffusion process. The acceleration effect of the new hyperparameter is quantified and it is not an artificial one created by time-rescaling. Instead, acceleration beyond underdamped Langevin in $W_2$ distance is quantitatively established for log-strongly-concave-and-smooth targets, at both the continuous dynamics level and the discrete algorithm level. Empirical experiments in both log-strongly-concave and multi-modal cases also numerically demonstrate this acceleration.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether an acceleration effect associated with Nesterov optimization can also improve sampling. The starting observation is that finite-step Nesterov updates can outperform their usual continuous-time limit. The authors seek sampling dynamics that retain the relevant extra structure and can produce accelerated gradient-based Markov chain Monte Carlo methods.

A coefficient in this equation becomes a tunable hyperparameter. The authors then add appropriate noise and discretize the resulting diffusion process, turning the optimization-inspired dynamics into sampling algorithms.

The result covers both continuous dynamics and discrete algorithms, and the acceleration is not merely an effect of rescaling time. Experiments show acceleration for log-strongly-concave and multimodal cases, with the latter extending the empirical evidence beyond the stated theoretical target class.
summary.tldr: A Hessian-free, Nesterov-inspired diffusion yields sampling acceleration over underdamped Langevin for log-strongly-concave, smooth targets.

title: Hessian-Free High-Resolution Nesterov Acceleration For Sampling

abstract: A main theoretical puzzle is why over-parameterized Neural Networks (NNs) generalize well when trained to zero loss (i.e., so they interpolate the data). Usually, the NN is trained with Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) or one of its variants. However, recent empirical work examined the generalization of a random NN that interpolates the data: the NN was sampled from a seemingly uniform prior over the parameters, conditioned on that the NN perfectly classifying the training set. Interestingly, such a NN sample typically generalized as well as SGD-trained NNs. We prove that such a random NN interpolator typically generalizes well if there exists an underlying narrow “teacher NN" that agrees with the labels. Specifically, we show that such a ‘flat’ prior over the NN parametrization induces a rich prior over the NN functions, due to the redundancy in the NN structure. In particular, this creates a bias towards simpler functions, which require less relevant parameters to represent — enabling learning with a sample complexity approximately proportional to the complexity of the teacher (roughly, the number of non-redundant parameters), rather than the student’s.

paragraphs: A large neural network can fit every training label while having many more parameters than the data seem to require. This paper studies why even a randomly sampled network can generalize when sampling is conditioned on perfectly classifying the training set. The question separates the effect of the parameter distribution from the usual role of gradient-based training.

The authors prove typical generalization under a specific condition: there exists a narrow teacher network that agrees with the labels. Their explanation is that a flat distribution over parameters does not produce a flat distribution over functions. Redundancy in neural network representations creates a preference for simpler functions that require fewer relevant parameters.

As a result, the sample complexity is approximately proportional to the teacher's complexity, roughly its number of nonredundant parameters, rather than the larger student's complexity. This provides a theoretical explanation for why parameter count alone can be misleading in this setting. The result concerns typical interpolating samples under the narrow-teacher condition; it does not claim that every randomly chosen network generalizes.
summary.tldr: Under a narrow-teacher condition, random interpolating networks typically generalize because flat parameter priors favor simpler functions.

title: How Uniform Random Weights Induce Non-uniform Bias: Typical Interpolating Neural Networks Generalize with Narrow Teachers

abstract: Motivated by recent advances in large language models for Natural Language Processing (NLP), we design a time-series foundation model for forecasting whose out-of-the-box zero-shot performance on a variety of public datasets comes close to the accuracy of state-of-the-art supervised forecasting models for each individual dataset. Our model is based on pretraining a decoder style attention model with input patching, using a large time-series corpus comprising both real-world and synthetic datasets. Experiments on a diverse set of previously unseen forecasting datasets suggests that the model can yield accurate zero-shot forecasts across different domains, forecasting horizons and temporal granularities.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether one pretrained model can forecast many kinds of time series without being trained again for each new dataset. The motivation comes from language models: broad pretraining might produce reusable predictive capabilities. Here, the desired capability is estimating future values from past observations across different forecasting settings.

The authors build a decoder-style attention model that processes the input using patches. They pretrain it on a large collection containing both real-world and synthetic time series. This combines a forecasting architecture with varied training data, aiming to make the resulting model useful immediately on previously unseen datasets.

Experiments suggest that this approach can produce accurate zero-shot forecasts across different domains, prediction horizons, and temporal granularities. On a variety of public datasets, its accuracy approaches that of leading supervised models trained for each dataset individually. The finding supports the possibility of broadly reusable forecasting models; it does not establish that a single pretrained model always matches a specialized one.
summary.tldr: A pretrained decoder-style model produces zero-shot time-series forecasts approaching specialized supervised models on varied public datasets.

title: A decoder-only foundation model for time-series forecasting

abstract: The problem of nearest neighbor condensing has enjoyed a long history of study, both in its theoretical and practical aspects. In this paper, we introduce the problem of weighted distance nearest neighbor condensing, where one assigns weights to each point of the condensed set, and then new points are labeled based on their weighted distance nearest neighbor in the condensed set. We study the theoretical properties of this new model, and show that it can produce dramatically better condensing than the standard nearest neighbor rule, yet is characterized by generalization bounds almost identical to the latter. We then suggest a condensing heuristic for our new problem. We demonstrate Bayes consistency for this heuristic, and also show promising empirical results.

paragraphs: Nearest-neighbor condensing replaces a larger labeled dataset with a smaller collection of representative points. New examples receive labels according to their nearest retained point. This paper extends that setup by assigning weights to the retained points and using weighted distances to decide which point supplies the label.

The authors analyze the resulting model and show that weighting can permit dramatically greater condensation than the standard nearest-neighbor rule. Despite that added flexibility, the model has generalization bounds almost identical to those of the unweighted approach. The result connects a potentially much smaller retained set with a similar theoretical account of prediction beyond the training data.

The paper then proposes a practical condensing heuristic for the weighted formulation. It establishes Bayes consistency for the heuristic, an asymptotic property concerning approach to the best possible classification error, and reports promising empirical results. The contribution combines a more flexible representation of the retained dataset with theoretical support and an algorithmic route to constructing it.
summary.tldr: Weighted distances can substantially shrink nearest-neighbor representative sets while preserving similar generalization bounds.

title: Weighted distance nearest neighbor condensing

abstract: Class-imbalanced node classification tasks are prevalent in real-world scenarios. Due to the uneven distribution of nodes across different classes, learning high-quality node representations remains a challenging endeavor. The engineering of loss functions has shown promising potential in addressing this issue. It involves the meticulous design of loss functions, utilizing information about the quantities of nodes in different categories and the network’s topology to learn unbiased node representations. However, the design of these loss functions heavily relies on human expert knowledge and exhibits limited adaptability to specific target tasks. In this paper, we introduce a high-performance, flexible, and generalizable automated loss function search framework to tackle this challenge. Across 15 combinations of graph neural networks and datasets, our framework achieves a significant improvement in performance compared to state-of-the-art methods. Additionally, we observe that homophily in graph-structured data significantly contributes to the transferability of the proposed framework.

paragraphs: When a graph contains many nodes from some classes and few from others, learning useful node representations becomes difficult. The training loss matters because it determines which prediction errors receive attention. Carefully designed losses can use class counts and the graph's connections to address imbalance, but creating them requires expert judgment and may produce choices poorly suited to another task.

This paper proposes a framework that searches for loss functions automatically. It moves the task-specific design work into a search process, aiming to make loss selection more adaptable across graph neural networks and datasets. The contribution centers on choosing how a model learns from imbalanced graph data, where both category frequencies and relationships between nodes are relevant.

Across 15 combinations of graph neural networks and datasets, the authors report significant performance improvements over state-of-the-art methods. They also observe that homophily, the tendency of connected nodes to share similar characteristics, contributes substantially to transferability. This finding connects the usefulness of a searched loss across tasks to the structure of the graphs involved.
summary.tldr: Automated loss-function search improves class-imbalanced node classification, with graph homophily contributing to transferability.

title: Automated Loss function Search for Class-imbalanced Node Classification

abstract: Active learning is increasingly adopted for expensive multi-objective combinatorial optimization problems, but it involves a challenging subset selection problem, optimizing the batch acquisition score that quantifies the goodness of a batch for evaluation. Due to the excessively large search space of the subset selection problem, prior methods optimize the batch acquisition on the latent space, which has discrepancies with the actual space, or optimize individual acquisition scores without considering the dependencies among candidates in a batch instead of directly optimizing the batch acquisition. To manage the vast search space, a simple and effective approach is the greedy method, which decomposes the problem into smaller subproblems, yet it has difficulty in parallelization since each subproblem depends on the outcome from the previous ones. To this end, we introduce a novel greedy-style subset selection algorithm that optimizes batch acquisition directly on the combinatorial space by sequential greedy sampling from the greedy policy, specifically trained to address all greedy subproblems concurrently. Notably, our experiments on the red fluorescent proteins design task show that our proposed method achieves the baseline performance in 1.69x fewer queries, demonstrating its efficiency.

paragraphs: When evaluating candidates is expensive, active learning must choose useful batches for problems with several objectives. Selecting a batch is difficult because its value depends on relationships among candidates, and the number of possible subsets is enormous. Optimizing candidates individually can miss those relationships, while searching a latent space can introduce discrepancies with the actual combinatorial space.

The paper proposes learning a greedy policy that directly targets batch acquisition in the combinatorial space. Ordinary greedy selection breaks the problem into smaller steps, but those steps depend on earlier choices and are difficult to parallelize. Here, the policy is trained to address all greedy subproblems concurrently, then used for sequential greedy sampling when constructing a batch.

In a red fluorescent protein design task, the method reaches baseline performance using 1.69 times fewer queries. This provides evidence of improved evaluation efficiency in that application. The main contribution is a way to train for dependent batch-selection decisions together while retaining sequential construction and explicitly considering the acquisition value of the batch.
summary.tldr: A jointly trained greedy policy selects candidate batches directly in combinatorial space and reduces evaluation queries in a protein design task.

title: Training Greedy Policy for Proposal Batch Selection in Expensive Multi-Objective Combinatorial Optimization

abstract: Data subsampling is one of the most natural methods to approximate a massively large data set by a small representative proxy. In particular, sensitivity sampling received a lot of attention, which samples points proportional to an individual importance measure called sensitivity. This framework reduces in very general settings the size of data to roughly the VC dimension $d$ times the total sensitivity $\mathfrak S$ while providing strong $(1\pm\varepsilon)$ guarantees on the quality of approximation. The recent work of Woodruff & Yasuda (2023c) improved substantially over the general $\tilde O(\varepsilon^{-2}\mathfrak Sd)$ bound for the important problem of $\ell_p$ subspace embeddings to $\tilde O(\varepsilon^{-2}\mathfrak S^{2/p})$ for $p\in[1,2]$. Their result was subsumed by an earlier $\tilde O(\varepsilon^{-2}\mathfrak Sd^{1-p/2})$ bound which was implicitly given in the work of Chen & Derezinski (2021). We show that their result is tight when sampling according to plain $\ell_p$ sensitivities. We observe that by augmenting the $\ell_p$ sensitivities by $\ell_2$ sensitivities, we obtain better bounds improving over the aforementioned results to optimal linear $\tilde O(\varepsilon^{-2}(\mathfrak S+d)) = \tilde O(\varepsilon^{-2}d)$ sampling complexity for all $p \in [1,2]$. In particular, this resolves an open question of Woodruff & Yasuda (2023c) in the affirmative for $p \in [1,2]$ and brings sensitivity subsampling into the regime that was previously only known to be possible using Lewis weights (Cohen & Peng, 2015). As an application of our main result, we also obtain an $\tilde O(\varepsilon^{-2}\mu d)$ sensitivity sampling bound for logistic regression, where $\mu$ is a natural complexity measure for this problem. This improves over the previous $\tilde O(\varepsilon^{-2}\mu^2 d)$ bound of Mai et al. (2021) which was based on Lewis weights subsampling.

paragraphs: Sensitivity sampling compresses a dataset by selecting points according to their individual importance. The goal is a small representative sample that approximately preserves the quantities needed for subsequent computation. This paper studies the sample size required for ℓp subspace embeddings when p lies between one and two.

The authors show that a previous bound is tight when sampling uses plain ℓp sensitivities. They then improve the sampling rule by adding ℓ2 sensitivity information. This augmented rule achieves sample complexity proportional to the dimension divided by the squared approximation tolerance, up to logarithmic factors. The result reaches an optimal linear dependence on dimension in the stated range of p.

This brings sensitivity sampling into a regime previously achieved using Lewis weights and resolves the stated open question for p between one and two. An application to logistic regression also improves the dependence on its complexity parameter μ from quadratic to linear. The gains come from modifying the importance measure used for sampling.
summary.tldr: Adding ℓ2 sensitivities to ℓp sensitivity sampling achieves optimal dimension-linear sample complexity for p between one and two.

title: Optimal bounds for $\ell_p$ sensitivity sampling via $\ell_2$ augmentation

abstract: Permutation equivariant neural networks are typically used to learn from data that lives on a graph. However, for any graph $G$ that has $n$ vertices, using the symmetric group $S_n$ as its group of symmetries does not take into account the relations that exist between the vertices. Given that the actual group of symmetries is the automorphism group Aut$(G)$, we show how to construct neural networks that are equivariant to Aut$(G)$ by obtaining a full characterisation of the learnable, linear, Aut$(G)$-equivariant functions between layers that are some tensor power of $\mathbb{R}^{n}$. In particular, we find a spanning set of matrices for these layer functions in the standard basis of $\mathbb{R}^{n}$. This result has important consequences for learning from data whose group of symmetries is a finite group because a theorem by Frucht (1938) showed that any finite group is isomorphic to the automorphism group of a graph.

paragraphs: Graph-based data has structure in the relationships between vertices. This paper argues that treating every permutation of vertices as a symmetry overlooks those relationships. For a particular graph, the relevant symmetries are its automorphisms: vertex rearrangements that preserve the graph’s structure. The goal is to build neural networks that respect precisely this group.

The authors fully characterize the learnable linear functions that are equivariant to a graph’s automorphism group between layers formed from tensor powers of the vertex-coordinate space. Equivariance requires transforming the input and then applying the layer to agree with applying the layer and transforming its output. They provide a spanning set of matrices that describes these allowable linear layer functions.

This characterization supplies concrete building blocks for networks whose symmetry matches a given graph. Its theoretical reach extends to data with any finite symmetry group: an established theorem states that every finite group is isomorphic to some graph’s automorphism group. The paper therefore connects graph-specific layer construction with a broader framework for finite-group-equivariant learning.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes linear neural-network layers that respect a graph’s actual automorphisms, with implications for learning under any finite symmetry group.

title: Graph Automorphism Group Equivariant Neural Networks

abstract: Concept-based interpretability methods offer a lens into the internals of foundation models by decomposing their embeddings into high-level concepts. These concept representations are most useful when they are compositional, meaning that the individual concepts compose to explain the full sample. We show that existing unsupervised concept extraction methods find concepts which are not compositional. To automatically discover compositional concept representations, we identify two salient properties of such representations, and propose Compositional Concept Extraction (CCE) for finding concepts which obey these properties. We evaluate CCE on five different datasets over image and text data. Our evaluation shows that CCE finds more compositional concept representations than baselines and yields better accuracy on four downstream classification tasks.

paragraphs: Concept-based interpretability aims to explain a foundation model’s internal representations using high-level concepts. For those concepts to explain a complete example, they need to work together compositionally. This paper shows that existing unsupervised extraction methods produce concepts that lack that property, creating a gap between identifying concepts and explaining how they jointly account for a sample.

The authors identify two salient properties of compositional representations and introduce Compositional Concept Extraction, or CCE, to find concepts obeying them. The approach makes compositionality an explicit target of concept discovery. Its purpose is to produce a collection whose members combine meaningfully, so the explanation depends on how the concepts relate to the whole example.

Evaluation across five image and text datasets finds that CCE produces more compositional representations than the compared baselines. It also improves accuracy on four downstream classification tasks. These findings connect the explanatory goal to predictive usefulness: the extracted concepts better support joint descriptions of samples and provide representations that improve classification in the evaluated tasks.
summary.tldr: CCE extracts concepts that combine more compositionally and improve downstream classification in the reported evaluations.

title: Towards Compositionality in Concept Learning

abstract: Lithography, transferring chip design masks to the silicon wafer, is the most important phase in modern semiconductor manufacturing flow. Due to the limitations of lithography systems, Extensive design optimizations are required to tackle the design and silicon mismatch. Inverse lithography technology (ILT) is one of the promising solutions to perform pre-fabrication optimization, termed mask optimization. Because of mask optimization problems’ constrained non-convexity, numerical ILT solvers rely heavily on good initialization to avoid getting stuck on sub-optimal solutions. Machine learning (ML) techniques are hence proposed to generate mask initialization for ILT solvers with one-shot inference, targeting faster and better convergence during ILT. This paper addresses the question of whether ML models can directly generate high-quality optimized masks without engaging ILT solvers in the loop. We propose an implicit learning ILT framework: ILILT, which leverages the implicit layer learning method and lithography-conditioned inputs to ground the model. Trained to understand the ILT optimization procedure, ILILT can outperform the state-of-the-art machine learning solutions, significantly improving efficiency and quality.

paragraphs: Lithography transfers a chip's mask design onto silicon, but limitations in the manufacturing system create differences between the intended design and the resulting pattern. Inverse lithography technology addresses this through mask optimization before fabrication. Its constrained, non-convex optimization problem makes numerical solvers sensitive to their starting point and vulnerable to suboptimal solutions.

Earlier machine learning approaches generate initial masks for those solvers. ILILT asks whether a learned model can instead produce high-quality optimized masks directly, without an ILT solver in the generation loop. The framework uses implicit layer learning and inputs conditioned on lithography, grounding the learned mapping in the mask optimization problem.

The model is trained to capture the ILT optimization procedure, moving the role of learning beyond initialization. The authors report that ILILT can outperform state-of-the-art machine learning solutions, with significant improvements in efficiency and quality. The stated findings support direct learned mask optimization as a promising way to reduce reliance on subsequent numerical refinement while improving the generated masks.
summary.tldr: ILILT learns to generate optimized lithography masks directly, reporting better efficiency and quality than state-of-the-art machine learning approaches.

title: ILILT: Implicit Learning of Inverse Lithography Technologies

abstract: Knowledge Graph Foundation Models (KGFMs) are at the frontier for deep learning on knowledge graphs (KGs), as they can generalize to completely novel knowledge graphs with different relational vocabularies. Despite their empirical success, our theoretical understanding of KGFMs remains very limited. In this paper, we conduct a rigorous study of the expressive power of KGFMs. Specifically, we show that the expressive power of KGFMs directly depends on the motifs that are used to learn the relation representations. We then observe that the most typical motifs used in the existing literature are binary, as the representations are learned based on how pairs of relations interact, which limits the model’s expressiveness. As part of our study, we design more expressive KGFMs using richer motifs, which necessitate learning relation representations based on, e.g., how triples of relations interact with each other. Finally, we empirically validate our theoretical findings, showing that the use of richer motifs results in better performance on a wide range of datasets drawn from different domains.

paragraphs: Knowledge graph foundation models can transfer to entirely new graphs whose relation vocabularies differ from those encountered previously. Despite that empirical success, the paper identifies a gap in understanding what these models can represent. It investigates expressive power, focusing on how a model builds representations of the relationships within a graph.

The theoretical analysis shows that expressive power directly depends on the motifs used to learn relation representations. Existing approaches commonly use binary motifs, capturing interactions between pairs of relations. The authors show that this choice restricts expressiveness and design models using richer motifs, including interactions among triples of relations, to represent more complex relational structure.

Experiments across datasets from different domains support the theoretical findings: richer motifs produce better performance. The contribution therefore connects an architectural choice to both representational capability and observed results. It gives a concrete reason to examine which relation interactions a model can encode when developing transferable graph models, rather than treating relation representations as an interchangeable component of the architecture.
summary.tldr: The paper shows that richer relation motifs increase knowledge graph foundation models’ expressive power and improve performance across diverse datasets.

title: How Expressive are Knowledge Graph Foundation Models?

abstract: Language recognition tasks are fundamental in natural language processing (NLP) and have been widely used to benchmark the performance of large language models (LLMs). These tasks also play a crucial role in explaining the working mechanisms of transformers. In this work, we focus on two representative tasks in the category of regular language recognition, known as ’even pairs’ and ’parity check’, the aim of which is to determine whether the occurrences of certain subsequences in a given sequence are even. Our goal is to explore how a one-layer transformer, consisting of an attention layer followed by a linear layer, learns to solve these tasks by theoretically analyzing its training dynamics under gradient descent. While even pairs can be solved directly by a one-layer transformer, parity check need to be solved by integrating Chain-of-Thought (CoT), either into the inference stage of a transformer well-trained for the even pairs task, or into the training of a one-layer transformer. For both problems, our analysis shows that the joint training of attention and linear layers exhibits two distinct phases. In the first phase, the attention layer grows rapidly, mapping data sequences into separable vectors. In the second phase, the attention layer becomes stable, while the linear layer grows logarithmically and approaches in direction to a max-margin hyperplane that correctly separates the attention layer outputs into positive and negative samples, and the loss decreases at a rate of $O(1/t)$. Our experiments validate those theoretical results.

title: How Transformers Learn Regular Language Recognition: A Theoretical Study on Training Dynamics and Implicit Bias

abstract: Bayesian optimization has attracted huge attention from diverse research areas in science and engineering, since it is capable of efficiently finding a global optimum of an expensive-to-evaluate black-box function. In general, a probabilistic regression model is widely used as a surrogate function to model an explicit distribution over function evaluations given an input to estimate and a training dataset. Beyond the probabilistic regression-based methods, density ratio estimation-based Bayesian optimization has been suggested in order to estimate a density ratio of the groups relatively close and relatively far to a global optimum. Developing this line of research further, supervised classifiers are employed to estimate a class probability for the two groups instead of a density ratio. However, the supervised classifiers used in this strategy are prone to be overconfident for known knowledge on global solution candidates. Supposing that we have access to unlabeled points, e.g., predefined fixed-size pools, we propose density ratio estimation-based Bayesian optimization with semi-supervised learning to solve this challenge. Finally, we show the empirical results of our methods and several baseline methods in two distinct scenarios with unlabeled point sampling and a fixed-size pool, and analyze the validity of our methods in diverse experiments.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimization guides the search for good inputs when evaluating a function is expensive. A common approach predicts function values probabilistically. This paper builds on an alternative that separates observations into relatively promising and less promising groups, then uses density ratios or classification probabilities to guide the search.

The authors identify overconfidence in supervised classifiers as a problem for this approach. A classifier can be too certain about what the available evaluations reveal about global solution candidates. Their proposed method introduces semi-supervised learning, allowing the model to use candidate inputs whose function values have not been evaluated as well as the labeled observations.

Access to these unlabeled points is an explicit assumption, with a predefined pool offered as one example. The experiments examine both sampled unlabeled points and a fixed-size pool, comparing the proposed methods with several baselines. The stated contribution is a way to incorporate unevaluated inputs into classifier-based optimization and an empirical investigation of its validity across varied experiments; the abstract does not claim a quantified or universal improvement.
summary.tldr: Semi-supervised learning incorporates unevaluated candidate inputs into density-ratio-based Bayesian optimization to address classifier overconfidence.

title: Density Ratio Estimation-based Bayesian Optimization with Semi-Supervised Learning

abstract: Time-series forecasting plays a critical role in many real-world applications. Although increasingly powerful models have been developed and achieved superior results on benchmark datasets, through a fine-grained sample-level inspection, we find that (i) no single model consistently outperforms others across different test samples, but instead (ii) each model excels in specific cases. These findings prompt us to explore how to adaptively leverage the distinct strengths of various forecasting models for different samples. We introduce TimeFuse, a framework for collective time-series forecasting with sample-level adaptive fusion of heterogeneous models. TimeFuse utilizes meta-features to characterize input time series and trains a learnable fusor to predict optimal model fusion weights for any given input. The fusor can leverage samples from diverse datasets for joint training, allowing it to adapt to a wide variety of temporal patterns and thus generalize to new inputs, even from unseen datasets. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of TimeFuse in various long-/short-term forecasting tasks, achieving near-universal improvement over the state-of-the-art individual models. Code is available at https://github.com/ZhiningLiu1998/TimeFuse.

paragraphs: A forecasting model that performs well overall may still be a poor choice for particular inputs. Through inspection of individual test samples, this paper finds that different models excel in different cases, with no single model consistently winning. TimeFuse uses this observation to make model combination depend on the time series being forecast.

The framework describes each input through meta-features and feeds them to a learned fusion component. That component predicts how much weight to give each forecasting model for the current sample. Because the underlying models can differ, the framework can combine distinct forecasting strengths. Its fusion component can also train jointly on samples from several datasets, exposing it to a wider variety of temporal patterns.

Experiments cover both short-term and long-term forecasting and report improvements over state-of-the-art individual models in nearly all evaluated cases. The authors also describe generalization to inputs from previously unseen datasets. These findings support adapting the combination to each input, while the near-universal improvement claim remains an empirical result rather than a guarantee.
summary.tldr: TimeFuse learns input-specific weights for combining forecasting models, producing improvements over individual models in nearly all reported evaluations.

title: Breaking Silos: Adaptive Model Fusion Unlocks Better Time Series Forecasting

abstract: Probabilistic survival analysis models seek to estimate the distribution of the future occurrence (time) of an event given a set of covariates. In recent years, these models have preferred nonparametric specifications that avoid directly estimating survival distributions via discretization. Specifically, they estimate the probability of an individual event at fixed times or the time of an event at fixed probabilities (quantiles), using supervised learning. Borrowing ideas from the quantile regression literature, we propose a parametric survival analysis method based on the Asymmetric Laplace Distribution (ALD). This distribution allows for closed-form calculation of popular event summaries such as mean, median, mode, variation, and quantiles. The model is optimized by maximum likelihood to learn, at the individual level, the parameters (location, scale, and asymmetry) of the ALD distribution. Extensive results on synthetic and real-world data demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms parametric and nonparametric approaches in terms of accuracy, discrimination and calibration.

paragraphs: Survival analysis estimates when an event may occur given information about an individual. Many recent approaches learn event probabilities at selected times or event times at selected probability levels. This paper instead learns the parameters of a complete probability distribution for each individual, using the Asymmetric Laplace Distribution.

The model learns three parameters: location, scale, and asymmetry. Together, these determine the distribution's position, spread, and unevenness around its center. Training uses maximum likelihood, and the approach draws on ideas from quantile regression. Once the parameters are learned, quantities such as the mean, median, mode, variation, and quantiles can be calculated in closed form.

This provides a common distributional basis for multiple event-time summaries, rather than learning only selected points of interest. Experiments on synthetic and real-world data report better accuracy, discrimination, and calibration than the evaluated parametric and nonparametric alternatives. The findings support this particular parametric choice as an effective way to learn individualized survival distributions in the studied settings.
summary.tldr: The method learns individualized Asymmetric Laplace survival distributions, yielding closed-form event-time summaries and strong reported predictive performance.

title: Learning Survival Distributions with the Asymmetric Laplace Distribution

abstract: Message-passing graph neural networks (MPNNs) and structural features (SFs) are cornerstones for the link prediction task. However, as a common and intuitive mode of understanding, the potential of visual perception has been overlooked in the MPNN community. For the first time, we equip MPNNs with vision structural awareness by proposing an effective framework called Graph Vision Network (GVN), along with a more efficient variant (E-GVN). Extensive empirical results demonstrate that with the proposed frameworks, GVN consistently benefits from the vision enhancement across seven link prediction datasets, including challenging large-scale graphs. Such improvements are compatible with existing state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods and GVNs achieve new SOTA results, thereby underscoring a promising novel direction for link prediction.

paragraphs: Link prediction asks which connections should exist in a graph. Message-passing neural networks and structural features are established tools for this task, but this paper explores an additional source of information: visual awareness of graph structure. The proposal is to equip graph models with a form of perception that has received little attention in this setting.

The authors introduce Graph Vision Network, or GVN, along with a more efficient variant called E-GVN. Their framework adds vision-based structural awareness to message-passing models. This positions visual information as a complement to existing graph-learning machinery and motivates testing whether it can improve methods that already perform well.

Across seven link-prediction datasets, including challenging large-scale graphs, the reported experiments consistently show benefits from vision enhancement. The improvements are compatible with existing state-of-the-art methods, and the resulting networks achieve new state-of-the-art results. These findings establish visual structural awareness as a promising direction for link prediction, with evidence spanning several datasets and extending to large graphs rather than only small examples.
summary.tldr: Graph Vision Networks add visual structural awareness to message passing and improve link prediction across seven evaluated datasets.

title: Open Your Eyes: Vision Enhances Message Passing Neural Networks in Link Prediction

abstract: In this paper, we present DiffusionVLA, a novel framework that integrates autoregressive reasoning with diffusion policies to address the limitations of existing methods: while autoregressive Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models lack precise and robust action generation, diffusion-based policies inherently lack reasoning capabilities. Central to our approach is autoregressive reasoning — a task decomposition and explanation process enabled by a pre-trained VLM — to guide diffusion-based action policies. To tightly couple reasoning with action generation, we introduce a reasoning injection module that directly embeds self-generated reasoning phrases into the policy learning process. The framework is simple, flexible, and efficient, enabling seamless deployment across diverse robotic platforms. We conduct extensive experiments using multiple real robots to validate the effectiveness of DiVLA. Our tests include a challenging factory sorting task, where DiVLA successfully categorizes objects, including those not seen during training. The reasoning injection module enhances interpretability, enabling explicit failure diagnosis by visualizing the model’s decision process. Additionally, we test DiVLA on a zero-shot bin-picking task, achieving 63.7% accuracy on 102 previously unseen objects. Our method demonstrates robustness to visual changes, such as distractors and new backgrounds, and easily adapts to new embodiments. Furthermore, DiVLA can follow novel instructions and retain conversational ability. Notably, DiVLA is data-efficient and fast at inference; our smallest DiVLA-2B runs 82Hz on a single A6000 GPU. Finally, we scale the model from 2B to 72B parameters, showcasing improved generalization capabilities with increased model size.

summary.tldr: DiffusionVLA injects language-model reasoning into diffusion policies, enabling fast robot control and improved generalization in real-robot experiments.

title: DiffusionVLA: Scaling Robot Foundation Models via Unified Diffusion and Autoregression

abstract: We investigate the transformer’s capability for in-context learning (ICL) to simulate the training process of deep models. Our key contribution is providing a positive example of using a transformer to train a deep neural network by gradient descent in an implicit fashion via ICL. Specifically, we provide an explicit construction of a $(2N+4)L$-layer transformer capable of simulating $L$ gradient descent steps of an $N$-layer ReLU network through ICL. We also give the theoretical guarantees for the approximation within any given error and the convergence of the ICL gradient descent. Additionally, we extend our analysis to the more practical setting using Softmax-based transformers. We validate our findings on synthetic datasets for 3-layer, 4-layer, and 6-layer neural networks. The results show that ICL performance matches that of direct training.

paragraphs: This paper investigates whether a Transformer can carry out the training process of a deep neural network through in-context learning. Its contribution is a constructive positive example: the authors explicitly specify a Transformer that implicitly simulates gradient descent on another network using the information provided in context.

The construction uses a Transformer with (2N+4)L layers to simulate L gradient descent steps for an N-layer ReLU network. This formula connects the depth of the constructed Transformer to both the depth of the network being trained and the number of simulated updates. The authors provide guarantees for approximation within any specified error and for convergence of the in-context gradient descent procedure.

The analysis also extends to Transformers using Softmax, bringing the construction closer to that practical architecture. Experiments on synthetic datasets examine three-, four-, and six-layer neural networks, with in-context performance matching direct training. The findings establish that this form of deep learning through context is possible in the constructed setting; they do not assert that every trained Transformer automatically implements the same procedure.
summary.tldr: An explicit Transformer construction can simulate gradient descent on deep ReLU networks through in-context learning, with approximation and convergence guarantees.

title: In-Context Deep Learning via Transformer Models

abstract: N:M sparsity stands as a progressively important tool for DNN compression, achieving practical speedups by stipulating at most N non-zero components within M sequential weights. Unfortunately, most existing works identify the N:M sparse mask through dense backward propagation to update all weights, which incurs exorbitant training costs. In this paper, we introduce BAME, a method that maintains consistent sparsity throughout the N:M sparse training process. BAME perpetually keeps both sparse forward and backward propagation, while iteratively performing weight pruning-and-regrowing within designated weight blocks to tailor the N:M mask. These blocks are selected through a joint assessment based on accumulated mask oscillation frequency and expected loss reduction of mask adaptation, thereby ensuring stable and efficient identification of the optimal N:M mask. Our empirical results substantiate the effectiveness of BAME, illustrating it performs comparably to or better than previous works that fully maintaining dense backward propagation during training. For instance, BAME attains a 72.0% top-1 accuracy while training a 1:16 sparse ResNet-50 on ImageNet, eclipsing SR-STE by 0.5%, despite achieving 2.37 training FLOPs reduction. Code is released at https://github.com/BAME-xmu/BAME

paragraphs: N:M sparsity constrains each group of M consecutive weights to contain at most N nonzero values. This structured compression can produce practical speedups, but finding a useful sparse pattern can itself be expensive. Many existing methods still update every weight during backward propagation, keeping a substantial part of training dense even when the forward computation is sparse.

BAME maintains sparsity in both forward and backward propagation throughout training. It adapts the mask, which specifies which weights remain active, by pruning and regrowing weights within selected blocks. Block selection combines two signals: how often the mask has changed and how much loss reduction a mask adjustment is expected to provide. This directs adaptation toward selected portions of the model.

The experiments report performance comparable to or better than methods that retain dense backward propagation. One example reaches 72.0% top-1 accuracy for a 1:16 sparse ResNet-50 on ImageNet, exceeding SR-STE while reducing training computation. The finding matters because it demonstrates that updating the sparse pattern need not require dense gradient computation throughout training.
summary.tldr: BAME adapts structured sparse masks while keeping both forward and backward training computations sparse.

title: BAME: Block-Aware Mask Evolution for Efficient N:M Sparse Training

abstract: Current causal discovery methods for time series data can effectively address a variety of scenarios; however, they remain constrained by inefficiencies. The significant inefficiencies arise primarily from the high computational costs associated with binning, the uncertainty in selecting appropriate time lags, and the extensive sets of candidate variables. To achieve both high efficiency and effectiveness of causal discovery, we introduce an accelerator termed ARROW. It incorporates an innovative concept termed “Time Weaving” that efficiently encodes time series data to well capture the dynamic trends, thereby mitigating computational complexity. We also propose a novel time lag discovery strategy utilizing XOR operations, which derives a theorem to obtain the optimal time lag and significantly enhances the efficiency using XOR operations. To optimize the search space for causal relationships, we design an efficient pruning strategy that intelligently identifies the most relevant candidate variables, enhancing the efficiency and accuracy of causal discovery. We applied ARROW to four different types of time series causal discovery algorithms and evaluated it on 25 synthetic and real-world datasets. The results demonstrate that, compared to the original algorithms, ARROW achieves up to 153x speedup while achieving higher accuracy in most cases.

paragraphs: ARROW addresses the computational expense of discovering causal relationships in time series. The paper identifies three sources of inefficiency: organizing observations into bins, choosing appropriate time lags, and searching through large sets of possible explanatory variables. Its contribution is an accelerator that can be applied to existing discovery algorithms.

The method combines three components. Time Weaving encodes time series to capture their changing trends while reducing computational complexity. A lag discovery strategy uses XOR operations, together with a theorem for obtaining the optimal lag. A pruning strategy then narrows the candidate variables to those judged most relevant, reducing the search required to identify causal relationships.

The authors apply ARROW to four types of causal discovery algorithms and evaluate it on 25 synthetic and real-world datasets. They report speedups reaching 153 times those of the original algorithms, with higher accuracy in most cases. These results support the usefulness of improving data encoding, lag selection, and candidate search together; the maximum speedup is a reported outcome, rather than a uniform gain across every case.
summary.tldr: ARROW accelerates time series causal discovery through efficient encoding, lag selection, and candidate pruning, reaching 153-fold speedups in the reported evaluations.

title: Arrow: Accelerator for Time Series Causal Discovery with Time Weaving

abstract: For researchers and practitioners in finance, finding synergistic formulaic alphas is very important but challenging. In this paper, we reconsider the discovery of synergistic formulaic alphas from the viewpoint of sequential decision-making, and conceptualize the entire alpha discovery process as a non-stationary and reward-sparse Markov decision process. To overcome the challenges of non-stationarity and reward-sparsity, we propose the AlphaQCM method, a novel distributional reinforcement learning method designed to search for synergistic formulaic alphas efficiently. The AlphaQCM method first learns the Q function and quantiles via a Q network and a quantile network, respectively. Then, the AlphaQCM method applies the quantiled conditional moment method to learn unbiased variance from the potentially biased quantiles. Guided by the learned Q function and variance, the AlphaQCM method navigates the non-stationarity and reward-sparsity to explore the vast search space of formulaic alphas with high efficacy. Empirical applications to real-world datasets demonstrate that our AlphaQCM method significantly outperforms its competitors, particularly when dealing with large datasets comprising numerous stocks.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to discover formula-based financial signals that work well together. It treats this search as a sequence of decisions, modeled as a Markov decision process with changing conditions and sparse rewards. This framing makes both challenges explicit: feedback is infrequent, and the search cannot assume that its reward environment remains fixed.

AlphaQCM addresses these challenges through distributional reinforcement learning. One network learns the Q function, which evaluates decisions, while another learns quantiles describing the reward distribution. A quantiled conditional moment method then uses those potentially biased quantile estimates to learn unbiased variance. The resulting search is guided by both learned value and variance, rather than relying on the Q function alone.

Applications to real-world datasets show that AlphaQCM significantly outperforms its competitors, especially on large datasets containing many stocks. The stated finding concerns the effectiveness of discovering complementary formulaic alphas. Its methodological contribution is to connect sequential search with distributional information that helps navigate sparse feedback and non-stationarity.
summary.tldr: AlphaQCM uses learned values and reward variance to search efficiently for complementary financial signals under changing conditions and sparse feedback.

title: AlphaQCM: Alpha Discovery in Finance with Distributional Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) contain large amounts of facts about the world. These facts can become outdated over time, which has led to the development of knowledge editing methods (KEs) that can change specific facts in LLMs with limited side effects. This position paper argues that editing LLMs poses serious safety risks that have been largely overlooked. First, we note the fact that KEs are widely available, computationally inexpensive, highly performant, and stealthy makes them an attractive tool for malicious actors. Second, we discuss malicious use cases of KEs, showing how KEs can be easily adapted for a variety of malicious purposes. Third, we highlight vulnerabilities in the AI ecosystem that allow unrestricted uploading and downloading of updated models without verification. Fourth, we argue that a lack of social and institutional awareness exacerbates this risk, and discuss the implications for different stakeholders. We call on the community to (i) research tamper-resistant models and countermeasures against malicious model editing, and (ii) actively engage in securing the AI ecosystem.
